Paratex Light – Fabric

 

Introduction

Lightweight, highly windproof, water repellent fabrics, exceptionally breathable and able to wick moisture away from the source, ideal for sleeping bag linings and mid-layer insulated clothing.

Windproof Rating

Windproof to the industry standard of 3 cubic feet per minute.

Water Repellency

DWR – Durable Water Repellent, a British Standard Spray Rating of 4 Minimum

Breathability

Breathability rating of 12l/m²/24h

Wicking

Exceptionally breathable and able to wick moisture away from the source.

 

Black to top

Paratex Dry – Fabric

 

Paratex Dry is a 100% waterproof fabric (hydrophilic polyurethane coating) with a hydrostatic head in excess of 5000mm (items with a hydro static head in excess of 1500mm are generally considered waterproof)

Detailed information

What it is:  
100% waterproof fabric (Hydrophilic Polyurethane Coating)

How it works: 
Closely constructed fabric with a ripstop construction. Teamed with a Hydrophilic Polyurethane (PU) which transfers water vapour chemically    from the inside to the outside (due to the temperature differential between the inside of the product and out)

Features:

  • 100% Waterproof with a Hydrostatic Head in Excess of 5000mm (Items with a Hydrostatic Head over 1500mm are generally considered waterproof)
  • Only ever used in fully taped seamed systems.
  • Ripstop Weave
  • Lightweight
  • Tough
  • Breathable (will transmit up to  7.5 litres of moisture per m2 per 24 hours)
  • Soft to the touch
  • Completely Windproof (trapping and stopping the movement of warm air in the sleeping bag or Garment)
  • Outer Fabric treated with a Durable Water Repellant. (water repellency can be maintained by a cool tumble dry after washing and periodic retreatment with suitable aftercare products such as Nikwax or Grangers)

Where it is used:
As a breathable Bivvi Bag (Waterproof sleeping bag outer) or a shell fabric in waterproof jackets. It is important to note that as this solid coating air can not pass so care should be taken not to completely seal any bivvi bag system to prevent suffocation.

 

 

Back to Top

 

Paratex Micro

 

Tough, lightweight, highly windproof and water repellent. A heavy-duty, closely constructed fabric, Paratex micro is exceptionally hard-wearing but still remains soft to the touch, ideal for outer casings of sleeping bags and jackets where durability is a prerequisite.

Features

  • Highly Windproof
  • Water Repellent and breathable

Back to Top

Paratex Steelplate

Paratex Steelplate, as the name, suggests this fabric is used on the cream of Snugpak’s products giving a great balance between aesthetics and performance.

Features
• Lightweight
• Tough Fabric
• Highly Breathable (will transmit 12 litres of moisture per m2 per 24 hours)
• Great Wicking Properties
• Soft to the touch
• Windproof to the industry standard of 3 cubic feet per minute (this keeps strong winds out or when used as a lining warm air and loft in)
• DWR – Durable Water Repellent, a British Standard Spray Rating of 4 Minimum (water repellency can be maintained by a cool tumble dry after washing and periodic re-treatment with suitable aftercare products such as Nikwax or Grangers)

Back To top

Supersoft – Fabric

 

This inner lining is ‘Supersoft’. A silky smooth fabric which is specially woven to produce a highly durable and comfortable wicking breathable lining.

Back to top

Reflectatherm – Insulation

 

Reflectatherm, this metallised fabric is designed to reflect heat and retain warmth. A highly breathable material, which adds little to the weight or pack size of the product and provides at least 15% additional warmth whilst being undetectable by touch in the sleeping bag or garment.

Features

  • Specially coated with metallic dots which help to trap heat
  • Excellent weight-to-warmth ratio
  • The coating does not affect breathability

Back to top

Paratex Antibacterial – Fabric

The latest breakthrough in antibacterial technology this specialist antibacterial and antimicrobial treatment on the outer and linings of our sleeping bags acts to discourage the growth of bacteria. This results in a reduction of odours and the need for regular laundering of the sleeping bag to keep it smelling fresh, ideal for prolonged tropical travel where temperatures may be high and facilities limited. The Paratex® base fabrics wicking properties and high breathability remain unaffected by the bacteria busting treatments.

 

Back to top

 

TS1 Thermal Suede– Fabric

 

Thermal suede is a lightweight polyester fabric with a suede finish, which uses a combination of yarns with different thicknesses. Microfibre yarns (less than 1 decitex) go on the outside and Macrofibre (3 decitex) go on the inside. The Macrofibre yarns are raised to produce a short pile, similar in feel to suede. The construction exploits a basic physical property – that water will always move from a low to high surface area or from the macro to microfilament yarns, thus moving water from the body outwards.

Features

  • Quickly perspires and wicks away unwanted moisture
  • Highly breathable
  • Fibres create a warm insulating layer

Back to top

Micro Diamond – Fabric

 

‘Micro Diamond Ripstop’ provides a lightweight, water repellent casing, produced to Snugpak’s exact specification. The mini diamond weave and the lustre of the yarn give a unique look.

Back to top

CoolMax

Coolmax works by mopping up any perspiration created by the active body. Ideal for hiking, sports, working outdoors and pretty much any other activity where you need to stay cool or warm and dry. The superfine internal hairs search for excess moisture to absorb then wick over a larger surface area keeping the body warm when cold and cooling the body off when it starts to over-heat. Coolmax doesn’t only adjust the body’s temperature to the climate but also keeps the body more hygienic

Back to top

Silvadur – fabric

SILVADUR™ Technology binds silver molecules (silver ions) microscopically to the travel towel surface. This specialist antibacterial and antimicrobial treatment discourages the growth of bacteria, reducing any odours and the need for regular laundering.

Back to top

Softie Premier – Insulation

 

As part of our continuing development process to keep our synthetic insulation at the leading edge we are pleased to introduce the next generation in sleeping bag technology. Softie® Premier uses the same basic principles as traditional Softie® but improvements in extrusion technology and binding resins result in a finer, softer and more durable insulation. Both Softie® and Softie® Premier are exclusive to Snugpak.

Features

  • Retains heat even when wet
  • Washable
  • High Loft
  • Super-fine filaments
  • Natural soft touch

Back to top

Softie – Insulation

Softie® – The brand name for the synthetic (Polyester) filling we use for the Softie® ranges of sleeping bags. It utilises superfine yarns bound with special resins to produce a luxurious down-like feel. It is created from staple yarns which mirror the compositions of natural insulation (As opposed to continuously extruded as in most synthetic fills) a variety of yarn processes are applied to give a more random effect, that is some are curled, some crimped and some are just left as they are. The random nature of the process results in a product that closely resembles the structure of natural insulators and the way they perform. Given all this technology Softie® is still easy to care for, washable and retains a lot of its thermal properties when wet.

Features

  • Retains heat even when wet
  • Super-fine filaments
  • Natural soft touch

Back to top

Travelsoft – Insulation

 

 

Travelsoft insulation is tailored to Snugpak’s exact brief. Ultra-lightweight high loft fine fibres are used which have excellent compressibility.

By design, these travel orientated fibres provide less bulk of fill, yet are still able to perform very efficiently. The weight of the fibres makes it the perfect fill for adventure travel-orientated equipment.

Features:

  • Retains heat when wet
  • Washable
  • High Loft, Superfine Filaments

Back to top

IsoFibre – Insulation

 

Filled with ‘Isofibre’ siliconised hollowfibre. The synthetic fibres are structured to trap warm air between tiny cavities in the fibre. When unpacked the ‘Hollowfibres’ Decompress and spring back to gain maximum re-loft.

Features

  • Retains heat when wet
  • Easy to wash and care for.

Back to top

Merino Wool – Insulation

Merino Wool is a Natural Fibre, which is naturally soft against sensitive skin areas. Merino Wool is a warm fibre, but also allows heat and moisture to escape; Merino Wool naturally absorbs moisture to keep you dry.

Synthetic fibres can be ideal for technical insulation, but for sensitive skin areas, the natural fibres from Merino Sheep, Merino Wool, is a soft wool product that is much lighter than other sheep’s wool, making it the ideal choice for next to skin items. Merino Wool can retain heat in colder climates, as well as allow convection, conduction and evaporative heat loss in warm weathers; your feet can sweat up to 250mls (each) per day under normal conditions, and a lot more in warm weather or during increased aerobic activity.

Back to top

Pile – Fabric

Luxuriously thick fleece-effect pile lining. Designed to be worn next to the skin to draw perspiration from the source.

title: Cooking With Confidence: How Cast Iron Cookware Became an Industry Standard
author: Laurence
excerpt: Durable, versatile, and very much in vogue. Cast iron cookware can sometimes appear a little bit intimidating to some - its weight alone can scare off some suitors - but there’s a clear reason why kitchens worldwide pref
html:
Durable, versatile, and very much in vogue. Cast iron cookware can sometimes appear a little bit intimidating to some - its weight alone can scare off some suitors - but there’s a clear reason why kitchens worldwide prefer to cook with cast iron as opposed to steel.

The creation of cast iron cooking products is wholly unique and leaves users with a rich and strong product that can perform its duties again and again over extremely long periods of time.

Speaking to NBC, renowned US chef Michael Gulotta confirmed that “cast iron products last a lifetime. They’re naturally non-stick when properly maintained, and hold their heat evenly no matter what surface you’re cooking on."

Notably, the versatility of cast iron products is still largely unrecognised. When it comes to cooking, cast iron is often solely associated with the searing of steaks. While the thermal density of cast iron is capable of keeping it hotter all over for longer - making it perfect for steaks - its potential extends way beyond the world of red meats:

Entering The World of Cast Iron Cookware

The significance of cast iron cooking products is that they’re all cast from molten steel and iron, and our PetroMax cast iron cookware is no different. While non-cast iron cookware is made from lighter materials like aluminium and stainless steel, cast iron products are capable of withstanding incredible levels of heat and are virtually indestructible.

Dutch Ovens have become synonymous with cast iron cooking over time. Consisting of a deep pot made from cast iron, Dutch Ovens are excellent for cooking food while on-the-go or camping. PetroMax cast iron Dutch Ovens have been lovingly crafted with a pre-seasoned finish for immediate use - so if you’re looking to go camping, you can simply pack your oven up and take it with you.

Cast iron cooking isn’t just limited Dutch Ovens, and plenty of products, from pans to skillets and bakeware, can be crafted from the material for great results.

Weighing Up The Advantages of Cast Iron Cookware

We’ve already looked at the excellent durability of cast iron Dutch Ovens and cookware, but cast products carry a wide range of benefits that have ultimately led them to become the favoured choice of cookware around the world.

Firstly, if well seasoned, cast iron cookware can be easier to clean than their steel counterparts. Their greater thermal density also ensures that the metal becomes comprehensively hotter for longer.

Significantly, cooking in cast iron can add valuable iron into your mealtimes. Cast iron also comes as cheaper to buy than enamelled cast iron but maintains a significantly high level of quality.

Contrary to what some believe, cast iron cookware is much more versatile than simply products to aid the cooking of steaks and red meat - with a variety of bakeware and griddles available.

The Cons of Cast Iron

While there are certainly plenty of advantages associated with embracing cast iron products in the kitchen, there are some disadvantages to be aware of. Due to its density, cast iron can take longer to heat up than stainless steel. It’s also notably heavier to operate.

Bare cast iron products may also need re-seasoning before use and might not be effective for boiling water or cooking with acidic food.

Ultimately, cast iron cooking products have operated as an industry standard for generations of restaurant owners. Today high quality cast iron goods are more accessible than ever, and companies like PetroMax are striving to supply cost-effective high-quality cast iron cookware to more budding chefs both outside of restaurants and homes altogether - with highly effecting and great quality camping and outdoor-ready Dutch Ovens, skillets and grills.

title: 5 Genius Hacks for Outdoor Cooking
author: Laurence
excerpt: Travelling to the great outdoors is an opportunity to be at one with nature and get away from the stress of everyday life. However, for some, the idea of outdoor cooking can bring some stress of its own. If you’re not su
html:
Travelling to the great outdoors is an opportunity to be at one with nature and get away from the stress of everyday life. However, for some, the idea of outdoor cooking can bring some stress of its own. If you’re not sure how to prepare for your next camping trip, take a look at these 5 outdoor cooking hacks…

Prepare your Meals in Advance

A lot of us prepare meals on a regular basis and it’s no different from when we go camping, in fact, it’s super helpful! Chop and prepare your ingredients from home so that they're ready for outdoor cooking! A good tip is to invest in some Ziploc bags, with these you can preserve all of your fresh needs as well as marinade things like meat on the go.

Limit the Cookware

It’s a good rule of thumb to pack lightly and you won’t need as much cookware as you think. Find disposable alternatives and invest in a good camping cookware set. Camping sets are built to be portable and compact but fitting in all the key essentials like cookware, dishes, and cutlery!

Minimise Dirty Dishes

Instead of lugging around your favourite pots and pans, try using disposable alternatives like tin foil. Not only is tin foil efficient to cook with, but you can eat straight from it, try cooking individual pocket meals so you can skip the pans and the plates!

Backup Stove

Many of us might be keen to start a fire the old fashion way, but it’s always good to have a backup. Weather and other circumstances can seriously affect your ability to start a fire and you don’t want to be caught off guard and unable to cook. Take a portable stove with you for the worst-case scenario, or hey, just for the sheer convenience! 

Salt as Disinfectant 

This might sound like a weird one but it’s an old trick for keeping things hygienic and spotless. Obviously we want to keep our dishes both clean and disinfected, but things like soap and disinfectant can be cumbersome to carry around, instead, throw some salt onto your dirty dishes, it acts as a disinfectant and it’s coarseness helps to remove dirt and grime. Feeling inspired? Explore our range of outdoor cookware and camping stoves now and start getting ready for your next adventure.

title: 3 skills to master to take your bushcraft to the next level
author: Laurence
excerpt: The most basic and satisfying bushcraft skills to learn are building a shelter and making a fire. These skills are fun to master and you get to see immediate visible results from your efforts. However, if you want to tak
html:
The most basic and satisfying bushcraft skills to learn are building a shelter and making a fire. These skills are fun to master and you get to see immediate visible results from your efforts. However, if you want to take your bushcraft skills to the next level, you need to take the time to learn the three skills listed below.

Tree and plant identification

Bushcraft is about interacting with your natural surroundings, so being able to identify trees and plants is an essential, though often overlooked skill. Plant identification isn’t as fun as building a shelter or making a fire with your hands, but it is a skill that can vastly improve your bushcraft ability. Most dry wood will burn, but you need a deeper understanding than that. For example, you need to know that while birch burns well, it also burns quickly. This makes it great if you want to heat up a kettle, but not so good if you need to cook a meal. If you’re foraging for wild food, you need excellent plant identification skills. You shouldn’t eat anything you find in the wild if you’re not 100% sure it's safe. 

Water Purification

Access to water can be one of the biggest barriers to wild camping and developing your bushcraft skills. We need 3-5 litres a day, but if you’re hiking through the woods with a lot of gear, you will need more than that. When you’re out for several days, you’ll also need more than you can carry. Far too many people think buying some water purification tablets is enough. It isn’t. What happens if you lose those tablets? At a minimum, you will need to understand the five contaminants and how to purify them. The five contaminants are: • Turbidity • Protozoa • Bacteria • Viruses • Chemical pollutants. 

Outdoor Cooking

Eating the same meal out of a can every time you go camping quickly gets boring. There’s no reason why you can’t eat a healthy and varied diet while engaging in bushcraft. There are many single pot dishes that you can create from fresh ingredients. If you’ve spent the time learning about plant identification, you can also add ingredients from your surroundings. Sausages and beans can be improved by adding foraged mushrooms, but you need to be able to identify which ones are safe to eat, as many varieties of mushroom are poisonous to humans. Practise making a variety of meals at home to determine what tasty but practical meals you can make.

Check out our blog on 5 genius hacks for outdoor cooking next for more great wild camping tips.

title: FILTER VS. WATER PURIFIER: WHAT’S THE DIFFERENCE?
author: Laurence
excerpt: WHAT’S THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A BACKPACKING WATER FILTER AND WATER PURIFIER? (MSR BLOG) Put simply, the main difference lies in the level of protection these two treatment devices provide against the harmful microorganis
html:
WHAT’S THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A BACKPACKING WATER FILTER AND WATER PURIFIER? (MSR BLOG)

Put simply, the main difference lies in the level of protection these two treatment devices provide against the harmful microorganisms that may be lurking in backcountry water sources. Generally speaking, a water filter is designed to remove waterborne protozoa and bacteria, but not viruses. A water purifier is designed to remove protozoa, bacteria and viruses, offering a higher level of defence.

WHY THE TWO TREATMENT DEVICE OPTIONS?

Traditionally, tackling viruses has been tough for water treatment devices. On the microscopic scale, viruses are far smaller than protozoa and bacteria. Because of this, they’re too small for backpacking filters to catch; they simply slip through the filter media that filters use.

Until recently, UV light, chemical treatments or boiling your water were required to deactivate viruses by scrambling their DNA. Now, however, advancements in mechanical pump purifiers mean you have a convenient way to physically remove viruses along with bacteria and protozoa, all in one easy step.

While pump purifiers and other purifying agents are great when you need them, a purifier isn’t always considered necessary on every trip. Let’s take a look at why.

(Please note, the COVID-19 virus has not been detected in drinking water supplies, according to the World Health Organization. Municipal systems readily tackle waterborne pathogens in their treatment methods.)

WHEN SHOULD I USE A BACKPACKING WATER FILTER?

While purifiers offer greater defence than microfilters, they may be considered a bit overkill for some types of trips.

If you’re traveling in the backcountries of the U.S. and Canada, a filter is typically considered sufficient protection. In those pristine landscapes, where human traffic is relatively low, the main threats are considered to be protozoa (like Cryptosporidium and Giardia), and bacteria (like E. coli and Salmonella). These microorganisms can be transferred to you through human or animal faecal matter in the water.

Viruses, in contrast, are, most often, species-specific. That means, viruses that are harmful to humans are transferred primarily by the fecal matter of other humans. Therefore, where fewer humans exist, we assume the risk of viruses is also lower.

It is important to ensure that your microfilter is built to handle backcountry-type water. Some filters in outdoor shops are designed to remove only unpleasant tastes from tap water. Backcountry-grade microfilters are designed to remove contaminants down to 0.2 microns and should meet NSF protocol p231 and/or the U.S. EPA’s Guide Standard and Protocol for Testing Microbiological Purifiers (for removal of bacteria and protozoa).

Learn about these testing standards here.

 

WHEN SHOULD I USE A BACKPACKING WATER PURIFIER?

If you’re traveling to less-developed countries, where water treatment and sanitation infrastructure is poor, a water purifier is the safer option. You might also choose a purifier in your local backcountry zones if you notice that people aren’t practising good hygiene near water supplies—such as at popular lakes.

Common waterborne viruses found in water sources include Norovirus and Hepatitis A.

If you own a microfilter, you can combat viruses by adding a purifying agent to the water after you’ve sufficiently filtered it of protozoa, bacteria and any particulate, like dirt. Chemical tablets make a great back-up purifier to any microfilter, rendering the water safe to drink of viruses.

Using a purifying agent, like chemical tablets or UV light, alone won’t remove particles like dirt from the water. It’s important to note that particulate in the water can impede the effectiveness of UV light and to a lesser degree, chemicals.

This is why mechanical pump purifiers offer a big advantage!

Mechanical purifiers are designed to physically remove contaminants down to 0.02 microns (notice the extra zero in front of the 2). All mechanical purifiers should meet the NSF Protocol P231, NSF Protocol P248, or EPA drinking water testing standards.

As our local backcountries see a rise in traffic, and the risk of viruses increases with it, purifiers may become the more popular tools of choice.

THREE USE SCENARIOS TO CONSIDER:

Here are a few scenarios that you might find yourself in while adventuring and the type of treatment device we recommend.

BACKPACKING IN WASHINGTON’S NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK:

You’ll be collecting water from subalpine streams and lakes along established hiking trails during the summer. Any pathogenic risks in the water will come from humans and animals, but are usually light in concentration. Here, bacteria and protozoa are the primary threats; the likelihood of encountering viruses is very low. The water may also contain particulate like dirt or sediment, which will need to be removed.

Treatment choice: A microfilter is typically recommended, but you might bring a purifying agent as a backup if you suspect viruses could contaminate the water.

CAMPING ON A HOLIDAY WEEKEND AT VERY POPULAR LOWLAND LAKE:

You’ll be collecting water from the lake, the shores of which are packed with campers. The higher concentration of humans leads to a higher risk of viruses. The water also contains particulates, which you’ll want to remove.

Treatment choice: A mechanical pump purifier, or microfilter plus purifying agent.

title: How to Keep Your Tent Dry in the Rain
author: Laurence
excerpt: Camping in the rain isn't always a pleasant experience. There's nothing worse than waking up in a pool of water and then having to spend the day in soggy clothes. Luckily, with a little preparation, you should be able to
html:
Camping in the rain isn't always a pleasant experience. There's nothing worse than waking up in a pool of water and then having to spend the day in soggy clothes. Luckily, with a little preparation, you should be able to keep your tent dry in even the harshest of weather. Here are a few tips for keeping the rain at bay.

  1. Don't forget your groundsheet When it comes to camping in the rain, a groundsheet is your most important piece of equipment. A groundsheet sits under your tent, forming a waterproof barrier between the inside of your tent and the ground. A properly installed groundsheet will allow rainwater to flow under or around the tent instead of seeping into the interior. If you don't have a groundsheet, try using a waterproof tarp as an alternative. The tarp should be bigger than the tent, but you should fold the edges under your tent to prevent the pooling of water at the corners.
  2. Think about the angle of your tent When setting up your tent, you can use angles to your advantage. Putting your tent on a slight slant will cause rainwater to run around it rather than collecting underneath. If there is a strong wind, you should point the entrance of your tent away from it to prevent rainwater from blowing in.
  3. Leave your fire burning If possible, you should leave your campfire burning on rainy nights. Set up a nearby tarp to prevent the rain from putting out the fire. The fire will not only provide heat and warmth throughout the night, but will help to evaporate excess water that has collected nearby.
  4. Consider a hammock This is an extreme solution, but it's worth remembering that a tent is not your only camping option. If you find yourself camping in a spot where the ground is completely saturated, a hammock might be your best option for keeping dry. If you're planning to spend the night in a hammock, remember to wrap up warm, wear waterproof clothing, and keep your gear above the ground as well.

title: Travelling Light: 5 Things You Don't Need to Take on a Camping Trip
author: Laurence
excerpt: If you're preparing for a camping trip, you've probably read dozens of lists of the items that you mustn't forget. From torches to spare socks, there are many essentials for those braving a night in the wilderness. But i
html:
If you're preparing for a camping trip, you've probably read dozens of lists of the items that you mustn't forget. From torches to spare socks, there are many essentials for those braving a night in the wilderness. But is it possible to over-prepare? Camping should be about getting back to basics, so overpacking will only slow you down. Here are 5 items that you absolutely don't need to take on your next camping trip.

  1. Glass or ceramic items Taking breakable items on a camping trip is a big no-no. Broken glass can tear through a rucksack and can also be a serious hazard at a campsite. Leave your breakable bowls and mugs at home and bring plastic or paper crockery instead.
  2. A mirror Camping should be about losing yourself in nature, so your appearance is the last thing you should be worrying about. Leaving your mirror at home is liberating, and also removes another potential source of broken glass.
  3. Smartphone and laptop One of the big attractions of camping is the opportunity to get away from the stresses of the modern world. Taking an internet device with you defeats the point by keeping you connected to life back at home. Spending the whole trip checking your work emails will leave you feeling like you haven't been on holiday at all. Take a basic phone with you for safety and leave it at that. The battery life will be better too.
  4. Kids' toys If you are taking your children camping, you may be tempted to bring lots of toys to keep them entertained. This is a big mistake as it means that your kids won't make the most of the experience. Nature is endlessly entertaining for children, so give them a chance to enjoy it fully by leaving the toys at home.
  5. White clothing This one should go without saying. Trying to keep white clothing clean on a camping trip simply isn't worth the hassle. Only bring clothes that can handle a bit of mud! For more information or advice on camping supplies, contact us at JustSupplies today.

title: 3 Survival Mistakes to Avoid in the Great Outdoors
author: Laurence
excerpt: If you're planning a camping trip to the great outdoors, you will no doubt be excited to get going and have fun. Before you set off though, you should think seriously about survival. Being able to stay safe and handle em
html:
If you're planning a camping trip to the great outdoors, you will no doubt be excited to get going and have fun. Before you set off though, you should think seriously about survival. Being able to stay safe and handle emergencies is very important on any trip. As well as knowing what you should do, it can often be just as useful to know the things that you should not do! But what survival mistakes should you avoid?

Not packing the right kit

This mistake is very important to avoid for survival. This is especially true if you will be hiking or engaging in activities such as rock climbing. It is key to pack all the kit you need for your trip, equipment to deal with accidents and the correct gear to perform any activities safely. This includes essentials like first aid kits, maps, a compass, food and drink, a knife, spare clothes, specific kit for certain activities, tents and cooking equipment.

Panicking if things go wrong

Another mistake to avoid when it comes to survival in the great outdoors is losing your head if things go wrong. Panicking will just make the situation worse and stress everyone out even more. It could also see you lose the ability to think rationally and make poor judgement calls on how to handle things. Spending time in the great outdoors can throw up curveballs at times - try to stay calm and work out how best to deal with them.

Not having the basic knowledge

A mistake that you see some people make is heading out into nature with no basic survival knowledge to call on. You may think that you are going for a short hike and not need to know how to start a fire or make a shelter but what if you need too? If the weather comes in and you get stranded, this could end up being a lifesaver. The same is true for any specific activities you might try when outdoors. Do not assume you can simply give it a go without any prior knowledge and it will be ok. This is often when accidents happen.

title: 3 Safety Tips for Using a Knife When Camping
author: Laurence

Always store them safely

If you have a fixed blade knife, make sure you put it back in its sheath. If the knife blade folds up or is retractable, make sure it is closed and put somewhere secure. Keep the blade sharp

Many people think that sharper knives are more dangerous but the opposite is true. Keeping the blade sharp means you have to put less pressure on it to cut things and therefore have less chance of the knife slipping. Wounds from sharper knives are also more precise which usually makes them simpler to stitch. Be aware of your surroundings

This is common sense but something that people can sometimes forget about. When you are using your knife, you must always be aware of who and what is around you. While you need to focus on the task in hand, being aware of your surroundings is also crucial. title: 4 more top tips for camp cooking
author: Laurence
excerpt: If you're enjoying the great outdoors for an extended period of time, you're going to need to think about cooking. Whether it's just a long day's hike or a week-long adventure in the wilderness, it's essential to know th
html:
If you're enjoying the great outdoors for an extended period of time, you're going to need to think about cooking. Whether it's just a long day's hike or a week-long adventure in the wilderness, it's essential to know the basics of outdoor cooking. These four top tips can help make sure you're able to cook comfortably.  

1. Keeping things cold

If you're bringing ice with you, block ice lasts a great deal longer than ice cubes. If you don't want to bring ice, however, you can still keep things cold while maximising your storage space. Consider freezing meat, cans of juice, or bottles of drink - they will act as a cooler without taking up unnecessary space in your pack.

2. Covering your cooking pot

If you're going to be cooking in a pot, make sure you bring a pot with a lid. There are several benefits to this - the first is that food in a covered pot will cook quicker, so you won't need to use so much fuel to heat it. The lid will also protect it from flies and insects, and prevent the smell from attracting animals from further afield.

3. Using charcoal to cook

Using charcoal is one of the best ways to cook outdoors because it provides an even and manageable heat which allows you to better ensure that your food is cooked all the way through. To prepare your charcoal faster, use a charcoal chimney to heat them before pouring them out into your designated cooking area to cook over.

4. After-meal cleaning hacks

Rubbing some liquid soap around the outside of your pots can prevent them from burning and leaving scorch marks. While you're eating, put a pan of water to warm over your charcoals while they're still hot. This will mean you have hot water ready when you need it. Make sure to bring bread for mopping up the very last of soups and stews - you don't want anything going to waste. title: Wild Camping Myths Debunked
author: Laurence
excerpt: If you're new to the idea of wild camping, you might be wondering what it's all about, and how it differs from the usual camping. In order to get your facts right, here are some common wild camping myths to avoid. Myth 1
html:
If you're new to the idea of wild camping, you might be wondering what it's all about, and how it differs from the usual camping. In order to get your facts right, here are some common wild camping myths to avoid.

Myth 1: You can camp anywhere

There's often the idea that with wild camping you can pitch up your tent anywhere you like. This isn't strictly the case. You'll need permission from a landowner if you wild camp in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. The rules are less strict in Scotland, although you'll still need to adhere to the Scottish Outdoor Access Code, which means that you must be responsible, respect the environment and the interests of others. Bear in mind also that you aren't allowed to just pitch up outdoors in nature reserves or national parks, with the exception of Dartmoor National Park in Devon.

Myth 2: Wild camping is only for the hardcore

Contrary to what you might think, you don't have to be a hardcore camper to enjoy the benefits of wild camping. As long as you've got the right camping equipment, you'll enjoy the feeling of really connecting with nature that wild camping brings. It's also a great opportunity to put those bushcraft and foraging skills into good use!

Myth 3: There are no rules like at normal campsites

Just because you're not staying within the confines of an organised campsite, doesn't mean to say that you can do exactly what you want when wild camping. While you might not have a list of dos and don'ts put under your nose when pitching up your tent, it's still important to respect the land and follow the Countryside Code. It goes without saying that you shouldn't leave any litter or trace of your stay behind. When it comes to outdoor cooking, never light a fire unless you've gained permission from a landowner. Camp in small groups, away from areas of wildlife or livestock, and don't outstay your welcome.

Myth 4: There'll be too much to carry

Going wild camping doesn't necessarily mean you'll have to be weighed down by an enormous, heavy backpack. These days, it's easy to find lightweight camping gear and camp cooking equipment that are compact and easy to fit into a pack. Seek quality gear from a reputable camping provider and you'll be amazed at just how much you can squeeze into your backpack, without feeling overburdened.

title: Wild Camping in the Winter
author: Laurence
excerpt: Let’s be honest, camping in the winter isn’t for everyone. And that is exactly what is so joyous about it. Campsites are closed, fair-weather holidaymakers are snuggled up inside their centrally heated homes … and those
html:
Let’s be honest, camping in the winter isn’t for everyone. And that is exactly what is so joyous about it. Campsites are closed, fair-weather holidaymakers are snuggled up inside their centrally heated homes … and those of us who know the true wonders of being outdoors at this time of year have all the prime spots to ourselves. If you are one of the hardy bushcraft fans who isn’t put off by a spot of cold weather, this post is for you.

Equipment is king

The absolute key to wild camping in the winter is having the right gear. No one wants a miserable night spent wondering if you are about to lose your toes to frostbite. Take only the essentials and choose your kit wisely.

  1. Small tent This isn’t an occasion for your full family tent with the porch and a separate living area. Make sure you only go as big as you need so that your body heat will be enough to warm the space and give you a good night’s sleep, which means opting for a small tent as far as possible.
  2. Other sleeping equipment A good sleeping bag is a must-have for winter wild camping. Choose one that is both warm and lightweight – you burn extra calories when it is cold, so you don’t want to be carrying any unnecessary weight. A sleeping mat is a good idea too to raise you off the cold ground.
  3. Good socks Heavyweight merino wool socks are the way to go in the wintertime. Bring an extra pair for sleeping so that you have some that are dry and warm for the night.
  4. Cooking equipment You are going to want a hot meal, especially if you are foraging or fishing and want to cook your catch. Choose light, folding outdoor cooking equipment that won’t weigh you down or take up too much space in your pack.
  5. Water bottle Even in the cold, it is important to stay well-hydrated while exploring the great outdoors. Make sure you have a water bottle with a decent capacity.
  6. Carrying equipment It won’t matter how carefully you have chosen the rest of your gear if you don’t have the right bag to carry it all in. Choose a pack that fits everything you need but no more – you don’t want to be tempted into adding extra weight unnecessarily. A waterproof bag or two is useful to keep your valuables (and those spare socks) dry in wet weather.

If you're new to outdoor adventures, choosing a camping tent can be a confusing and overwhelming task. Thankfully, here at JustSupplies, we've put together this handy guide to help you make the best purchase for your intended camping trip.

So, if you want to know your tent footprint from your groundsheet and your semi-geodesic tent from your air tents, read on for our breakdown!

First, Consider Your Camping Needs

Before you even start looking at tents, it's important to consider the type of camping you'll be doing. 

Will you be backpacking and hiking long distances to your campsite or setting up a base camp near your car? The answer to this question will determine the size, weight, and design that would be best for you.

If you're going on a long-distance trek, a lightweight tent will be essential. However, if you'll be driving to your campsite, size and weight may not be as much of a concern since you won’t have to lug it around.

You also need to think about the number of people and the amount of kit that's going to be in the tent at night to make sure everyone has enough room to be comfortable.

So, in summary, you should consider:

  1. Size and space required – As mentioned earlier, it's essential to consider the number of people and equipment that will be inside the tent.
  2. Seasonality & weather conditions – Will you be camping in winter or summer? The season will determine the type of tent suitable for your trip.
  3. Ease of setup – Consider how much time and effort you're willing to spend pitching your tent. A pop-up tent may seem easy, but you're sacrificing stability.
  4. Durability and weather resistance – Your tent must be able to withstand various elements, such as wind, rain, and snow.
  5. Weight and pack size – Depending on the type of trip you'll be taking, weight and pack size can play a significant role in the suitability of a tent.
  6. Price range – Tents for camping are available in a wide range of prices, so it's important to determine your budget before making a purchase.

The Most Popular Styles of Tents

There are a few different styles of tents that you're likely to come across when looking for a new tent, Below are some of the common types of tents available and what kinds of camping trips they're good for.

Dome Tents

Dome tents are among the most commonly used styles of tents, primarily due to the following reasons. Dome tents are typically designed with 2 or 3 poles that, once inserted, create the tent's shape. This makes pitching the tent a straightforward process.

Dome tents are also known for their rigidity, making them ideal for setting up in harder areas where strong fixing points may be limited. They offer stability and reliability in various camping conditions.

Overall, dome tents offer a practical and reliable solution for outdoor enthusiasts seeking a convenient and functional shelter option.

Tunnel Tents 

Tunnel tents are highly suitable for larger groups and families, offering superior headroom and spaciousness. These tents are constructed using similar poles to dome tents, but they are inserted widthways, resulting in a tunnel shape. 

It is important to note that stability is reliant on the guy ropes, and a strong peg hold is crucial to avoid any potential issues.

A-frame/Ridge tents

These tents are highly popular among backpackers, primarily because they allow for weight reduction by replacing tent poles with walking sticks or hiking poles. Tarps can also be utilised to create this type of tent or shelter.

Geodesic Tents 

Often referred to as top-tier tents, these shelters are commonly utilised by individuals camping in extreme climates. They are available in a variety of styles tailored to specific needs. Geodesic tents, for instance, resemble dome tents but boast additional poles to enhance stability and weather resistance.

author: Ben Barnes

html:
Choosing the right backpack or rucksack can be tricky. They come in a variety of styles, sizes, and prices, making it difficult to decide which one is best for you. When it comes to choosing a rucksack vs backpack for the trip you have planned, there are a few things that you need to take into account.

To help make the decision easier, we’ve put together this buying guide. It covers the different types of backpacks, the main uses for each, and the things to consider before making a purchase.

Explore the Best Rucksacks & Backpacks

The Difference Between Rucksacks & Backpacks

Of course, rucksacks and backpacks sound like they're two terms for the same thing, but there are some crucial differences that can affect your decision depending on the trip or expedition that you're embarking on.

What is a Backpack?

A backpack is a bag carried on the back, similar to a shoulder bag. It is typically smaller than a rucksack and has only one main compartment for storage.

What is a Rucksack?

A rucksack is a type of backpack that is made from heavy-duty materials, tends to be larger and offers way more storage opportunities via a range of pockets and compartments.

What are the Differences?

The main difference between rucksacks and backpacks is that backpacks are designed for smaller loads, such as a laptop, lunchbox, or reading materials.

Rucksacks usually have more storage space and compartments, making them better for carrying heavier loads such as tents, sleeping bags, and bulkier camping items.

What are the Different Types of Backpacks?

  • Classic backpacks
  • Daypacks
  • Hiking backpacks
  • Travel backpacks
  • School/college backpacks
  • Sports backpacks
  • Fashion & lifestyle backpacks

For camping purposes, you'll only be interested in the top four types of backpacks, but daypacks and hiking backpacks are most commonly chosen by campers.

A day pack is smaller than a hiking backpack and designed for carrying just enough supplies for a short trip, such as going to work or running.

What Should I Look for When Choosing a Backpack?

When looking to buy a new backpack, make sure to take the following factors into account:

Size

Backpacks come in different sizes, so it’s important to find one that fits your needs perfectly.

Weight

Make sure the backpack you’re buying is light enough for you to carry without feeling weighed down.

Features

Some hiking backpacks only have a single compartment, so it’s important to select one with plenty of storage space.

Comfort

Make sure the backpack is comfortable to wear and fits your body well.

How to Choose the Best Rucksack

When it comes to selecting the right rucksack for you, there is no one-size-fits-all answer. That’s why it’s important to take measurements and choose the rucksack that is perfect for your needs.

Rucksacks come in different sizes, so it’s important to choose the right one based on your needs and preferences. For example, if you prefer a backpack for prolonged travel, a large rucksack may be the right fit for you.

Additionally, rucksacks are perfect for camping and hiking due to their versatility and capacity to carry a range of gear, such as tents, sleeping bags, food and water.

Contents are usually secured by a drawstring or zipper, and some rucksacks offer a waterproof lining to protect clothes and valuables.

Other rucksack features worth mentioning are pockets for water bottles, top compartments for any tools and camping accessories you need quick access to, and a hardened base that further protects the contents from damage.

What Should I Look for When Choosing a Rucksack?

Again, like a backpack, you should think about size, weight and features. When it comes to size, make sure the rucksack you’re buying will fit your body well and can cope with the strain of a heavy load.

If you are tall or have a big waist, then look for a rucksack that can be secured firmly to your body. Similarly, if you are short or have a small waist, select a shorter rucksack that has more capacity and less weight overall.

One thing to mention about rucksacks is that they are typically measured in litres to identify the total capacity.

Pros & Cons of Rucksacks & Backpacks

When it comes to the best rucksack or backpack for the job, it all comes down to what you need it for.

Backpacks

+ Perfect for students and people who want a single fuss-free compartment.

+ They’re also less restrictive when it comes to movement, making them better for active people.

- A single main compartment restricts what you can pack into it.

Rucksacks

+ Rucksacks are the more versatile of the two, as they can be used for a variety of activities.

+ Can carry a range of camping and hiking equipment due to their high capacity and multiple compartments.

- Tend to be bulkier and take up more room than backpacks.

So, the choice comes down to what you’re the most comfortable carrying and what you need the bag for. Remember to take the time to try them out and find the perfect one for you!

Why Choose a Rucksack or Backpack?

Backpacks are better for everyday use because they’re more space-efficient. They’re also lightweight and can be packed small, making them the perfect travel companion. 

They are also great for carrying daily essentials like school materials or laptop computers. Ultimately, the best choice for you depends on what type of activities you’ll be using the backpack for.

Rucksacks, on the other hand, are better for longer trips or activities where you’ll need to carry a lot of gear and supplies. They’re designed with more space in mind and often come with additional compartments and features to help organise your belongings.

So, consider what you need the rucksack for and choose the one that best suits your needs!

Key Takeaways: Is a Rucksack or Backpack Right for You?

When choosing between a backpack and a rucksack, the differences can be subtle. It really comes down to functionality and personal preference. Both bags can be used for various activities, so it's important to think about the type of trip you're taking and find the one that suits you best.

Types of solid fuel camping stoves

Choosing the right camping stove can be a daunting task, but it's important to do your research.

There are a variety of types of solid fuel camping stoves available on the market, so it's important to know what you're looking for. Some of the most common stoves include gas stoves, propane stoves, and solid fuel stoves.

Each stove has its own benefits and drawbacks, so it's important to choose the right one for your needs. If you're looking for a stove that will fit your needs and enjoy campfire cooking all season long, determining which type of solid fuel stove you need is a must.

Pros and cons of using solid fuel camping stoves

If you're considering using a solid fuel camping stove, it's important to do your research first.

Make sure you choose the right one for your needs - for example if you're looking for an easy-to-use stove that doesn't require any special gear or preparation, a solid fuel camping stove may be the best option for you.

However, be aware that solid fuel camping stoves can be unpredictable and dangerous in cold weather conditions. Make sure you have enough fuel and lighter fluid so that you can start the fire easily, and always take safety precautions when using a stove in cold weather.

Pros include:

  • They're friendly on the environment. Solid fuel stoves burn cleanly and don't produce any harmful fumes, so they're a great option if you want to cook with minimal waste.
  • They're cheaper! A standard propane or gas camping stove can cost upwards of £40, but a solid fuel stove may only cost around £5 - £20.
  • More portable. This is a close one, but on the whole solid fuel stoves can be packed more compactly due to not having any extra tubing or connectors that are required with gas stoves.
  • They're easy to use. With few exceptions, solid fuel stoves are similar in design and operation to gas stoves - so you should have no trouble getting started if you've used one before.

Cons include:

  • If the weather gets cold, a solid fuel camping stove can be difficult to start. Some models require you to use lighter fluid or an electric starter - which can become difficult in cold weather.
  • Not as convenient as a gas stove. Typical gas stoves can be ignited and burn in even the coldest conditions.
  • They can be unpredictable. Solid fuel stoves are designed to work with a specific type of wood or lump of coal, so if you get an incorrect fuel or lighter fluid, your stove may not fire at all.
  • Solid fuel blocks burn out much quicker than gas canisters.

Remember that regardless of which solid fuel camping stove you choose, make sure to read the product description and safety instructions carefully before using it - and always take proper precautions when outdoors in cold weather when fire is involved.

Gas vs. Solid Fuel Camping Stove - Which is Better?

It might just come down to preference - but there is something about a solid fuel stove that resonants with wild camping. Maybe it's the simplicity or the fact that you can pack your stove down into smaller and more compact spaces than gas stoves.

Either way, solid fuel camping stoves are a great alternative to propane or gas campfires when it comes to reducing environmental impact and wastefulness.

However, gas stoves are convenient, albeit more expensive. Ultimately, it comes down to what you're looking for in a camping stove - and whether or not convenience is more important to you.

title: Your All-Inclusive Guide to Peak District Camping
author: Ben Barnes
excerpt: If you’re yearning for a truly authentic and immersive camping experience, there is no better place to venture into the great outdoors than the magnificent Peak District. With its sprawling landscapes, picturesque trails
html:
If you’re yearning for a truly authentic and immersive camping experience, there is no better place to venture into the great outdoors than the magnificent Peak District. 

With its sprawling landscapes, picturesque trails, and enchanting wildlife, the Peak District offers a haven for nature enthusiasts and wild campers.

Whether you desire peaceful stargazing nights in the dark peak area or exhilarating hikes through rugged terrain, this captivating destination promises an unforgettable camping experience that will leave you feeling connected to nature in the most profound way.

So pack your gear, embrace the spirit of exploration, and embark on an extraordinary journey in the breathtaking embrace of the Peak District.

Camping In The Peak District

Camping in the Peak District is a popular pastime for locals and visitors alike. There are many campsites to choose from, both in the towns and villages within the National Park and in the surrounding areas.

The area attracts plenty of outdoor enthusiasts who are interested in wild camping. However, this isn't always possible – especially in the national park that covers a lot of the area to protect conservation efforts.

You can find some of the most stunning scenery in the country in the Peak District, and campers can enjoy waking up to views of rolling hills, woodlands and sparkling rivers. 

There are also plenty of activities to keep campers busy – from hiking and cycling to rock climbing and fishing (but we’ve got more on that later). Camping in the Peak District is a great way to experience this beautiful area of England, and with so many campsites to choose from, there’s sure to be one that’s perfect for you and whatever you want to get from your trip.

Our Favourite Peak District Camping Spots

The Peak District is a large area, so it’s important to pick a campsite that is close to the activities and attractions that you want to experience. There are numerous campsites within and surrounding the area, so do your research in advance and pick one that best suits your needs.

Because the park is perfect for hiking, you can choose multiple campsites and go backpacking during the day. If you're camping during peak times, booking a campsite is recommended. If you're visiting during off-peak times, you can get away with just turning up.

Some of the best campsites in the Peak District include:

  • North Lees Campsite, Hathersage, Hope Valley
  • Combs Valley Campsite, Combs, High Peak
  • Lathkill Dale Campsite, Monyash, Bakewell
  • Derbyshire Hills Campsite, Grindlow, Buxton
  • Upperhurst Farm Campsite, Hulme End, Buxton
  • Hayfield Camping & Caravanning Club Site, Hayfield, High Peak
  • Scaldersitch Farm, Sheen

Can You Wild Camp in the Peak District?

Of course, wild camping is always a tempting option. If you're looking for wild camping locations, you should avoid the national park as it is not permitted. You can find wild camping spots on private land. 

Just make sure to seek permission first, as it's technically illegal.

Some of the best spots for wild camping in the Peak District include:

  • Burbage Valley
  • Bamford Edge
  • Chee Dale
  • Derwent
  • Kindeu
  • Surprise View Car Park (a registered 'Dark Skies' stargazing spot)
Read Our Wild Camping Essentials Checklist to Prepare for Your Trip

Our Top 5 Peak District Outdoor Activities While Camping

As well as camping, the Peak District offers a whole host of other outdoor activities that are perfect for a summer’s day. Here are five of the best:

Hiking on the Peak District Trails

The Peak District is home to some of the most stunning hiking trails in the country. With miles of breathtaking scenery to explore, it’s the perfect place to get your hiking boots on and explore the great outdoors.

Some of our favourite walks include:

  • Mam Tor and Cave Dale
  • The Limestone Way
  • Bamford and Stanage Edge Circuit
  • Kinder Scout Plateau Circuit

Peak District Cycling Routes

There are lots of excellent cycling routes around the Peak District, both for beginners and more experienced cyclists. There are gentle routes suitable for all abilities, as well as more challenging routes for those looking for a workout.

Some of the most popular routes are:

  • Ashbourne Circuit
  • Monsal Trail
  • Manifold Trail
  • Rudyard and Roaches

Peak District Rock Climbing

For those who like a bit of adventure, rock climbing is the perfect activity. The Peak District is home to some of the best climbing spots in the country, so it’s the perfect place to give it a go – if you know what you’re doing, that is!

Some fun climbing locations include:

  • Burbage South Boulders
  • Stanage Edge
  • Froggatt Edge
  • Wind Gather Rocks

Fishing in Designated Peak District Rivers & Lakes

The Peak District is home to a number of rivers and lakes, although fewer than the Lake District, making it the perfect place to enjoy a spot of fishing. Whether you’re a seasoned angler or have never fished before, there are plenty of spots where you can cast your line.

Some of our favourite fishing spots include:

  • Barlow Lakes Fishery
  • Ogston Reservoir
  • Blithfield Reservoir
  • Holymoorside Dam

Pony Trekking in the Peak District

For those who want to explore the Peak District on horseback, pony trekking is the perfect activity. There are a number of companies that offer treks around the area, so you can trot through stunning scenery and take in the views at a leisurely pace.

Some popular pony trekking centres are:

  • Peak District Guided Horse Rides
  • Northfield Farm Riding and Trekking Centre
  • Derbyshire Pony Trekking

Peak District Star Gazing

This may sound like an odd activity, but there are multiple designated 'dark sky' zones throughout the Peak District that offer the perfect conditions for uninterrupted star gazing (weather permitting). 

These dark areas are one of the many things that attract wild campers to the Peak District region. They certainly make the ideal first wild camping spot.

Get the Most Out of Authentic Peak District Tent Camping

The Peak District is one of the most popular places in the country to get back to nature and spend some time camping. Because there are so many stunning places to choose from, it can be easy to overlook things when planning your trip.

Here are a few of our top tips to make sure you have the best possible time.

Bring the Right Gear

This may seem like a no-brainer, but it’s important to bring all the essentials with you when peak district tent camping. 

In addition to your tent and sleeping bags, don’t forget to pack food, water, a first-aid kit, and any other essential camping items you might need for your trip.

If you're planning to find a wild camping spot, it's essential to make sure you bring all the supplies you'll need to stay safe and enjoy your wild camping adventure.

Be Respectful of the Environment

When you’re in nature, it’s important to be respectful of the environment around you. This means packing up all of your trash, being careful with campfires, and being mindful of your impact on the area.

This is additionally important for wild campers. Many private landowners are happy to let you use their land as a wild camping spot, provided that you respect the area and leave no trace. 

This means following certain unwritten rules, including:

  • Taking all your rubbish with you
  • Not leaving food waste behind
  • Camp overnight and leave early
  • Be mindful of open fires

By taking care of the environment, we can ensure that future generations will be able to enjoy the same experiences that we get today.

Disconnect From Technology

One of the best parts about peak district tent camping is getting away from everything and disconnecting from technology for a while. Use this opportunity to unplug from your electronic devices and really connect with nature (and maybe even yourself).

If you're wild camping or planning on hiking some trails, make sure you have a charged phone with you in case you need to call for help in an emergency.

Have Fun!

Last but not least, don’t forget to have fun! This is your chance to relax and enjoy all the Peak District offers. 

Take some time to explore, play some games, sit around the campfire, and just soak up the environment. Enjoy spending time with your friends and family or by yourself and recharge with the power of nature.

Final Thoughts On Camping in the Peak District

With so much to see and do, camping in the Peak District is the perfect way to spend a summer.

Whether you’re looking for adventure or just want to relax in beautiful surroundings, there’s something for everyone in this stunning part of the country. 

By following these tips, you can ensure that you have the best possible time while peak district tent camping – just don’t forget to pack all of your camping essentials from JustSupplies!So what are you waiting for? Pack your camping gear and head to the Peak District!

title: What Is Cliff Camping? The Ultimate Camping Experience!
author: Laurence
excerpt: Nothing brings us as much joy as getting out in the open with nature. Camping allows us to go full-fledged outdoors and get away from the stress of everyday life, being at one with the scenery around us. And we certainly
html:
Nothing brings us as much joy as getting out in the open with nature. Camping allows us to go full-fledged outdoors and get away from the stress of everyday life, being at one with the scenery around us.

And we certainly all have our go-to camping locations and spots where we like to relax. But, sometimes, we crave something a little more daring and adventurous than the typical camping spot in the woods.

If you've ever found yourself thinking this exact thought, cliff camping might just be what you're after!

You can completely take your camping game to the next level with cliff camping. Of course, you obviously can't be afraid of heights if you want to try this type of camping. 

But if you're an adrenaline-junkie camping-lover, this could be just what you're after!

What is Cliff Camping?

Cliff camping is quite simply camping on the side of a cliff (who would have thought!). It's an extreme form of camping that requires both physical fitness and mental toughness.

You've got to be strong enough to carry all of your camping gear up and down the cliffs, secure enough to stay in a tent on the narrowest of ledges and brave enough to enjoy the impressive views!

When done correctly, cliff camping can provide unbeatable views and an incredible sense of achievement. However, it's important to remember that this is not a form of camping for beginners. If you're new to camping, stick to more traditional forms until you build up your experience, like tent camping in the Peak District.

If you've never camped on a cliff edge before, it might be wise not to go at it alone for your first trip. Experienced climbers are best suited to advising you on the safest routes and methods for camping, so you could see if there are any camping groups you can join who are experienced in cliff camping.

What is Night Cliff Camping?

The counterpart to day cliff camping is night cliff camping. It is usually done by experienced climbers as well, but with a few extra risks that come with it. 

Although the views and adrenaline-pumping experiences are still there, the risks increase when you camp on cliffs in the dark!

It's important to note that if you're going to do night cliff camping, you must have extensive knowledge about the area, as well as all of your climbing equipment. You don't want to put yourself in a vulnerable position.

That being said, the rewards that come from cliff camping at night are very real. The sights of the stars and the moon from a cliff edge at night can be truly mesmerising, giving you an unmatched sense of peace and calm that you won't find anywhere else!

It will surely be an unforgettable night.

Where Did Cliff Camping Originate?

Some say the concept of cliff camping originated in the 1980s in Yosemite National Park in California when climbers began finding ledges to camp on as they traversed the cliff walls.

Today, though it is still considered an extreme activity, more and more people are turning to cliff camping for a unique camping experience. 

It's become increasingly popular in areas around the world that have plenty of steep cliffs and dramatic landscapes.

Where Are The Most Popular Places For Cliff Camping?

If you're planning on going cliff camping, you'll need to choose your destination carefully. Not all cliffs are created equally! When choosing a place to camp, make sure to pick a spot that is safe and has easy access to food and water.

Europe

Europe is home to some of the most spectacular cliff camping spots in the world, including Cliffs of Moher in Ireland, Salto del Gitano in Spain, and Mont Aiguille in France. Countries like Switzerland and Italy also offer plenty of opportunities for cliff camping, with their stunning mountain ranges.

The Dorset coast in England is also popular for its dramatic cliffs and stunning ocean views.

North Wales has some of the best cliff camping spots in the UK, so it's definitely a spot to check out.

North America

For those in North America looking for an extreme camping experience, there are plenty of options too! Yosemite National Park in California is one of the best spots for cliff camping in the USA (where it all started!), as well as Zion National Park in Utah.

Canada also has some incredible spots for cliff camping, like the Canadian Rockies and Lake Superior Provincial Park in Ontario.

Asia

For those looking to camp on a cliff ledge in Asia, Thailand is one of the best options. With its limestone cliffs, beaches and islands, there are plenty of adventurous places to explore!

Cliff camping in Japan is also popular, with Mount Fuji offering some of the most stunning views. Other popular spots include Mount Hakuba, Kashimayari and Inokashira Park.

What Do You Need To Take Cliff Camping?

First and foremost, you'll need to pick out your cliff tent, and you need to carefully select the right tent for your needs. It should be lightweight and sturdy enough to withstand the elements, as well as big enough to fit both you and your camping supplies comfortably.

You must double-check the set-up instructions, stakes and tripods to ensure everything is in place - the sturdiness of your cliff camping tent is essential!

A portaledge is a type of tent specifically designed for cliff camping, and it allows you to attach your tent to the cliff wall. Make sure that your portaledge is properly secured before you go to sleep.

You never know what the weather forecast will be like when you're out camping on a cliff edge, so it's important to bring some layers with you. Pack a rain jacket and waterproof trousers (just in case!), as well as some warm clothes for colder nights.

The shoes you wear are also essential. You'll need sturdy shoes with good grip - preferably climbing shoes or specialised cliff camping boots.

A sleeping bag is a must, as it will help you stay warm and comfortable during the night. If you plan on doing any rock climbing, you should also bring some safety equipment such as a rope, harness and carabiner with you. The DD Jura 2 Sleeping Bag is a great option - it will keep you warm and comfortable in temperatures as low as -5C.

Finally, don't forget to pack some food (and snacks!) and plenty of water to keep you going. If you're in a cold climate, you will need to bring a thermos with you to keep your drinks warm. You can't go wrong with hot chocolate!

How To Stay Safe While Cliff Camping

As with any extreme sport, there is always some element of risk involved with cliff camping. It seems obvious to say that you should never camp on a cliff ledge without the proper safety equipment and knowledge. 

If you're ever feeling unsure, it's best to err on the side of caution and not take any risks.

Make sure that your tent is securely fastened to the cliff face rocks and packed with plenty of padding for extra protection from the elements. It's also a good idea to double-check your equipment, such as ropes and carabiners before you set off.

Make sure you fully stock your emergency or first-aid kit and know how to use it. Bring a friend with you in case of an emergency, or make sure someone knows exactly where you're going and when you plan on returning.

It will be a good idea to take a few light sources with you - a flashlight, headlamp, and lantern are all essential for camping in the dark. If one breaks or fails, you'll have a backup.

Summarising Cliff Camping: Your Next Adventure!

Whether you feel as if you've exhausted your usual camping spots or you're looking for a new type of thrill, cliff camping is an excellent adventure! With its spectacular views and rugged terrain, this extreme activity is perfect for those who are seeking adrenaline and exploration.

To make sure you have the most fun and stay safe while cliff camping, it's important to double-check your equipment before setting off - and it's probably best to go with a friend or group who have some experience in the field.

It's undeniable that you'll experience some of the most breathtaking views and exciting moments on your cliff camping adventure. Here at JustSupplies, we’ve got a huge selection of essential camping gear so that you can prepare yourself for the adventures that await  - so what are you waiting for?

Get packing and hit the cliffs!

title: The Essential Family Camping Checklist For Your Next Adventure
author: Laurence
excerpt: It's no secret that there is a certain level of preparation and planning that goes into a successful camping trip. And when you're taking the kids away for a fun family adventure, you need to be especially prepared. Not
html:
It's no secret that there is a certain level of preparation and planning that goes into a successful camping trip. And when you're taking the kids away for a fun family adventure, you need to be especially prepared.

Not only do you have to make sure everyone has the right supplies and equipment, but you need to make sure that your campsite is set up properly and safely.

It can feel impossible trying to juggle all the details, but we've made it a little easier for you with this handy family camping checklist.

Whether you're going on a short weekend trip or a week-long stay, you'll find everything you need to make sure your camping experience is comfortable and safe.

1. Tent

It might seem obvious, but you will need to pack a suitable tent for your family trip. That means taking into account the size of your family, the environment you'll be camping in and the temperature.

A tent should be big enough to comfortably fit all your family members with enough space for sleeping bags, backpacks and other items.

You will also need to make sure that the tent is suitable for the conditions you anticipate. In wetter climates, waterproof tents are essential, and in colder temperatures, four-season tents will provide the best protection.

Generally, it's best to go for a good quality tent that will last you through multiple trips. That way, you won't have to replace it every time you go camping.

Shop now

2. Sleeping Bags or Blankets

Sleeping bags are essential if you want a comfortable camping experience. Not only will they keep you warm and insulated, but they are also easier to transport than bulky blankets.

It's best to get sleeping bags for each family member that is rated for the conditions you plan on camping in. If it's colder, then opt for a bag with extra insulation or a liner.

If you decide to use blankets instead, make sure they are thick enough to keep you warm and dry. Keep in mind that you'll need a few extra for when you need to cover your sleeping bags or if one gets wet.

We recommend: DD Scarba Sleeping Bag

Shop now

3. Torchor Headlamp

No camping trip is complete without a good source of light. A torch or headlamp will come in handy if you need to take a bathroom trip in the middle of the night or if you need to light up your campsite after dark.

If you have young children, it's a good idea to get them their own torch so that they have a source of light during the night if they need it.

You can hang up a light in your tent if you're camping in an area with electricity, or you can opt for a battery-powered torch or headlamp.

We recommend: Petzl Actik Core 600 Lumens

Shop now

4. Family Games & Gadgets

Camping breaks are the perfect opportunity for families to get some quality time together. 

And what better way to do this than with a few fun family games and gadgets?

Pack a deck of cards, board games or travel-sized versions of popular party games. Or you can go with something more modern like portable video game consoles, water-proof speakers and a tablet for watching movies.

Of course, you don't want to spend all your time indoors. So, pack some outdoor games, like horseshoes or badminton sets, to keep everyone entertained in the great outdoors.

5. Cooking Supplies

No camping trip is complete without a good meal. And that means you'll need to pack the right supplies for cooking over the campfire or on the grill.

Make sure you have all the necessary utensils, pots and pans and any other items needed to make your meals.

Cooking pots, like cast-iron cookware that are made for camping, are ideal. 

They're lightweight and can be used in a variety of settings, so you won't need to worry about finding the right type of cooking surface or worrying about food burning inside them.

You'll also want to think about bringing along some fire starters, lighters or matches so that you can get the fire roaring.

Don't forget to pack some basic ingredients, like seasonings and oils, as well as any pre-made food items you might need for a quick meal. Because why can't you enjoy a home-cooked meal while camping in the great outdoors?

Shop now

6. Food & Water

No camping trip is complete without some delicious food and plenty of water. When packing for your trip, make sure you have enough food to last you the entire duration of your stay.

Pack non-perishable items such as canned goods, dried fruit, nuts and granola bars. Also, don't forget to bring along a cooler to store any perishable items.

Most importantly, make sure you have plenty of clean drinking water. If you're not camping in an area with a water source, then fill up several containers before leaving

7. First Aid Kit

No matter how prepared you are, accidents can still happen. That's why it's important to bring along a first aid kit on your camping trip.

Your kit should contain the basic items such as bandages, gauze, antiseptic wipes, ointment and pain relievers.

Don't forget to bring along any medications your family may need while camping. And make sure you pack enough for the entire duration of your stay.

We recommend: Care Plus Family First Aid Kit

Shop now

Where are the Best Locations for Family Camping in the UK?

Now that you've got everything on your family camping checklist ticked off, you might be wondering where the best locations are for family camping in the UK.

1. Lake District, Cumbria

The stunning scenery of the Lake District makes it a great destination for family camping in the UK. With its array of lakes, mountains and forests, this region offers an incredible variety of outdoor activities that the whole family can enjoy

2. Pembrokeshire Coast National Park, Wales

The rugged coastline of Pembrokeshire Coast National Park makes it a great place for family camping. From the stunning beaches to the breathtaking cliffs and coves, there's plenty to explore in this beautiful corner of Wales

3. The Norfolk Broads, East Anglia

This network of rivers and lakes is the ideal place for a family camping trip. With its rich wildlife and numerous outdoor activities, the Norfolk Broads provide the perfect opportunity to reconnect with nature and make some lasting memories with your loved ones

4. The New Forest, Hampshire

The ancient woodland of The New Forest provides the perfect backdrop for a peaceful family camping trip. From the heathland and forests to the wildlife-rich wetlands, there's plenty to explore in this stunning corner of England

5. Peak District National Park, Derbyshire

A family camping trip to the Peak District National Park is sure to be one you won't forget. With its rolling hills, rocky outcrops and peaceful trails, this stunning region is a great place to explore and make some lasting memories

Wrapping Up: Ticking Off Your Family Camping Checklist

A family camping holiday is a great way to explore the great outdoors, reconnect with nature and make some lasting memories with your loved ones.

With our family camping checklist, you can ensure that you're well-prepared for your trip. From essential items like tents and sleeping bags to the extras such as food and water, JustSupplies has got you covered.

So grab your gear and head out into the great outdoors!

FAQs

What do I need to go camping with family?

When going camping with family, you will need a tent, sleeping bags, flashlights, matches or lighters, portable stove and cookware, food and water, first aid kit and any other essentials that you might need while out in the wild

What should I pack for camping with kids?

When camping with kids, you should make sure to pack a few extra items such as child-sized sleeping bags, kid-friendly snacks, games and activities to keep them entertained, and any other items that your children might need while out in the wild.

What not to forget when camping with kids?

When camping with kids, you should make sure to pack enough food and water for everyone; sunscreen, bug spray and a first aid kit; as well as anything to keep them entertained, such as books, toys or games.

What do most people forget when camping?

Many people forget to pack essential items such as a flashlight, matches or lighters, extra clothes and shoes, as well as items like sunscreen and/or bug spray. It is also important to remember to bring along any medications your family may need while camping.
