title: The 45 Best Campsites in England by Region
author: Laurence
excerpt: England is home to some of the most stunning campsites in the UK. Whether you’re looking for a peaceful retreat in the countryside or an adventurous camping trip by the coast, England has something to offer for every typ
html:
England is home to some of the most stunning campsites in the UK. Whether you’re looking for a peaceful retreat in the countryside or an adventurous camping trip by the coast, England has something to offer for every type of camper.

In this post, we’ll explore some of the best campsites in England by region to help you plan your next camping trips with ease.

The best campsites in England by region:

  • South West England
  • South East England
  • East Midlands
  • West Midlands
  • North West England
  • North East England
  • Yorkshire
  • London
  • East of England

Best Camping Sites in South West England

South West England boasts some of the most iconic coastlines in the UK, making it a popular destination for camping enthusiasts. 

From the historic Jurassic Coast to the green hills of Somerset and the sandy beaches of Cornwall, this region offers a variety of campsites for both families and solo travellers.

Here are some of the best campsites in this region:

1. Golden Cap Holiday Park, Bridport, Dorset

Nestled amidst the stunning landscapes of the Jurassic Coast, Golden Cap Holiday Park in Bridport, Dorset, stands out as a prime camping destination. 

This campsite offers a unique blend of natural beauty, with panoramic sea views and direct access to tranquil beaches. 

Facilities include:

  • Well-maintained pitches
  • Modern washrooms
  • A play area for children

2. Burton Springs Holiday Camping Site, Bridgwater, Somerset

Burton Springs Holiday Camping Site in Bridgwater, Somerset, is a hidden gem surrounded by nature's serenity. Offering both fishing lakes and scenic walking paths, it boasts facilities including:

  • Electric hook-ups
  • A clean shower block
  • Dedicated areas for both camping and caravanning


They also have glamping pods and teepee-style “Belle Tents’ for those who prefer a little more luxury during their camping experience. 

3. Petruth Paddocks, Cheddar, Somerset

Petruth Paddocks in Cheddar, Somerset, provides a luxurious camping experience with spacious pitches and stunning views of the Cheddar Gorge, making it an ideal choice for both adventure seekers and relaxation enthusiasts. 

Facilities include:

  • Free WiFi
  • A friendly animal paddock
  • Fire pit rentals

4. Trewan Hall, St. Columb Major, Cornwall

Trewan Hall, nestled in Cornwall's lush countryside, offers a captivating camping experience. 

The site is known for its grand 17th-century manor house, providing a unique backdrop to your camping adventure.

It also has a heated swimming pool, so you can take a dip and relax after a day of exploring the nearby stunning beaches or let the kids tire themselves out. They also put on evening entertainment (from July) for the whole family to enjoy.

5. Hele Valley Holiday Park, Ilfracombe, Devon

Hele Valley Holiday Park in Ilfracombe, Devon, is a must-visit for its serene beauty and pristine environment, making it perfect for family holidays that blend relaxation with coastal adventure.

They offer campervan and motorhome pitching, as well as large tent and XL all-weather pitch options, all with water, electricity options, and modern facilities.

The site also has direct access to Hele Bay Beach, where you can spend hours soaking up the sun, building sandcastles, or taking a refreshing swim in the waters.

Best Camping Sites in South East England

South East England has some of the most stunning campsites in England, with a mix of coastal and countryside destinations. 

Depending on the type of camping holiday you are looking for, you can choose from a range of options, including family-friendly sites with plenty of activities and facilities or secluded sites for a peaceful getaway.

Here are some of our favourites:

1. Mercury Yacht Harbour & Holiday Park, Southampton, Hampshire

Nestled by the serene waters of the River Hamble, Mercury Yacht Harbour & Holiday Park stands out for its stunning waterfront views and boating opportunities. It's a must-visit for both marine enthusiasts and families looking for a peaceful getaway. 

Facilities include:

  • Boat Moorings
  • Children's play area
  • On site cafe

It’s also located close to Southampton city (8 miles), so it’s a great base to explore the bustling port city and its attractions.

2. Bluebell Coppice Park, Crowhurst, Battle, East Sussex

Bluebell Coppice Park in Crowhurst, Battle, East Sussex, is an enchanting retreat surrounded by woodland and bluebell fields.

There are facilities for trailer tents, campervans, caravans, and tents, so no matter your preferred camping style, there is a spot for you.

3. Painters Farm Campsite, Faversham, Kent

Painters Farm Campsite in Faversham, Kent, is a must-visit for its tranquil countryside setting, offering a peaceful retreat.

Tents, campervans, and caravans are welcome with electric hookups if needed, and there are clean and modern facilities on site, as well as fire pits for cosy evenings under the stars.

4. Cotswold Hills Country Park, Chipping Norton, Oxfordshire

Cotswold Hills Country Park in Chipping Norton, Oxfordshire, is a gem amidst rolling hills and picturesque landscapes, making it a must-visit for nature lovers and tranquillity seekers. 

Facilities include:

  • Stunning countryside views
  • Close proximity to Cotswold walking paths
  • Peaceful and spacious camping environment

The site is also open 12 months of the year, allowing visitors to enjoy the beauty of each season.

5. The Barn Caravan Park, Lancing, West Sussex

The Barn Caravan Park in Lancing, West Sussex, is a must-visit for its close proximity to the stunning South Downs and the Sussex coast, providing the perfect blend of countryside and seaside experiences. 

Facilities include:

  • Scenic walks and bike routes
  • Family-friendly atmosphere
  • Excellent local amenities

They offer both electric and non-electric pitching, as well as clean facilities, a clubhouse on-site and a play park for children. 

Best Camping Sites in the East Midlands

The East Midlands is home to a surprising amount of beautiful and tranquil camping destinations. If you’re searching for a peaceful escape from the hustle and bustle of everyday life, look no further than these sites…

1. Barn Farm Campsite, Matlock, Derbyshire

Barn Farm Campsite, located near the picturesque village of Matlock in Derbyshire, is a must-visit for its stunning Peak District views and family-friendly atmosphere. It has a wealth of facilities, such as:

In fact, the site even won 2 awards in 2023 for the Best Campsite (East Midlands) and the Best Family Campsite (East Midlands), so you know you’re in for a top-notch camping experience.

2. The Nurseries Caravan Park, Mumby, Lincolnshire

The Nurseries Caravan Park in Mumby, Lincolnshire, is a must-visit for its quiet, countryside setting, which is perfect for a peaceful retreat. 

It’s an adults-only site with scenic nature trails, a well-stocked fishing lake, and close proximity to local beaches, so there’s plenty to do for those looking to relax or get active. 

The park also has a variety of pitches available, from grass and hardstanding only to pitches with electric hookups, so you can choose the perfect spot for your stay.

3. Sherwood Pines Campsite, Edwinstowe, Nottingham, Nottinghamshire

Sherwood Pines Campsite in Edwinstowe, Nottinghamshire, is a must-visit for its immersive forest experience and outdoor activities for all ages. 

The site has direct access to Sherwood Forest with bike hire and trails available to explore the beautiful surroundings. It also offers a range of accommodation options, including pitches for tents, caravans and motorhomes, as well as luxury camping pods.

4. Longnor Wood Holiday Park, Longnor, Buxton, Derbyshire

Longnor Wood Holiday Park in Buxton, Derbyshire, is an adults-only retreat offering a peaceful and serene environment. It's a must-visit for couples seeking tranquillity, with hot tubs and tranquil nature walks on offer.

There are spacious hard-standing pitches for tents, with all-weather gravel spaces available in their Peak District location.

5. Brook Meadow, Sibbertoft, Leicestershire

Brook Meadow in Sibbertoft, Leicestershire, is a must-visit for its picturesque lakeside setting, offering a serene escape from the hustle and bustle.

Facilities include:

  • Fishing opportunities
  • Eco-friendly amenities
  • Quiet, family-friendly environment

Best Camping Sites in the West Midlands

The West Midlands also has a wide variety of beautiful campsites to explore, with stunning countryside and plenty of outdoor activities. Here are some top picks:

1. Springfields Countryside Caravan & Camping, Stoke-on-Trent, Staffordshire

Springfields Countryside Caravan & Camping in Stoke-on-Trent, Staffordshire, is celebrated for its peaceful surroundings and close proximity to the Peak District. A haven for nature enthusiasts, it provides:

  • Walking trails
  • Fishing lakes nearby
  • Kid-friendly amenities
  • Pet-friendly environment


This combination makes it a top choice for family camping trips.

2. Bredon-Vale Caravan & Camping, Evesham, Worcestershire

Bredon-Vale Caravan & Camping in Evesham, Worcestershire, is renowned for its idyllic setting amidst orchards and rolling hills, making it a perfect countryside escape. 

Facilities include:

  • Pitches with stunning views
  • Kid's play area
  • Walking and cycling paths

3. Woodside Country Park, Ledbury, Herefordshire

Woodside Country Park in Ledbury, Herefordshire, is a hidden gem amongst England's camping destinations, offering unparalleled peace and natural beauty. 

The site has secluded woodland pitches for tents and caravans, with luxury glamping options also available.

There are fantastic nature trails and wildlife-watching spots nearby, as well as a fishing lake and on-site cafe for refreshments

4. Gopsall Hall Farm, Atherstone, Warwickshire

Gopsall Hall Farm in Atherstone, Warwickshire, is a must-visit for its historical significance and picturesque settings. It's perfect for tranquil retreats amidst nature. 

Facilities include:

  • Historical ruins exploration
  • Spacious pitches
  • Walking trails
  • Close proximity to local attractions

5. Cayo Retreat, Hereford, Herefordshire

Cayo Retreat in Hereford, Herefordshire, stands out for its unparalleled natural beauty and relaxed atmosphere, making it a top choice for a serene getaway. Pitches are available for tents and touring caravans, with non-electric hookups.

Facilities include:

  • Private bathrooms & wetrooms
  • Panoramic views of the Black Mountains
  • Exclusive woodland walks
  • Situated on a working farm

The close proximity of this campsite to the Brecon Beacons National Park makes it ideal for hikers and backpacking enthusiasts

North West England

Take a trip to the North West of England to find some of the country's most stunning campsites. Here are our top picks:

1. Wallace Lane Farm, Caldbeck, Wigton, Cumbria

Wallace Lane Farm in Caldbeck, Wigton, Cumbria, is a must-visit for its breathtaking views of the Lake District's northern fells. Pitches at this site include Glamping pods, fully serviced pitches, tent pitches, and motorhome service points. This tranquil retreat offers:

  • Fully equipped tents and cabins
  • Farm animals on site & pet friendly
  • Access to walking and biking trails
  • Hot tub pitches

2. Moss Howe Farm Campsite, Witherslack, Grange-Over-Sands, Cumbria

Facilities include:

Little Acre Holiday Park, in Crooklands, Milnthorpe, Cumbria, is celebrated for its serene ambience, making it a must-visit.

Facilities include:

  • Spacious pitches
  • Close proximity to the Lake District
  • On-site café for refreshments

This stunning campsite is pet and family-friendly, making it the perfect spot for a true family holiday.

4. Welltrough Hall Farm, Macclesfield, Cheshire

Welltrough Hall Farm in Macclesfield, Cheshire, is acclaimed for its luxury glamping experience with stunning countryside views. This site boasts grass and hardstanding pitches. Fully serviced pitches are also available. 

A must-visit for its:

  • Luxurious glamping pods
  • Private hot tubs
  • Dedicated walking trails
  • On-site farm shop

With a dedicated dog shower, laundry facilities, and a direct path to the local pub, this campsite is ideal for escaping into the wild with your four-legged friends.

5. Ream Hills Holiday Park, Blackpool, Lancashire

Ream Hills Holiday Park, located near Blackpool, Lancashire, stands out for its adventurous wakeboard park and proximity to Blackpool's iconic attractions. Choose from luxury lodges, touring pitches, geodesic domes, and novelty helicopter pitches. 

Facilities include:

  • Wakeboarding park
  • Lakeside views
  • On-site accommodations

A must-visit for thrill-seekers and families alike, you can easily access Blackpool Pleasure Beach (only 4 miles away) and Beacon Fell for a challenging nature hike. 

North East England

Travel to the other side of the country to find even more stunning campsites in North East England. Here are our top picks for this region:

1. Tranwell Farm Certificated Site, Morpeth, Northumberland

Tranwell Farm Certificated Site in Morpeth, Northumberland, is a verdant getaway characterised by its quietude and beauty, offering an authentic camping experience. Pitches include camping pods, bell tents, shepherd's huts, and tent pitches.

Facilities include:

  • Ideal location for exploring Northumberland
  • Basic amenities for a comfortable stay

Walkmill Campsite in Warkworth, Northumberland, is a charming destination nestled in a picturesque setting by the river, making it perfect for nature enthusiasts and those seeking peace. 

Facilities include:

  • Close to Warkworth Castle
  • Ideal for fishing and kayaking
  • Shower and toilet facilities

Pitches at this campsite include tent, campervan, and motorhome pitches. The close proximity to local walks and trails makes it perfect for hikers. 

3. Thorpe Farm Centre, Barnard Castle, County Durham

Thorpe Farm Centre, located near Barnard Castle in County Durham, is a must-visit for its unique blend of history and recreation, set within a beautiful country setting. 

Facilities include:

  • Animal petting area
  • Gourmet farm shop
  • Walks around the historical site

Pitches include EHU, non-EHU, and tent options. Seasonal pitches are available for extended stays.

4. Sharpley Camping, Seaham, County Durham

Sharpley Camping in County Durham is celebrated for its panoramic coastal views and tranquil atmosphere, making it an idyllic escape for the whole family. 

Facilities include:

  • Stunning sea views
  • Spacious tent and caravan pitches
  • Direct access to coastal walks
  • Family and pet-friendly environment

There are spacious camping pitches available for tents and campervans, as well as a select number of EHU pitches. 

5. Bankfoot Camping, Stocksfield, Northumberland

Bankfoot Camping in Stocksfield, Northumberland, is noted for its impressive views of the Tyne Valley, presenting a peaceful retreat. It is essential for:

  • Breathtaking valley views
  • Access to Hadrian’s Wall paths
  • Family & pet-friendly
  • Basic yet comfortable amenities

An ideal choice for history enthusiasts and nature lovers, this campsite offers 27 non-EHU grass pitches on a level field. Pitches are unallocated, so turn up and pick a spot!

Yorkshire

Yorkshire is home to some of the most beautiful and fun campsites in England. If you're planning a camping trip to this region, be sure to check out these top picks:

1. Nurseries Caravan Park, Askham Bryan, York, North Yorkshire

Nurseries Caravan Park in Askham Bryan, York, is a must-visit for its tranquil setting and proximity to historic York. 

Facilities include:

  • Peaceful environment
  • Close to York's attractions
  • Well-maintained amenities
  • Family-friendly

Pitches include tent spaces with room for a car and super pitches with EHU and water. Seasonal pitches are available too for those looking to make Nurseries Caravan Park their home away from home.

2. Middlewood Farm Holiday Park, Whitby, North Yorkshire

Middlewood Farm Holiday Park in Whitby, North Yorkshire, stands out for its proximity to the stunning Robin Hood's Bay and the historical town of Whitby. 

Pitches at this campsite are available for holiday caravans, glamping pods, touring pitches, and tents. No gazebos or groups are allowed, though, so bear this in mind when booking!

3. Butt Farm Caravan & Camping Site, Beverley, East Yorkshire

Butt Farm Caravan & Camping Site in Beverley, East Yorkshire, is renowned for its unique combination of historical charm and modern amenities, set amidst the serene Yorkshire countryside. 

It’s located close to the town of Beverley, and there is an on-site shop, which makes it easy to stock up on essentials. 

There are tent and campervan pitches available with and without EHU, so you can choose the level of comfort that suits you best.

4. Mill Farm Country Park, Skipsea, East Yorkshire

Mill Farm Country Park in Skipsea, East Yorkshire, is a must-visit for its traditional charm and tranquil atmosphere, making it ideal for a relaxing getaway. 

Facilities include:

  • Picturesque walking trails
  • Fully equipped fishing pond
  • Children’s play area
  • Close to beautiful Skipsea beach

5. Castle Howard Lakeside Holiday Park, York, North Yorkshire

Castle Howard Lakeside Holiday Park in York, North Yorkshire, is a must-visit for its stunning location within the grounds of the historic Castle Howard estate. 

Facilities include:

  • Walking and cycling routes
  • Elegant setting and landscaping

Camping pitches include EHU hardstanding touring pitches, EHU grass pitches, and non-EHU grass pitches.

London

Change up your camping adventures with London's hidden gem campsites. Here are our top picks for camping near the bustling city:

Lee Valley Campsite Sewardstone, in Chingford, London, offers a unique blend of city convenience and serene countryside. A must-visit for its:

  • Access to Lee Valley's vast parkland
  • Family-friendly facilities
  • Pitch options for tents and caravans

A perfect city escape within nature's lap, pitches here include hardstanding touring and grass tent pitches. Tent hire is also available – just in case!

2. Waggoners Campsite, Farnham, Surrey

Waggoners Campsite in Farnham, Surrey, provides a peaceful retreat within close reach of London's vibrant scene. This haven offers guests:

  • Scenic countryside views
  • Direct access to hiking trails
  • Family and pet-friendly grounds

A must-visit for those seeking a tranquil escape with easy city access. Pitches available include spacious grass tent pitches. This is an off-grid campsite, so there is no electricity at all.

3. Walton on Thames Camping & Caravanning Club Site, Surrey

The Walton on Thames Camping & Caravanning Club Site in Surrey is a must-visit for its remarkable tranquillity beside the River Thames. 

Facilities include:

  • Riverfront pitches
  • Boating and fishing opportunities
  • Close to Hampton Court Palace
  • Excellent walking and cycling routes

Pitches at this campsite include grass only, grass with EHU, and hardstanding with EHU. There is also a motorhome service point available.

4. Apps Court, Walton-on-Thames, Surrey

Apps Court in Walton-on-Thames, Surrey, is renowned for its extensive range of outdoor activities and stunning natural scenery, making it a top camping destination. 

Facilities include:

  • Archery and fishing
  • Spacious event fields
  • Family and pet-friendly
  • Near attractions like Thorpe Park

Pitch options at Apps Court include motorhomes, campervans, touring caravans, and tent spaces. EHU and non-EHU pitches are available.

5. Aldenham Country Park, Elstree, Hertfordshire

Aldenham Country Park in Elstree, Hertfordshire, is a key destination for nature lovers and families, offering a peaceful escape with ample recreational activities. 

Facilities include:

  • Interactive farm experience
  • Nature trails and woodland walks
  • Children’s Adventure playground
  • Picnic areas and scenic lake views

A serene countryside haven near the city, pitches in this stunning campsite include open grass tent pitches, bell tent hire, glamping, and cabins. 

East of England

Venture to the East of England to find some of the most picturesque and relaxing campsites. Here are our top picks for this region:

1. Galley Hill Farm Camping, Blakeney, Holt, Norfolk

Galley Hill Farm Camping in Blakeney, Holt, Norfolk, is a must-visit for its stunning coastal views and proximity to nature reserves. Pitches include 13 x non-EHU grass pitches, 6 x EHU grass pitches, and a glamping pod.

Facilities include:

  • Coastal access for bird-watching
  • Nearby seal spotting locations
  • Tranquil setting for relaxation
  • Basic amenities for a comfortable stay

2. King's Lynn Caravan & Camping Park, North Runcton, Norfolk

King's Lynn Caravan & Camping Park, located in North Runcton, Norfolk, is renowned for its extensive facilities and serene environment, earning its must-visit status for both families and solo adventurers. 

Facilities include:

  • Spacious pitches

  • Proximity to King's Lynn's historical sites
  • Play area for children

Pitches available at King’s Lynn Camping Park are suitable for tents, motorhomes, caravans, and folding campers.

3. Shottisham Campsite, Shottisham, Woodbridge, Suffolk

Shottisham Campsite in Shottisham, Woodbridge, Suffolk, is a scenic gem celebrated for its harmony with nature. Grass pitches are available for tents, caravans, and campervans with EHU available for some. A must-visit due to:

  • Proximity to Suffolk's coastal beauty
  • Family and pet-friendly site
  • Tranquil surroundings ideal for relaxation
  • Essential facilities ensure a comfortable stay

4. Walnut Farm, Norwich, Norfolk

Walnut Farm in Norwich, Norfolk, is a must-visit for its unique blend of farm life and camping luxury, offering a peaceful retreat. Grass pitches are available for tents, touring caravans, and static caravans. EHU and non-EHU pitches are available. 

Facilities include:

  • Hands-on farm experiences
  • Luxury glamping options
  • Close proximity to Norwich City
  • Natural beauty and wildlife

5. The Pretty Thing, St. Osyth, Clacton-on-Sea, Essex

The Pretty Thing in St. Osyth, Clacton-on-Sea, Essex, is an idyllic escape for beach lovers and families. A must-visit for its:

  • Direct access to sandy beaches
  • Family-friendly atmosphere
  • Close to local attractions in Clacton-on-Sea
  • Secluded pitches for privacy

A perfect blend of relaxation and seaside fun. Pitches at this site include non-EHU grass pitches for tents. There are also EHU tourer and trailer tent pitches available.

Summary: The Best Camping Sites Across England

Exploring England’s landscapes through camping is an unparalleled experience, offering a blend of adventure, relaxation, and natural beauty. Whether you're seeking tranquillity, historical exploration, or outdoor activities, these campsites are perfect for staycation camping trips.

Find more trip ideas and planning tips on our camping blog!

Read More Camping Trip Tips

FAQs

Can I Live On a Campsite UK?

Living permanently on a campsite in the UK typically isn't allowed due to planning and licensing restrictions. However, some sites offer long-term pitches for "holiday use" only, requiring you to have a permanent address elsewhere.

Where is Best to Camp?

The best place to camp depends on your preferences. For nature and tranquillity, Northumberland offers peaceful countryside. For history lovers, Yorkshire's sites are unbeatable. For beach enthusiasts, Essex's coastal campsites are ideal.

Where is the Biggest Camp Site in the UK?

The biggest campsite in the UK is Holgates Silverdale Holiday Park in Lancashire, offering extensive facilities across a sprawling area. With pitches for tents, caravans, and luxury holiday homes, it caters to all camping preferences

Where Can You Legally Wild Camp in England?

Legally, wild camping in England is restricted and mostly not permitted without the landowner's consent, except in parts of Dartmoor National Park. Always seek permission or check local guidelines before setting up camp.

author: Laurence
excerpt: Quick answer: The best camping foods without a fridge are ones that keep at room temperature: dehydrated meals such as FirePot, tinned fish, meat and beans, jerky, nuts and dried fruit, grains, bagels and cereal bars. Ad

Quick answer: The best camping foods without a fridge are ones that keep at room temperature: dehydrated meals such as FirePot, tinned fish, meat and beans, jerky, nuts and dried fruit, grains, bagels and cereal bars. Add instant coffee, tea bags and squash for drinks, and heat everything on a lightweight camping stove.

Breakfast Bagels, banana bread, cereal bars, jerky and pre-cooked bacon

No-refrigeration camping meals can make your trip a whole lot easier – and there are some really tasty options! 

Whether you're going on a weekend camping trip or a longer expedition, we have compiled a list of the best no-refrigeration meals that are easy to pack and will keep you satisfied and energised throughout your trip. 

Here are some of our favourites…

Breakfast Lunch Dinner Snacks & Drinks
  • Savoury muffins
  • Banana bread
  • Bagels
  • Pop tarts
  • Jerky
  • Pre-cooked bacon
  • Fresh eggs

  • Cereal bars

Best No-Fridge Breakfast Ideas for Camping

Breakfast is the most important meal of the day, and taking pre-baked goods with you is the perfect way to fuel your day. 

You can opt to bake your own breakfasts before you leave or lean into lazy camping food and get some pre-packaged items. Some of our favourite pre-baked breakfast items to take camping include:

1. Savoury Muffins, Banana Bread, Bagels & Pop-Tarts 

These can be eaten straight out of the packet or simply heated up over your camping stove. 

If you're taking unrefrigerated food that needs cooking, we'd recommend something like the Optimus Elektra FE Gas Cookset With Pans or the Trangia 25-5 Complete Cooking System. Both of these sets come with a selection of pans to help you heat your food.

If you already have a camping stove, the Petromax Camping Oven is a great addition to your kit to help you whip up delicious, unrefrigerated meals.

How to Choose the Best Camping Stove for Your Trip

2. Jerky & Pre-Cooked Bacon

If you really can't go without meat for breakfast, it's possible to still get your fix without having to take a cooler with you. Jerky is a great alternative to bacon and sausages and can double up as a delicious and convenient snack for hikes.

You can also get some precooked bacon from supermarkets that are fine to be left unrefrigerated. These crunchy rashers can be heated up and eaten like fresh bacon. 

Alternatively, they work really well crumbled into scrambled eggs for a nutritious and delicious start to the day.

3. Fresh Eggs & Fruit

Of course, there are plenty of options for non-perishable breakfast foods that you probably already have for breakfast.

Fresh eggs are always a great breakfast option, they can also double up as a great snack during the day. If you're camping near a farm, you might even be able to get a supply of fresh eggs each morning from the farmer.

Fresh fruit is another great option for breakfast. If you've got a day of hiking or mountain biking ahead of you, the fruit won't be enough on its own. However, it's an ideal accompaniment for eggs, bagels, or as a topping for porridge.

4. Classic Cereal Bars

If you want to keep things as simple as possible, cereal bars make the ideal no-refrigeration breakfast option. 

Gone are the days of having to choose between bland cereal bars and ones packed with sugar. There are so many brands on the market that offer healthy, nutritious cereal bars to kick-start your day.

This is another option that can double up as a hiking snack if you bring enough with you.

Nutritious No-Fridge Camping Lunch Foods

When you've got a day packed with hiking and physical activity, you need lunches that will sustain you and give you enough energy to keep going. 

Thankfully, there are plenty of options that are naturally non-perishable that can refuel you and keep you going until dinner.

5. Canned Protein

In the age of convenience, there are plenty of canned protein options that will keep you feeling full and energised for the rest of your excursion.

Tinned tuna or other fish is a great option for a quick and easy lunch. You can eat it straight from the can or pack some crackers to have with it.

Canned beans, chickpeas or lentils are also great options for protein-packed lunches. Simply drain and rinse them before adding them to a salad or serving them alongside your tinned fish.

Canned meals like chilli or stews are also a great option to fill you up and keep you warm.

6. Nuts & Dried Fruit

To boost the healthy fats, fibre, and calories in your lunches, nuts and dried fruit are great options. Not only do these items not need refrigeration, but they also make great snacks around the campfire when you're resting after a long hike.

If you don't want to have lots of packaging to dispose of, you can combine nuts and dried fruit into a homemade trail mix in a reusable tub. You can always take smaller pouches or snack boxes to decant the mix for a hiking snack.

The DD Organiser Bags are great for keeping your camp and tent neat, but they can also double up as snack bags for your day hikes.

7. Good Old Grains

Of course, you can't go wrong with classic grains as a camp lunch idea that doesn't need refrigeration or cooler packs to stay edible.

Cooking a pot of rice, quinoa, or barley for your lunch is a surefire way to boost your energy levels for the rest of the day. Eating grains at lunchtime instead of for dinner helps avoid that heavy, bloated feeling that can disrupt your sleep if you eat too close to bedtime.

Investing in a cast iron pot makes cooking a batch of grains much easier. We love the GSI Guidecast Dutch Oven Set for our campsite kitchen. It's available in various sizes to suit your needs.

Dutch Ovens: What Are They And What Can You Cook In Them?

8. Hearty Sandwiches

Sometimes, the best lunches are the classics. There are plenty of sandwich fillings that don't require cooling or refrigeration. 

Using canned meat is a great way to get some extra protein in for lunch. You can also use spreads like nut butter, honey, or jam that aren't perishable when they're unrefrigerated.

Fresh veggies like cucumber, tomato, and peppers are also great options for making delicious and nutritious sandwiches for lunch.

Top Tip: Stock up on individual sachets of sauces like mayonnaise and ketchup before your trip so you don't have to have dry, bland food!

Dehydrated No-Fridge Meals for Camping Dinners

Our favourite option for non-perishable food items when camping is dehydrated expedition meals that are packed with all the macro and micro-nutrients you need to sustain your trip. 

These handy meals don't require any cooking skill beyond boiling the pouches in water, so you don't have to bring lots of cookware with you either!

9. FirePot Dehydrated Meals

FirePot makes an extensive range of expedition meals that cover all three meals, so you only need to pack extra snacks.

You can start the day with their Baked Apple Porridge, then tuck into Barbecue Pulled Pork or Chilli Non-Carne with Rice for lunch. Round out your day with Mac 'n' Greens or Tuscan Stew.

They offer a range of vegan and vegetarian meals to suit various dietary restrictions.

If you like to have some variety for breakfast, or you like to finish your day with something sweet, Summit to Eat has the expedition meals for you!

Start the day with a choice of Chocolate Mousse with Granola & Cherry, Morning Oats with Raspberry, or Scrambled Egg with Cheese.

To round out your evening with a sweet treat, the Custard Apple Crunch and Rice Pudding with Strawberry are both delicious choices. They also offer a range of savoury meal choices, including pasta and curry options.

Handy No-Fridge Drinks & Snacks

Of course, you also need drinks for your camping trip. While water is the most important drink to have, it's nice to have other options, especially hot drink options, but these often require refrigeration. 

Here are our favourite beverages for camping that don't require a fridge.

12. Instant Coffee, Tea Bags & Hot Chocolate Sachets 

These are great options for unrefrigerated drinks. If you like milky coffee, latte and cappuccino sachets are perfect for camping. Otherwise, you can get individual jiggers of UHT milk that are ideal for creating hot drinks to enjoy around the campfire.

13. Squash & Iced Tea Bottles 

These are also ideal for giving you a break from plain water during your trip. This is especially useful if you have children camping with you.

14. Sports Drinks

If you're planning on doing a lot of physical activities during your camping trip, sports drinks are a great option for staying hydrated and replenishing electrolytes lost through sweating.

15. Marshmallows

Are any camping trips complete without roasted marshmallows? S'mores are a great way to finish any camp meal and perfect for snacking on the go.

FAQs

How Do You Keep Food Fresh Without a Fridge Camping?

To keep food fresh while camping without a fridge, coolers filled with ice packs are the easiest option. Alternatively, choose shelf-stable, dry, or dehydrated foods. Opt for fresh produce that doesn't require refrigeration, and consume perishable items early in your trip. Keep food out of direct sunlight

What Food Lasts Longest Without Refrigeration?

Foods that last the longest without refrigeration include dried fruits, nuts, jerky, canned goods, whole grain cereals, and hard cheeses. These items, stored properly, remain safe and consumable for a significant duration due to their low moisture content and preservative properties.

What Food Keeps Well for Camping?

For camping, food that keeps well includes dehydrated meals, canned foods, whole grain cereals, dried fruits, nuts, and hard cheeses. These options are durable, non-perishable, and don't require refrigeration, making them ideal for sustaining energy levels and nutrition while enjoying the great outdoors.

What Food to Bring Camping for 3 Days?

For a 3-day camping trip, pack a variety of dehydrated meals, canned protein, fresh fruits, whole grain cereals, nuts, and energy bars. Include dried fruits and hard cheeses for snacking. Opt for food items that are lightweight, nutritious, and do not require refrigeration to ensure convenience and sustainability.

title: Campervans Vs Tents: Which We Prefer & Why
author: Laurence
excerpt: If you’re planning your next camping trip, tossing up the idea of staying in a campervan or opting for a traditional tent, you’re not alone. Do you go for the convenience and comfort of a campervan, or do you stay true t
html:
If you’re planning your next camping trip, tossing up the idea of staying in a campervan or opting for a traditional tent, you’re not alone. Do you go for the convenience and comfort of a campervan, or do you stay true to nature and embrace the simplicity of a tent? 

Our team has been on many a camping trip, both in campervans and tents, and it’s something we’ve debated amogst ourselves many times. 

We’ve compared the good, the bad, and the ugly of campervans vs tents, and we’re here to share our thoughts with you to help you make the best decision for your next wilderness escape.

Campervan Camping Tent Camping
Can drive to different campsites & explore surrounding areas Can hike to remote, unique areas for a different experience
Good privacy with solid doors, walls, & windows Good privacy within the tent, but less when outside in shared campsites (although you can always use windbreaks as dividers)
Requires purchasing or renting a campervan Relatively inexpensive to purchase a tent
Provides shelter from elements, sleeping bed, & basic amenities Extra precautions needed for camping in poor weathers
Less practical for everyday use & need driveway space to keep when not in use Highly portable & can be stored easily
May require reservations at campsites with limited van spaces Fits in most campsites with tent pitches

Camping Mobility in a Tent Vs Campervan

Being able to move your kit around, including transporting, setting up, and packing down, is an important characteristic to consider when deciding which type of accommodation works best for you.

If you’re camping solo, you might not be so concerned with the time it takes to pitch and set up your outdoor living quarters. But if you’re headed on a group or family camping trip, you’ll probably be looking for an easy and quick solution.

Mobility of a Tent

Transporting a tent is generally straightforward due to its lightweight and compact design, making it ideal for those travelling to their camping location by car or even on foot.

Setting up a tent does require some effort, including assembling poles and pegs, but it becomes quicker with practice. Packing down is similarly efficient. 

We always recommend setting up and taking down your tent in the garden before each trip or having a few practices at it if it’s a new tent or you’ve never been camping before.

That way, you’ll figure out what goes where and see if there’s anything that needs to be repaired or replaced.

However, tent camping often necessitates additional gear, such as pots, pans, and sleeping bags, which can add to the overall load.

Shop Tent Parts & Add Ons

Mobility of a Campervan

Transporting a campervan requires simply driving to your destination, making it easy and convenient.

Unlike a tent, setting up involves minimal effort; parking in your chosen spot often suffices. Some campervans might need levelling or extending awnings, but these tasks are generally straightforward.

Packing down is equally hassle-free, involving securing internal items and retracting any extended parts. The campervan's self-contained nature means you travel with your amenities – like your bed, kitchen, and sometimes even a toilet – eliminating the need for additional camping gear most of the time.

That being said, you’ll still need to pack your daily essentials like clothing and toiletries, as well as bedding and cooking supplies.

Privacy & Security of Tents Vs Campervans

Another factor we think is pretty important is the privacy you want and the security that comes with either camping in a tent or a campervan.

Some of this will come from where you're planning on camping, but your accommodation also plays a significant role in your privacy and the security of your gear.

Privacy Given by Tents

Tents create a personal, enclosed space that separates campers from the outside environment, offering a sense of privacy in nature. 

While you may not have the solid walls of a campervan, a lot of people choose tent camping for the community and social aspects. However, keep in mind that the level of privacy can vary depending on the campsite and how close the tents are to each other.

We often use windbreaks if we want to create an additional layer of privacy around our tents. This not only blocks the wind, but also serves as a visual barrier between you and your neighbours.

We also recommend never leaving any items of value inside your tent if you’re going out for the day. While camping is relatively safe, it’s always better to be cautious and keep your belongings with you.

Consider investing in a large-capacity rucksack or backpack so you can keep your valuables with you when you leave the tent, like the Highlander Harrier 35L pack.

Shop Rucksacks & Backpacks

Privacy in a Campervan

Campervans excel in offering privacy and security. Solid walls and lockable doors provide campers with a secluded and safe living space.

The ability to lock the campervan not only secures your personal belongings but also ensures a private retreat from the outside world.

Initial Costs of a Campervan Vs a Tent

One of the biggest considerations when deciding between a campervan and a tent is the initial cost of purchasing your camping accommodation. Because of the nature of these two products, there's a considerable disparity between the initial costs.

Upfront Cost of a Campervan

The initial cost of purchasing a campervan can be quite substantial, often ranging from tens of thousands to over a hundred thousand pounds, depending on the make, model, and features.

A new, well-equipped campervan can cost around £30,000 to £70,000, while luxury models or those with custom fittings might exceed this range. Second-hand campervans offer a more affordable option, but prices still vary widely based on age, condition, and specifications.

This significant financial investment includes the vehicle itself, along with built-in facilities such as a kitchenette, sleeping area, and sometimes a bathroom.

Initial Costs of a Tent

Purchasing a tent is significantly more affordable than a campervan, with prices starting under £30 for basic models and reaching up to several hundred pounds for high-end, spacious tents designed for larger groups or extreme weather conditions.

However, it's important to factor in additional costs, such as sleeping bags, mats, and cooking equipment, which are essential for a comfortable camping experience.

We stock a selection of tents to suit any budget. These range from one-man tents under £50, like the Vango Soul 100 tent, to the Naturehike Nebula two-man 4-season tent, which costs over £200 – in other words, it’s much easier to find a tent within your budget than it is to find a campervan.

Shop now

Comfort & Quality in Campervans Vs Tents

The level of comfort you want from your trip is probably the second biggest deciding factor for many people. 

Getting a Good Night's Sleep in a Campervan

Sleeping in a campervan can significantly enhance the comfort of your camping experience. They’ll usually come equipped with built-in beds, often paired with high-quality mattresses.

This setup not only elevates you off the ground, away from the cold and uneven terrain, but also provides a level of comfort comparable to what you might experience at home.

The enclosed environment offers a controlled temperature, ensuring a cosy atmosphere regardless of the weather outside.

Getting Comfortable in a Tent

Sleeping in a tent brings you closer to nature and offers unique comfort despite its simplicity. With the right sleeping bag, pad, or air mattress, you can create a snug sleeping arrangement that cushions against the ground's hardness.

Tents allow you to choose your sleeping spot and often feature mesh doors, which allow for ample ventilation and a connection with the outdoor ambience.

In fact, the main reason why people go camping is to escape the hustle and bustle of everyday life and reconnect with nature. The sound of birds chirping, the rustling of leaves, and the fresh air all contribute to a peaceful night's sleep – with the addition of a good-quality sleeping bag and mat, of course!

Shop Sleeping Bags

The Practicality of Tents Vs Campervans

Of course, you want your camping trip to go smoothly, so considering the practicality of a tent vs. a campervan is essential to ensure you have the adventure you want.

How Practical is a Campervan?

Campervans provide a high level of convenience, allowing travellers to bring the comforts of home on the road. The in-built facilities, like a bed, kitchen, and sometimes a bathroom, enable spontaneous and flexible travel plans.

However, their size can be a drawback, limiting where you can park or camp, especially in more rugged or remote outdoor areas. Additionally, the initial and maintenance costs of a campervan are significantly higher compared to traditional tent camping.

Not only that, but you’ll have to think about where you’re going to keep the campervan when you’re not using it to roadtrip. You might have to make extra space on your driveway or garage. Or, if you don’t have the room at home, you may need to consider renting a storage space for it.

How Practical is a Tent?

Tents offer unparalleled practicality for those seeking an authentic camping experience. Their lightweight and compact design facilitates easy transportation, making them ideal for hikers and backpackers.

The weather will obviously affect your camping experience, but there are lots of tents that are designed to withstand wind and rain. In which case, a 4-season tent will be your best bet, as these are specifically designed for harsh weather conditions.

Plus, you won’t really have to worry about where you’re going to store it when you’re not using it. Tents can easily be folded and stored in your garage, the loft, or in a cupboard in your house.

Campsite Availability of Campervan Vs Tent

You need to be able to access campsites around the country unless you're camping in the wilderness or at the side of the road (which we don't recommend). 

While many campsites have pitches available for both campervans and tents, there might be some barriers to both types of camping.

Where Can You Camp in a Campervan?

Access for campervans to camping sites in England is generally good, with a wide selection of sites catering to vehicles of all sizes.

Many of these sites offer electric hook-up facilities, allowing campervan holidaymakers to connect their vehicles to an electricity supply for added comfort and convenience.

The availability of such amenities enhances the camping experience, ensuring that while away from home, one can still enjoy the modern conveniences.

However, it's important to note that these facilities might not always be available, which can affect your camping trip.

Where Can You Camp in a Tent?

Tent camping in the UK enjoys broad access to campsites equipped to accommodate tents of various sizes and types. These sites often include basic amenities like toilets, showers, and sometimes even communal kitchens.

Wild camping, although restricted in England and Wales, is freely permitted in most of Scotland, offering tent campers a unique opportunity to immerse themselves in the untouched beauty of the natural landscape, provided they follow the Scottish Outdoor Access Code.

This blend of options makes tent camping a more versatile choice for exploring the UK's outdoor spaces.

Final Thoughts: Which is Better, a Tent or a Campervan?

Choosing between a tent and a campervan for camping really depends on what you like and what's important to you. Both give you different but great ways to enjoy nature, so take the time to consider your choices and pick the one that fits the adventure you're looking for.

But if we had our final say, we'd have to go with tent camping. 

Not only does it provide a more authentic and immersive experience in nature, but it also allows for more flexibility in terms of location and terrain. Plus, there's something special about falling asleep under the stars and waking up to the sound of birds chirping!

If you want to get prepared and ready for your next camping trip, make sure you check out our range of camping gear from some of the best brands in the camping space. Whether it’s a new tent you’re after, cooking supplies, sleeping bags, or little gadgets to enhance your experience, we’ve got you covered.

And don't forget to pack some good company and a sense of adventure – those are the true essentials for an unforgettable camping trip!

Shop All Camping Equipment

FAQs

Is it Worth Having a Campervan?

Absolutely. A campervan is a great choice if it fits your style of camping. It's an investment in enriching experiences, exploring unseen places, and creating unforgettable memories, with a balance of comfort and adventure that's difficult to achieve with other forms of travel and accommodation.

What is the Lifespan of a Campervan?

The lifespan of a campervan can vary widely, typically ranging from 10 to 20 years, depending on its make, model, usage, and how well it is maintained. With diligent care and regular maintenance, some campervans can last even longer, offering many years of camping adventures.

What is the Lifespan of a Tent?

The lifespan of a tent can vary greatly, often lasting between 5 and 15 years, depending heavily on the material quality, frequency of use, and how well it is cared for. Proper cleaning and storage can significantly extend its life.

Is it Cold in a Campervan at Night?

The temperature in a campervan at night can vary. Proper insulation and heating options, such as built-in heaters or quality sleeping bags, can help you remain warm and comfortable. Without these, you might get cold, especially in cooler climates or during the winter months.

title: The Complete JustSupplies Camping First Aid Kit Checklist
author: Laurence
excerpt: Our complete camping first aid checklist includes everything you need to ensure your safety and well-being on your camping trips, no matter if you’re a first-time camper or a repeat adventurer. While safety might not be
html:
Our complete camping first aid checklist includes everything you need to ensure your safety and well-being on your camping trips, no matter if you’re a first-time camper or a repeat adventurer.

While safety might not be the first thing you think of when planning a camping trip, it should always be a top priority. Accidents and injuries can happen anywhere, anytime, so being as prepared as you can be is key.

We've taken our years of camping experience to give you a checklist to run through when packing your first aid kit for your next adventure. Here are our top first-aid essentials for any camping trip.

Our essential first-aid kit checklist to help you stay safe when camping
Basic first-aid pain relief
  • Paracetamol/Ibuprofen
  • Aspirin
  • Ice packs or cooling gels/spray
Basic first-aid wound care
  • Antiseptic wipes
  • Sterile gauze pads
  • Adhesive bandages (plasters)
  • Micropore tape
  • Antibacterial cream
  • Non-adhesive dressings
  • Tweezers
  • Scissors
Basic preventative measures
  • Sunscreen
  • Insect repellent
  • Hand sanitiser
  • Rehydration salts
  • Allergy medication
Auxillary wound essentials
  • Compression bandages
  • Sterile wound dressings
  • Elastic bandages
  • Butterfly stitches (steri-strips)
  • Triangular bandages
  • Wound closure strips
Auxillary medical supplies
  • Antihistamines
  • Anti-diarrhoeal medication
  • Oral rehydration solutions
  • Antacids
  • Antifungal cream
  • Hydrocortisone cream
  • Epinephrine auto-injector (if prescribed)
  • Prescription medications

Basic First Aid Kit Essentials

Any camping trip, even a weekend getaway or a festival trip, needs a basic first aid kit to handle common ailments and injuries that may occur. 

Here are our recommendations for your basic first aid kit to keep you and your campmates healthy.

Pain Relief

Pain relief is a critical component of any basic first aid kit, especially when you're out camping and far from medical facilities. The items focused on pain relief should include:

  • Paracetamol & ibuprofen: These over-the-counter medications are essential for reducing fever and alleviating mild to moderate pain, such as headaches, muscle aches, and menstrual cramps.
  • Aspirin: Useful not only for pain relief but also for its anti-inflammatory properties. However, it's important to note that aspirin is not recommended for individuals under 16 years of age without medical advice.
  • Ice packs or cooling gels: These are invaluable for immediate relief of sprains, strains, and swelling. We always take the IGLOO Ice Blocks with us and pop them in our freezer box. They're also good for keeping food cool, so they can double-up.

By including these items in your camping first aid kit, you can ensure you're prepared to manage common pains and aches that might occur during your outdoor adventures.

Wound Care

Effective wound care is fundamental to any first aid kit aimed at camping enthusiasts. Ensuring you have the tools to clean, disinfect, and protect wounds can prevent infections and speed up the healing process. 

Our recommended items include:

  • Antiseptic wipes: For cleaning wounds before dressing. It's essential to minimise infection risk.
  • Sterile gauze pads: To cover and protect a wound from infection. They are available in various sizes and can be cut to fit.
  • Adhesive bandages or plasters: These are available in a selection of sizes and shapes to cover and protect minor cuts and scrapes.
  • Micropore tape: For securing gauze pads in place without causing irritation to the skin.
  • Antibacterial ointment: To apply on a clean wound before dressing to reduce the risk of infection.
  • Non-adherent pads: Ideal for covering burns or abrasions, as they won’t stick to the wound.
  • Tweezers: For removing debris such as dirt, glass, or splinters from a wound.
  • Scissors: With rounded tips for cutting gauze or tape to the required size.
Shop First Aid Kits for Camping

Preventative Measures

Preventative measures are an often overlooked but vital component of any basic first aid kit, especially for camping. Incorporating items aimed at preventing injuries can significantly enhance safety during outdoor activities. 

Key items include:

  • Sunscreen: To protect the skin from harmful UV rays, reducing the risk of sunburn and sunstroke.
  • Insect repellent: To ward off insects and prevent bites which can lead to discomfort, allergic reactions, or even diseases.
  • Hand sanitiser: For maintaining hygiene, particularly before eating or after handling items that could be contaminated. This simple preventative measure can significantly reduce the risk of gastrointestinal infections.
  • Rehydration salts: To replenish fluids and electrolytes lost through sweat, helping to prevent dehydration, which can be a serious concern when camping, especially in hot weather.
  • Allergy medication: Including antihistamines for those who suffer from allergies. This is particularly important for outdoor enthusiasts who may be exposed to allergens like pollen, dust, or insect stings.

Include these preventative measures to reduce the likelihood of common camping ailments and ensure a safer, more enjoyable outdoor adventure.

Instead of building your own first aid kit, the Kombat UK Small First Aid Kit and the Highlander Forces Cadet First Aid Kit are both great options for ready-stocked kits.

Shop now

Auxillary First Aid Kit Equipment

In addition to your basic first-aid kit, you should include some heavy-duty first-aid essentials. These pieces of equipment should be considered essentials for off-grid trips that are far from medical attention.

Open Wound Essentials

In the case of more significant injuries, especially those involving open wounds, your camping first aid kit should be equipped with additional items aimed at managing these situations effectively. 

Being prepared for severe cuts, lacerations, or deep wounds is crucial when you're in remote areas. Here's what to include:

  • Compression bandages: These are vital for applying pressure to larger wounds or controlling bleeding before professional medical help can be accessed. They can also be used to support sprains or strains.
  • Sterile wound dressings: Larger than standard gauze pads, these dressings are designed for bigger wounds and provide a sterile barrier against infection.
  • Elastic bandages: For wrapping around sprains and strains, elastic bandages offer support and reduce movement, aiding in the healing process.
  • Butterfly stitches (steri-strips): For closing small to moderate lacerations that don't require professional suturing. They help to keep the wound edges together, promoting better healing.
  • Triangular bandages: Versatile and essential, these can be used as slings, for immobilisation, or to wrap around wounds as makeshift dressings.
  • Wound closure strips: Similar to butterfly stitches, these adhesive strips are used to close wounds and support optimal healing.

Medical First Aid Supplies

An extensive camping first aid kit should also include medications to manage a range of possible health issues that can occur in the wilderness.

  • Antihistamines: Essential for allergic reactions, including hay fever, insect bites, or unexpected allergies to plants. They can help reduce itching, swelling, and other allergic reaction symptoms.
  • Anti-diarrhoeal medication: This includes substances like loperamide. Given that changes in water and food can lead to gastrointestinal issues, anti-diarrheal medication can quickly address symptoms of diarrhoea.
  • Oral rehydration solutions: Critical for treating dehydration, which can result from diarrhoea, vomiting, or excessive sweating. These solutions help replenish lost fluids and salts.
  • Antacids: Useful for managing discomfort from heartburn or indigestion that can arise from campfire meals or unfamiliar foods.
  • Antifungal creams: For treating fungal infections, which are more common in damp environments, including athlete’s foot or ringworm.
  • Hydrocortisone cream: A 1% hydrocortisone cream can relieve skin irritations, rashes, insect bites, and minor skin inflammations, reducing discomfort.
  • Epinephrine auto-injector (if prescribed): For those with severe allergies, an Epinephrine auto-injector like an EpiPen can be life-saving in the event of anaphylactic reactions.
  • Prescription medications: If anyone in your camping group is on prescription medication, ensure a sufficient supply for the trip, plus a little extra in case of delays.

Must-Have First Aid Tools

For a well-prepared camping expedition, there are several first aid tools that are indispensable, and we always make sure to take on our own camping trips:

  • Safety pins: These are useful for securing bandages and slings in place. They can also come in handy for repairing gear in a pinch.
  • First aid manual: A compact, waterproof first aid manual can provide a quick reference for treating injuries and conditions when professional medical help is not immediately available.
  • Medical gloves: Disposable gloves are essential for protecting both the first aider and the patient from potential infection during wound care or any other direct contact.
  • Thermometer: A digital thermometer can help you monitor for fever, an important symptom of infection or illness.
  • Whistle: While not a medical tool per se, a whistle is a vital safety tool for signalling for help if you or someone in your group is injured and unable to return to camp.
  • Waterproof case or bag: Keeping your first aid supplies dry is essential, particularly in damp or rainy environments. A sturdy waterproof case or bag can protect your items from water damage.

Survival Kit Essential Items

A survival kit extends beyond medical emergencies, incorporating tools for shelter, sustenance, and safety.

Key items not found in a first aid kit include a fire starter (matches, lighter, or magnesium fire starter) for warmth and cooking, an emergency blanket to retain body heat, a multi-tool or knife for various tasks, water purification tablets to ensure safe drinking water, a compass for navigation, and non-perishable emergency food rations.

These items are crucial for survival in scenarios where you're waiting for rescue or need to move to safety.

For the ultimate ready-made survival kit, the BCB Elite Explorer's Kit is our favourite choice. It contains everything you need to treat minor injuries and survive away from your camp.

The BCB Ultimate Survival Kit is another comprehensive survival kit that can keep you going in adverse situations. It includes first aid tools and survival tools.

To find out more about what to include in a survival kit, read our blog about Survival Kit Essentials.

Final Thoughts: First Aid Kit Supplies for a Safe Camping Trip

Equipping yourself with a comprehensive first aid kit is crucial for any camping adventure. It ensures preparedness for both minor inconveniences and serious emergencies.

Always keep your first aid kit fully stocked between adventures so it's ready to go when you need it. Refer to this checklist to properly restock your kit.

We have a super range of first aid kits for camping that contain a variety of essential supplies. Whether you're a solo camper or heading out with a group, we have the perfect kit to fit your needs. You can never be over-prepared, after all!

Shop Camping First Aid

FAQs

Do I Need First Aid Training to Administer First Aid?

While not mandatory, a basic first aid course is highly recommended. It equips you with essential skills to effectively respond to common injuries and emergencies, potentially saving lives until professional medical help is available.

What First Aid Technique Should Be Used in Camping?

For common camping injuries, prioritise cleaning the wound with clean water, applying an antibacterial ointment, and covering it with a sterile dressing. For sprains, use the RICE method (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation). Always seek professional medical help for severe injuries.

What Are the 4 C's of First Aid?

The 4 C's of First Aid stand for Calm, Control, Comfort, and Call for help. They guide the initial response in an emergency: stay Calm, Control the situation, Comfort the injured person, and Call for professional medical help if the situation is beyond first aid treatment.

What Does ABCD Stand For in First Aid?

In first aid, ABCD stands for Airway, Breathing, Circulation, and Disability. Responders use this sequence of priorities to assess and manage a patient, ensuring that critical life-supporting functions are maintained and any immediate threats to life are addressed.

title: How to Choose the Right Size Gas Bottle for Your Campervan
author: Laurence
excerpt: Making sure you have enough gas for your campervan is essential for a comfortable and stress-free trip. But with so many different gas bottle sizes available, how do you know which one you need? From heating your camper’
html:
Making sure you have enough gas for your campervan is essential for a comfortable and stress-free trip. But with so many different gas bottle sizes available, how do you know which one you need?

From heating your camper’s water to powering your stove and fridge, gas is an essential resource for any campervan owner, and there are a lot of different types and sizes of gas bottles to choose from.

In this guide, we’ll walk you through everything you need to know about choosing the right size gas bottle for your campervan.

What Size Gas Bottle Do I Need for My Campervan?

Selecting the right size gas bottle for a campervan, caravan, or motorhome is super important in making sure you have enough gas to last your entire trip. 

The ideal size largely depends on the vehicle's size and the specific needs of your travel…

For Smaller Campervans

A 3.9kg propane gas bottle often does the job for short trips or where cooking is the primary use of gas.

This smaller size is lightweight, easy to handle, and convenient for tight storage spaces commonly found in compact campervans.

For Mid-Sized Campervans

These vehicles may use more gas, so they’ll need a bigger supply for heating, hot water, and cooking.

A 6kg gas bottle should give you enough gas for a few days to a week, depending on usage. Plus, this size bottle isn’t overly big, making it easier to store in a designated compartment or under your vehicle.

For Larger Campervans

A 13kg propane gas bottle might be required for a vehicle designed for long-haul travel or equipped with amenities that demand higher gas consumption, including central heating systems.

This larger size ensures a consistent gas supply over extended periods, reducing the frequency of replacements and offering peace of mind during lengthy trips.

Ultimately, the benefits of different bottle sizes range from enhanced portability and ease of storage with smaller bottles to greater autonomy and fewer concerns about running out of gas with larger sizes.

Selecting the appropriate size for your vehicle and travel needs is essential for a worry-free adventure.

What Type of Gas Do I Need for my Campervan?

Of course, it's not just the size that matters. There are different types of gas you can use in your campervan, and these gases have different properties that can affect their burn rate, making them last varying amounts of time regardless of their size.

Propane Gas Bottles

Propane gas is a popular choice for campervan gas bottles due to its excellent properties, which make it highly suited to the varying conditions encountered during travels.

One of propane's primary advantages is its ability to remain a gas at a much lower temperature than other gases like butane, making it an ideal fuel source in colder environments.

This characteristic ensures that your supply remains consistent and reliable – even in chillier conditions – providing a steady source of heat for cooking, heating, and hot water.

Also, propane burns cleanly, producing minimal soot and emissions. This clean combustion not only makes it an environmentally friendlier option but also reduces maintenance issues related to soot accumulation in appliances.

Overall, propane's properties make it an excellent choice for campervan enthusiasts seeking efficiency and reliability in their fuel source.

Butane Gas Bottles

Butane gas is another viable option for campervan gas bottles, offering advantages that can be particularly appealing for certain types of travellers.

One notable property of butane is its higher calorific value compared to propane, which means it can produce more heat from the same volume of gas.

This efficiency can be particularly advantageous in warmer climates where the gas's ability to remain liquid at higher temperatures does not pose a problem.

Butane is a cost-effective choice for campervan users who prioritise cooking and require a reliable heat source for longer periods without the need for frequent bottle replacements.

Also, butane typically burns slightly cleaner than propane, contributing to fewer emissions and a reduced environmental impact. Minimal soot production also means less maintenance for gas appliances.

However, it's critical to note that butane's performance is temperature-dependent; it remains liquid and struggles to vaporise at temperatures below freezing, which can limit its utility in colder climates.

How Long Does a Campervan Gas Bottle Last?

The duration of a gas bottle's life depends significantly on its size, frequency of use, and the type of appliance it powers.

Gas Bottle Size Usage Duration
3.9kg Cooking only A couple of days
6kg Cooking and occasional heating Several days to a week
13kg Heating, hot water, cooking Two weeks to a month

These estimates are broad, assuming moderate daily usage and actual durations can vary.

Assessing your trip's length and activities is essential to choosing the right size gas bottle. This will ensure you have a sufficient gas supply throughout your adventure without burdening yourself with unnecessary weight or space usage.

Camping 101: How Long Do Camping Gas Canisters Last?

What to Do With an Empty Gas Bottle

Disposing of an empty gas bottle requires careful consideration for safety and the environment.

Never throw it in general waste. Instead, return it to the supplier or a certified gas bottle retailer; many offer a return or exchange program for empty bottles.

Some locations also provide recycling services for these bottles. Always check the bottle for any specific disposal instructions from the manufacturer.

By responsibly handling empty gas bottles, you ensure environmental protection and adhere to safety regulations, making your camping experience both enjoyable and sustainable.

Find out more about disposing of your gas bottle from the British Compressed Gases Association (BCGA)

Is a Refillable Gas Bottle System Worth It?

Considering the environmental and economic aspects, investing in a refillable gas bottle system for your campervan can be remarkably worthwhile.

Refillable systems allow for more sustainable travel practices by reducing the need for disposable gas bottles, which in turn helps minimise waste and contribute to environmental conservation.

Economically, while the initial outlay for a refillable system may be higher than purchasing disposable bottles, the cost of refilling is generally lower than the cost of buying new bottles each time.

This means that over the lifetime of your campervan usage, the savings can be substantial.

Refillable systems also offer the convenience of topping up your gas supply at numerous refill stations, ensuring you're never far from a refill point during your travels.

However, it's essential to consider the availability of refill stations along your planned routes and whether the type of gas required by your system is readily accessible.

Gas Bottle Safety 101

A part of having a campervan gas bottle is making sure that it’s handled and maintained safely. This can involve checking the age of your gas bottle, ensuring it’s properly secured during travel, and regularly inspecting for any damage or wear. 

It's also crucial to know how to turn off the gas supply in case of an emergency, as well as how to properly handle and store the gas bottle when it's not in use.

Here are key safety tips to consider:

  • Regular checks: Periodically inspect gas bottles and connections for signs of wear, damage, or leaks. Use soapy water to check for leaks – bubbles will form if one exists.
  • Ventilation: Ensure adequate ventilation when using gas appliances inside the campervan to avoid the build-up of potentially harmful gases.
  • Emergency plan: Have an emergency plan in place. Know how to shut off the gas supply quickly and safely in case of a leak or fire.
  • Carbon monoxide detector: Install a carbon monoxide detector within the campervan to alert you to harmful gases produced by faulty gas appliances.
  • Professional installation and maintenance: Always have gas appliances and connections installed and serviced by a qualified technician.
  • Certified equipment: Use only certified gas bottles and equipment that meet the regulatory standards for safety and efficiency.

Summary: How to Choose the Right Size Campervan Gas Bottle

Whether you’re headed off on a short weekend getaway or a road trip round the country, you’ll want to make sure you have a sufficient supply of gas to power your camper. We’d recommend a 3.9kg bottle for small campervans, 6kg for mid-sized, and 13kg for large campervans. 

You should also think about how you’ll be using the gas. If you plan on using it for cooking, heating, and running your fridge, you may need a larger bottle. On the other hand, if you’re only using it for cooking, a smaller bottle could do you just fine.

For more camping tips and advice on making the most of your camper, head over to our blog!

FAQs

How Long Does a 6kg Gas Bottle Last in a Motorhome?

The duration of a 6kg gas bottle in a motorhome can vary, typically lasting from a few days to a week, depending on the level of cooking, heating, and hot water usage. For moderate use, expect it to last closer to a week.

What Gas Do I Need for My Campervan?

The type of gas you need for your campervan depends on your travel conditions and usage. Propane is ideal for colder weather due to its lower freezing point, whereas butane is better for warmer conditions and offers higher cooking efficiency.

Is it Safe to Have a Gas Bottle in a Campervan?

Yes, it is safe to have a gas bottle in a campervan if you follow proper safety protocols, such as using certified bottles, ensuring regular maintenance, proper installation, and adequate ventilation, along with having an emergency plan and carbon monoxide detector in place.

Do Campervans Need a Gas Certificate?

Yes, in many regions, campervans require a gas safety certificate issued by a qualified technician to ensure the gas system is installed and functioning safely. This certification is crucial for both legal compliance and peace of mind while travelling.

title: Wild Camping Rucksack Buying Guide: Best Size, Features, & Packing Tips
author: Laurence
excerpt: A rucksack will become your best friend while you’re wild camping, which is why it’s so important to choose one that’s not only the right size but also has the right features for your needs. Before you go ahead and buy a
html:
A rucksack will become your best friend while you’re wild camping, which is why it’s so important to choose one that’s not only the right size but also has the right features for your needs.

Before you go ahead and buy any old rucksack, take some time to consider what you’ll be using it for and what features are essential for your specific trip. 

Are you going to be hiking a long distance before you reach your pitching spot? What size tent are you bringing? What’s the bag made of? These are all important factors to consider when choosing the right rucksack for your wild camping adventures.

To make it easier for you to figure out which rucksack is the perfect fit for you, we’ve put together a buying guide that covers everything from size to features and even packing tips.

Rucksack Capacity Recommended Use Description
Under 10L Daypacking (short hikes, commutes) Small and lightweight, ideal for carrying essentials like water, snacks, and a light jacket.
10L - 30L Daypacking (longer hikes, day trips) It is comfortable for carrying more gear on day hikes, picnics, or day trips. It can fit additional layers, food, and basic emergency supplies.
30L - 50L Overnight backpacking It is ideal for weekend backpacking trips or overnight adventures. It provides enough space for sleeping gear, clothing, food, and other essentials.
50L+ Multi-day backpacking, expeditions It has a large capacity for extended backpacking trips or expeditions. It can accommodate a full backpacking kit, including a tent, sleeping bag, and additional supplies.

Rucksack Sizing Explained

Choosing the right rucksack size is crucial for your wild camping essentials because everything must fit on your back. 

The perfect rucksack size varies with your trip's length and the essential gear you need. 

A weekend trip might need a 30 to 50-litre rucksack for basic gear, food, and clothes. Longer trips or those needing extra equipment, like winter clothes or more camping gear, could require a 60 to 70-litre pack.

How is Rucksack Volume Measured?
Rucksack volume is measured in litres, representing the capacity of the main compartment and any additional pockets.
This measurement gives an idea of how much gear the rucksack can hold. For accuracy, manufacturers might fill the rucksack with small balls or beads and then empty these into a graduated container to determine the volume.
This standardised measurement allows you to compare different models and sizes effectively, ensuring you can find a rucksack that fits your needs.

What Are the Different Types of Rucksacks?

Rucksacks can be classified into several types, each designed to serve specific needs and purposes for the outdoor enthusiast.

  • Day Packs are small and light, perfect for short trips or day hikes. They hold between 10 to 30 litres, enough for water, food, a first-aid kit, and possibly a light jacket or raincoat.
  • Backpacks/Rucksacks are the larger, tougher versions of day packs, with capacities starting at 30 litres and going up to 70 litres or more. Designed for multi-day treks, they can carry camping gear, clothes, food, and sometimes specialised equipment.
  • Travel Backpacks combine the compactness of a day pack with the capacity and organisation of a larger backpack. They often have lockable zippers and compartments for electronics designed to meet airline carry-on requirements.
  • Hydration Packs are designed with a built-in water reservoir or bladder and a hose for easy drinking on the move. These packs vary in size but focus on keeping the wearer hydrated, especially during activities like running, cycling, or long hikes in warm climates.


Each type of rucksack serves a unique purpose, catering to different kinds of outdoor activities. Choosing the right one depends on the length of your trip, the items you need to carry, and how you prefer to travel.

Shop Rucksacks & Backpacks

Questions to Ask When Buying a Wild Camping Rucksack

When it comes to buying a rucksack for your wild camping trip, there are a few essential questions you should be asking to make sure you can effectively and safely carry all your gear to and from your camp set up.

How Much Can It Carry?

Understanding your rucksack's carrying capacity is pivotal for wild camping, as it directly impacts your comfort and mobility.

Carrying a rucksack that is too small could mean leaving essential items behind, compromising your experience and safety in the wilderness. 

Conversely, a rucksack that's too large may tempt you to pack unnecessary items, leading to excess weight that can cause physical strain over time, reduce your travel distance, and ultimately detract from the enjoyment of your adventure.

Knowing how much a rucksack can carry allows for efficient packing, ensuring you have all you need without the burden of overpacking.

Travelling Light: 5 Things You Don’t Need To Take On A Camping Trip

How Much Does it Weigh?

The weight of a rucksack, both empty and when fully packed, is a crucial consideration for any wild camping expedition.

An empty rucksack's weight is significant because it constitutes the base weight you'll be carrying, even before adding any gear or supplies.

A lightweight rucksack can considerably reduce your overall load, enhancing comfort and reducing fatigue over long distances.

When fully packed, the weight of the rucksack impacts your ability to manoeuvre easily and can affect your balance, especially on uneven terrain or during challenging climbs.

Also, carrying a rucksack that's too heavy may lead to unnecessary strain on your back, shoulders, and legs, potentially resulting in injuries that could cut your adventure short.

Is it Comfortable?

Comfort is paramount when selecting a rucksack for wild camping, especially when it's fully loaded. A rucksack that feels comfortable when empty can become a source of discomfort and strain once it's packed with gear, food, and equipment necessary for your adventure.

Look for rucksacks with adjustable chest and hip straps. These straps help distribute the weight more evenly across the body, reducing the burden on your shoulders and lower back.

Padding on the straps and back panel can also significantly enhance comfort, minimising the pressure points and the risk of chafing during long treks.

Ultimately, a comfortable rucksack makes it easier to cover longer distances, enjoy your surroundings, and fully engage with the wilderness experience.

Different Rucksack Features to Look For

Understanding the common features of rucksacks and their specific purposes can significantly impact your comfort and efficiency during an outdoor adventure. Here are some key features to look out for:

Feature Description Benefit
Adjustable Straps Shoulder straps, waist belts, and load adjuster straps Secure fit, minimises pack movement, distributes weight
Padded Back Panel Provides comfort and support Enhances comfort, improves ventilation
