Hiking Kit Non-Negotiables

This is the gear you should always take with you when hiking, no matter the length of your walk.

  • Hiking bag
  • Hiking footwear
  • Food
  • Water
  • Navigation tools and apps (if needed)
  • First-aid kit
  • Whistle
  • Personal items (phone, ID)

The specific item for each might change depending on the length of your walk, though. We’ve split out what you need for each length of hike below — click through to the length of hike you’re headed on, and you can jump straight to that section:

  • Hiking Gear Checklist for Short Hikes
  • Hiking Gear Checklist for Day-Long Hikes
  • Hiking Gear Checklist for Multi-Day Hikes

Hiking Gear Checklist for Short Hikes

Short hikes refer to those few hours spent trekking along the coast, up a mountain, or around a national park.

A few examples are Pen Y Fan, the Bright Angel Trail (Three-Mile Resthouse), and the Dubrovnik City Walls Walk. 

These only take a couple of hours to complete, so, as you can imagine, you won't need much specialist gear.

Here's exactly what we suggest for your short hikes.

Hiking Gear

As you won't be tackling Everest or spending your days trekking through the Alps, specialist gear isn't really required for short, few-hour hikes.

You, of course, need the basics, though, so here are our recommendations:

Backpack: This should be between 10 and 15L. You won't need much space, just enough room for water, extra layers, and snacks.



Trekking poles: These aren't just for long, tough hikes. If you need added stability or support for your joints, these poles can help relieve the pressure, helping you enjoy your hike.

Clothing

Our top recommendation? 

Always check the forecast!

Although the weather can be unpredictable, and you can't always rely on apps, you should still aim to give yourself an idea of the conditions to help you prepare what you're going to wear and bring as a spare.

Some mountainous walks will require you to prep for all types of weather, since the conditions up there are ever-changing.

Here are our recommendations to wear and pack as extra:

  • Moisture-wicking t-shirt: To help keep you dry while sweating.
  • Long-sleeve top: To help protect you from the cold or beating sunshine.
  • Quick-drying/waterproof shorts or trousers: Which one you choose depends on the weather forecast.
  • Lightweight fleece or jacket: If you're walking in the winter or anywhere that's cold, you'll need to bring something to keep warm. Ensure it's lightweight enough to carry, though, because you might not want to wear it all the time.
  • Lightweight waterproof: This is especially important if you're hiking in the UK. You never know when the next shower might be.
  • Winter hat/cap: If it's windy and cold, protect your ears and warmth with a woolly hat, and if it's hot and sunny, consider a cap to keep cool and shaded.

Footwear

Even on short hikes, you need to keep your feet and ankles happy. Here's what we recommend:

  • Hiking shoes: They should be comfortable, supportive, and offer good balance for the duration of your hike. If they're suited to multiple terrains — even better.
  • Moisture-wicking socks: Keep your feet nice and dry with some high-quality socks.

Food & Drink

You might not think you need snacks or drinks during a short hike, especially if you had a big breakfast, but that's incorrect, and you might become seriously dehydrated (and hangry) if you leave empty-handed.

To remain properly fuelled at all times, while giving yourself a good excuse for a well-deserved break, here's what you need:

  • Water bottles: You should try to bring at least half a litre for each hour you're walking, but this can be adjusted depending on the weather, your body type, sweat rate, and age.
  • Hiking snacks: This might be a trail mix, protein bars, nuts, or fruit. You don't need to go overboard, but take something for breaks and when you finish your walk.

Note: Don't leave rubbish anywhere, and always bring it home with you.

Health & Hygiene Products

Even though you're only heading out on a short hike, you still need to prepare for all eventualities.

Preparing for hiking is all about safety, so even if you think it's over the top (it's not), here are our top recommendations to bring on your hike:

  • First-aid kit: Bring a first-aid kit with you to deal with any injuries while you're walking.
  • Pain medication: Aspirin or Ibuprofen for any pain throughout the hike.
  • Antibacterial/antiseptic wipes: These should be in your first-aid kit, but it's worth checking. These wipes are useful for grazes, cuts, or general cleanliness.
  • Hand sanitiser: Self-explanatory.
  • Menstrual products: Don't forget feminine products, just in case.
  • Toilet paper: Most hikes have a toilet at the start or in a nearby car park, but it's best to bring your own to be safe.
  • Insect repellent: Don't let those annoying midges or mosquitoes ruin your hike.
  • SPF suncream and lip balm: It's always essential to be protected from the sun. UV rays can still be high with the sun behind clouds, so always apply an SPF where possible.

Optional & Extra Items

You won't always need this list of extras — it depends on the type of hike you're taking on — but we thought we'd list them here if you want to be extra prepared.

  • Knife or multi-tool:This might be useful if you run into any unexpected situations where you need to cut some wood, tighten something, open something, or in case of emergencies.



  • Gear-repair kit: If your bag or another piece of equipment becomes damaged, you might need some duct tape, ties, spare zips, or patches.
  • Flashlight or headlamp: This is necessary if you're hiking during the hours of darkness, but it might also be useful if you're prone to getting lost or think you might take longer to complete your hike.

Hiking Gear Checklist for Day-Long Hikes

Day hikes are a little different because you'll be tackling sometimes tough terrain for most of the day.

Single-day hikes, from the Seven Sisters to the Zion Narrows and the Aletsch Glacier Trail, are extremely rewarding, but require a bit more preparation.

Although the basic gear will stay the same, there are a few additions you should be aware of. Let's get into it.

Hiking Gear

Like we said, you need to ramp it up a bit in terms of hiking gear you'll bring on a half or full day hike, so here is what we recommend:

  • Backpack: This should be between 20L and 35L. You don't need much extra space, but you will need to account for more snacks, more water, and extra clothing if necessary.
  • Trekking poles: These are more of a non-negotiable for long hikes like these. Your knees and other joints will benefit from having some extra pressure relieved. You're also likely to encounter different terrains, and poles can help with your stability here.
  • Hydration Pack: If you're hiking for a full day, consider a hydration pack. This is a backpack containing a water reservoir (bladder) connected to a hose with a bite valve.
  • Flashlight or headlamp: On a full-day hike, whether in the morning or in the evening, you'll likely be hiking through some hours of darkness. It's best to bring some kind of light source, and it's especially useful if you find yourself in an emergency situation.

Clothing

You'll need more or less the same clothing for a single-day hike as you would for a hike only a few hours long.

However, it's likely, depending on where your hike is, that it'll be more gruelling and you'll experience more weather conditions, meaning you'll need more clothing options.

Here's what we recommend you wear and pack as spare or extra:

  • Moisture-wicking t-shirt: To help keep you dry while sweating.
  • Long-sleeve top: To help protect you from the cold or beating sunshine.
  • Quick-drying/waterproof shorts or trousers: Which one you choose depends on the weather forecast.
  • Lightweight fleece or jacket: If you're walking in the winter or anywhere that's cold, you'll need to bring something to keep warm. Ensure it's lightweight enough to carry, though, because you might not want to wear it all the time.
  • Lightweight waterproof: This is especially important if you're hiking in the UK. You never know when the next shower might be.
  • Winter hat/summer cap: If it's windy and cold, protect your ears and warmth with a woolly hat, and if it's hot and sunny, consider a cap to keep cool and shaded.
  • Moisture-wicking underwear: To help prevent discomfort and irritation while you sweat.
  • Spare layers: On a full-day hike, you never know what you might encounter, so it's best to come prepared as the temperature changes and the weather remains unpredictable.
  • Winter items: Depending on where your hike is located, you might want to consider bringing some gloves and a scarf, too.

Footwear

On a single-day hike, you need to be doubly sure your feet are comfortable in the footwear you choose. It's also essential that you break your shoes in before walking long distances in them. This will prevent discomfort and blisters that can hinder your walk.

Long and relatively challenging terrain calls for hiking boots that are ideally waterproof and supportive. Of course, they should also be well-fitting and broken in.

You’ll also want some moisture-wicking socks to keep your feet nice and dry.

Food & Drink

It's likely you'll be crossing a few, maybe even all the meal times during your day hike, which is why you need your pack to reflect that.

It's important to refuel yourself throughout the hike; otherwise, your energy levels will decrease, and you'll stop enjoying the experience.

Here's what we recommend taking with you: 

  • Water: As we said earlier, it's recommended that you bring half a litre for every hour you're hiking, but if you're on a 10-hour hike, this may not be possible. That's why we recommend bringing a water filter or a water purification method so you can fill up in rivers and streams if necessary.
  • Hiking snacks: This might be a trail mix, protein bars, nuts, or fruit. You don't need to go overboard, but take something for breaks and when you finish your walk.
  • Meals: You won't be able to cook yourself a hearty, energising meal while hiking through mealtimes, but you can bring one. Consider a packed lunch or even proper dehydrated meals, like those from Firepot or Blaband, which will give you all the nutrients you need to refuel.



  • Extra food: For emergency purposes, bring an extra day's worth of food so you're prepared for all eventualities.
  • Fire starter: Bring some matches or a lighter, so you can safely make a fire if you need to boil some water or find yourself in an emergency situation.

Health & Hygiene Products

Your health and hygiene products will largely stay the same, with a couple of important additions.

Since day hikes are longer, they can sometimes be more dangerous, so it's important to prepare for various situations.

Plus, since you're walking longer, you might want a few extras to make the hike a little more comfortable. Here’s what we suggest:

  • First-aid kit
  • Pain medication
  • Blister treatments
  • Antibacterial/antiseptic wipes
  • Menstrual products
  • Toilet paper: You'll need to relieve yourself in the great outdoors, because it's unlikely you'll come across many toilets. Read The British Mountaineering Council's guide to toileting in the wild to find out more if you're hiking in the UK.
  • Insect repellent
  • SPF suncream and lip balm
  • Deodorant: Day hikes are sweaty work, and if you don't want your hiking buddy to turn their nose up at you, we suggest bringing some deodorant.

Optional & Extra Items

If you're planning a full-day hike, you should add a few optional and extra items to the list. You won't always need them, but it's best to know what they are so you can judge.

Here are our recommendations:

  • Knife or multi-tool: This might be useful if you run into any unexpected situations where you need to cut some wood, tighten something, open something, or in case of emergencies.
  • Gear-repair kit: If your bag or another piece of equipment becomes damaged, you might need some duct tape, ties, spare zips, or patches.
  • Power bank and charging cable: If you're one to do a digital detox while on a hike, you might not need this. If you love taking pictures and using your phone as a trail map, you'll probably need to charge it at some point.
  • Emergency shelter: Depending on your hiking experience and length of your hike, you can judge whether you need this. It can be useful if you lose your way and the night is drawing in.
  • GPS: This might be necessary if you're going on a long hike and don't want to rely on your mobile phone.

Hiking Gear Checklist for Multi-Day Hikes

Multi-day hikes are a whole different ball game. Packing for a few days in one backpack can be difficult, but of course, you will need a lot more equipment than normal, so you need to find a way to make it work.

It's not just about bringing enough gear to get you through the day, but also about bringing equipment that makes your overnight stay comfortable and safe.

So, if you're taking on the Anapurna Circuit, heading up Kilimanjaro, or the South West Coastal Path Walk, here's your hiking kit list.

Note: The amount of equipment, including clothes, food, and hygiene products, will vary depending on the length of your hike.

Hiking Gear

For a multi-day hike, whether that be 3 days or 10, you'll need a lot more equipment than your regular day hikes, and that's because you need to account for your sleeping equipment.

To ensure you've got everything you need, here are our suggestions:

  • Backpack with a capacity between 50L and 70L. This will account for your solo tent, sleeping bag, and extra clothes you'll need to bring.
  • Trekking poles
  • Flashlight or headlamp: On a multi-day hike, whether in the morning or in the evening, you'll likely be hiking through some hours of darkness. It's best to bring some kind of light source, and it's especially useful if you find yourself in an emergency situation.
  • Tent: If you have arranged accommodation, you won't need a tent (unless you want it for emergency situations), but if not, you'll need one for your overnight stays. We have a selection of different-sized tents below if you're looking for one.
  • Sleeping bag: Bring one that's the appropriate temperature rating for the climate you're hiking in.
  • Sleeping mat: For added comfort and insulation in cold locations.

Clothing

Your clothing won't change much from what you'd wear/bring on a day hike, but you'll obviously need a lot more, plus overnight wear.

Here's what we suggest:

  • Moisture-wicking t-shirt
  • Long-sleeve top
  • Quick-drying/waterproof shorts or trousers
  • Lightweight fleece or jacket
  • Lightweight waterproof
  • Winter hat or a summer cap
  • Moisture-wicking underwear
  • Thermal layers for overnight
  • Spare clothes: If you're hiking for a few days, you'll need to change out of your dirty clothes into new ones.
  • Winter items: You might want to consider bringing gloves, a scarf, thermal wear, and more, especially if you're hiking in sub-zero temperatures.

Footwear

Footwear is no different to single-day hikes — you still need that extra comfort, support, and your shoes should be broken in.

You’ll want a really sturdy and supportive pair of hiking boots. Long and challenging terrain calls for hiking boots that are ideally waterproof and supportive. Of course, they should also be well-fitting and broken in.

Hiking socks with cushioning will also be key, as they’ll provide additional comfort.

Food & Drink

Your food and drink needs will differ depending on whether you're staying in hotels, designated campsites, or camping wild on your trek.

But for the purposes of this article, we'll explain what you'd need if you were staying in a tent, wild camping style, during your hike.

  • Water: No, you don't need to bring all the water you'll need for a 7-day hike with you. Bring a few water bottles, even a hydration pack if necessary, and fill them up each day. Water purification methods and filters are essential if you don't know where you'll next get the chance to fill up.
  • Hiking snacks: This might be a trail mix, protein bars, nuts, or fruit that won't spoil after a few days in your bag. Be sure to bring enough with you — taking breaks to refuel will feel luxurious.
  • Meals: You won't be able to cook yourself a hearty, energising meal while hiking through mealtimes, but you can bring one. Bring enough dehydrated meals, like those from Summit To Eat or Blaband, for mealtimes, which will give you all the nutrients you need to refuel.
  • Extra food: For emergency purposes, bring an extra few days' worth of food so you're prepared for all eventualities.
  • Cookware: To ensure you're not carrying too much, aim to bring a lightweight stove or small boiling system, a spork, a cup, and any cookware you may need to prepare the meals you're planning on bringing. Avoid overpacking, because you don't want to add too much extra weight.

Health & Hygiene Products

To stay clean and aid with any injuries, you'll need to bring quite an extensive product and equipment list during your hike.

Building upon our single-day hike checklist, here's what we recommend for multi-day hikes:

  • First-aid kit & pain medication
  • Blister treatments
  • Antibacterial wipes
  • Menstrual products
  • Toilet paper
  • Bug repellent
  • SPF suncream
  • Deodorant
  • Toiletries: If you're hiking for multiple days, you'll need soap, hair-washing products, and toothpaste. To save space and weight, be sure to take mini versions of these items.
  • Towel: A quick-dry towel is essential for showering during your hike.

You can bring a few extra items on your trip that would make the hike more comfortable or perhaps safer, but these aren't always essential:

  • Knife or multi-tools
  • Gear-repair kit
  • Power bank and charging cable
  • GPS
  • Lightweight camp seat: After a day's walking, you might want something comfortable to sit on if you want to hang out with your fellow hikers.
  • Dry bags or packing cubes: If you want to organise your bag because you have a lot of baggage, you can consider packing aids.
  • Documentation: Some national parks and protected areas require permits. You may also want to bring a credit card, cash, or ID in case of emergencies.

How to Pack a Backpack for Hiking

Hiking packing is all about balance and taking what you need without overloading your bag.

The general rule is to carry no more than 10% of your body weight on day hikes and 20% on multi-day hikes, but this isn't a requirement, and it will differ depending on fitness levels, experience, etc.

Heavier items, bulky items, like cooking gear and your sleeping bag, should be kept close to your back and centred to help with stability.

Lighter things like spare clothes and chargers can go around the outside of the bag, essentially anywhere you can squeeze them in.

Essentials, such as phones, snacks, a waterproof jacket, etc., should be packed nearer the top or in side pockets for easy access along the trail.

If you're hiking somewhere snowy or notoriously wet, we suggest packing your kit in dry bags or liners, not only to help organise it, but also to keep it protected from the weather.

Lastly, your tent. If space allows, you can place this inside your bag with pegs and poles at either side to distribute the weight. If not, you can securely strap it to the outside of your bag.

Conclusion: Be Prepared No Matter How Short or Long Your Hike is

Hopefully, you should now have your hiking checklist at the ready, whether you're heading out on a short, single-day, or multi-day hike.

If you need any more help and advice on hiking, head to our blog, where you'll find tons of expert information to help you through the trek.

And if you're looking for any gear, browse through our website and find everything you need for a professional, safe, and comfortable hike, no matter the location.

Enjoy your next hike, we hope it's a good one!

title: The Ultimate Dolomites Hiking Guide
author: Laurence Kay
excerpt: The Dolomites are quickly becoming one of the most popular hiking destinations, and it's not surprising — the scenery is mesmerising. But if this is your first time visiting the region, you'll need to prepare! As one of
html:
The Dolomites are quickly becoming one of the most popular hiking destinations, and it's not surprising — the scenery is mesmerising. But if this is your first time visiting the region, you'll need to prepare!

As one of the more family-friendly hiking holidays, with a couple of more challenging routes on offer, the Dolomites is the perfect location, but you already knew that.

What you need to know are the details. 

In this guide, we'll take you through everything you need to know before heading to Italy, including accommodation, the best walks, information on pricing, and much, much more.

So, let's get you prepared for taking on the Dolomites. Keep reading for all the details, or jump to the different sections if you're searching for something specific!

Here's what we cover:

  • FAQs About Hiking the Dolomites
  • Accommodation in the Dolomites
  • Top 5 Best Hikes in the Dolomites
  • A Typical 7-Day Dolomites Itinerary
  • The Dolomites Essential Packing List

FAQs About Hiking the Dolomites

Hiking the Dolomites isn't something you can just wake up and do one day (as much as we wish it was). There has to be a certain level of planning involved to get your feet off the ground and into the Italian region.

So, before you embark on your Alpine adventure (yes, technically it is the Alps), we've rounded up some of the most commonly asked questions so you can be better prepared for your hiking trip.

Are the Dolomites Part of the Alps?

Ah, our favourite questions. Despite the confusion, the Dolomites are in fact part of the Alps. 

They actually form part of the Southern Limestone Alps in the far corner of northeast Italy.

Despite being (technically) the Alps, the Dolomites are a totally unique mountain range and worth visiting even if you've been to other parts of the Alps.

The Dolomites are rapidly growing in popularity, with many avid hikers discovering the beauty on platforms like TikTok and Instagram.

Some say they're a great (and sometimes cheaper) alternative to visiting the Swiss Alps.

@natyexplora autumn in the dolomites is MAGICAL 🥹💘 #lagodibraies #dolomites #italy ♬ original sound - SedyyFilms

Credit: @jessionaquest on TikTok.com

When is the Best Time to Visit the Dolomites?

The best time to visit the Dolomites is during the summer months (June-August), when the weather is warmer and more suitable for outdoor activities. 

However, this is also peak tourist season, so expect crowds and higher prices.

If you prefer a quieter experience, consider visiting in the shoulder seasons of spring (April-May) or autumn (September-October).

The winter months are also popular for skiing and snow sports, but be prepared for colder temperatures. You should also bear in mind that some facilities may not be open during this time of year.

It just depends on the kind of experience you're after!

Do You Need a Guide to Hike the Dolomites?

This totally depends on your experience, level, familiarity with the region, and the types of trails you plan to tackle.

Many routes in the Dolomites can be explored independently by experienced hikers who are comfortable navigating marked trails and know basic map reading. 

The region offers well-maintained and signposted paths, making it accessible for those who prefer to plan their own adventure.

But, if you're more of a beginner or want to tackle more challenging routes, hiring a guide or going on an organised tour can enhance your experience.

Local guides provide invaluable insights about the terrain, weather, and hidden gems off the beaten path. They can also ensure your safety by assessing risks and adapting routes according to conditions.

Guided hikes can offer a more enriching experience, where you can meet new people and gain insight into history and culture. 

Equally, if you enjoy your own peace and quiet and like the freedom of roaming by yourself, an independent hike is possible.

How Expensive is it to Hike in the Dolomites?

The cost of hiking the Dolomites greatly varies depending on your preferences and style of travel.

For budget-conscious hikers, there are plenty of well-marked trails that require no guided tours or permits. But you'll likely still need accommodation, meals, and other extras.

For those willing to spend a little more, you can choose from more luxurious accommodations, hire tour guides, and take on more challenging hikes that may require special permits and equipment.

To give you a bit more of an idea, according to The Hiking Club, an 8-day hike on the Alta Via 1 trail costs 700 Euros. This is based on 2023 figures and includes 7 nights of shared accommodation in mountain huts, 7 days of breakfast and lunch at the accommodation, and 8 days of picnic lunches and snacks.

This doesn't include the flights to and from Italy, your hiking equipment, travel insurance, tour guides, and more.

 

So, as you can see, this isn't a budget trip, but there are ways to cut costs, like researching the cheapest accommodations, sharing accommodations, researching different hikes, and shortening the number of days you wish to hike.

Are there Any Restrictions or Permits Needed for Hiking the Dolomites?

For the most part, hiking in the Dolomites doesn't require any special permits or restrictions.

However, certain trails, especially those in national parks or protected areas, like the Ampezzo Dolomites Natural Park, might have specific guidelines to follow, such as staying on designated paths or observing seasonal closures to protect wildlife and plant life.

Some roads to trails or huts (especially the more famous ones, like Tre Cime) may also require booking and a fee for car access.

It’s also important to note that some routes via ferrata, as they're more technically demanding, may require specialised climbing equipment and experience.

Booking accommodation in advance during peak tourist seasons is highly recommended to secure a spot in popular mountain huts, too. You don't want to miss out on the one you've been eyeing.

Always check the local regulations for the area you plan to hike, and ensure you’re fully prepared for all eventualities.

Can You Hike the Dolomites as a Beginner?

Definitely! 

Beginners can hike the Dolomites, as there are some easy trails that don't require specialist knowledge, especially if you're planning on going on a tour or hiring a guide.

We recommend focusing on routes that are labelled easy or moderate, such as those around Alpe di Siusi or Lake Braies. These routes have less challenging terrain, but equally rewarding scenery.

Ensure you wear appropriate footwear, carry adequate water, and pack essentials. 




How Do You Get to the Dolomites from the UK?

Reaching the Dolomites from the UK is pretty easy, with several travel options available.

The quickest way is to fly to a nearby airport, such as Venice, Verona, or Innsbruck, which all offer good connections to the region and are easy to reach from the UK.

From the airport, you can hire a car or use public transportation to reach your destination in the Dolomites.

Alternatively, for those who prefer a more scenic (and eco-friendly) route, taking a combination of trains through France, Germany, or Switzerland is an excellent option, offering stunning views along the way. 

You can turn the trip into a bit of interrailing!

Is There Food Available in the Dolomites?

You can access food fairly easily when hiking the Dolomites, especially if you stick to popular routes.

Restaurants and mountain huts, known as rifugios, offer warm and welcoming spots to enjoy authentic meals after a day of exploring. But bear in mind, some may not be open depending on the season.

It's recommended to take some easily accessible hiking snacks with you, though. Hiking is hungry work, and you don't want a rumbling stomach when you're trying to enjoy breathtaking views!

Is Drinking Water Available When Hiking the Dolomites?

Yes, drinking water is generally available when hiking in the Dolomites, but it’s always wise to plan ahead. Many rifugios have water available, either for free or for a small fee, which can be a reliable source during your trek.

Additionally, natural water sources like streams and springs are common in the Dolomites, but you'll, of course, need to bring some bottles with you.

However, it’s essential to be cautious and ensure the water is safe to drink. Carrying a water filter, purification tablets, or a reusable bottle with a built-in filter can give you peace of mind.

Are there Any Hikes in the Dolomites Suitable for Children?

Absolutely! The Dolomites offer several family-friendly trails that are perfect for children. Many of these hikes are shorter and feature gentle gradients, making them ideal for younger hikers.

For example, the Resciesa Plateau near Ortisei is a popular choice, providing stunning views with minimal effort. 

Another great option is the Alpe di Siusi, Europe’s largest high-altitude meadow, where children can enjoy wide-open spaces and even spot cows or horses grazing along the way.

When planning a hike with kids, it’s always a good idea to factor in plenty of breaks and pack snacks to keep them motivated and energised.

With the right preparation, hiking in the Dolomites can be a great adventure for the whole family!

Accommodation in the Dolomites

You have several options depending on how remote you are, how rugged you want the experience, and how much comfort you want.

The most common type of accommodation people associate with the Dolomites is rifugios. These are mountain huts located along the hiking trails, where you can spend the night and enjoy a warm meal.

Here are some details of the types of accommodation you might find in the Dolomites. Please note that the prices listed may not be the exact price you'll pay; it's just to give you an indication.

Type of Accommodation Facilities/Comfort Where You’ll Find them Price
Rifugios (Mountain Huts):

Rustic huts in the mountains.

One of the most common types of accommodation in the Dolomites.		 Dorm-style rooms or mixed dorms. Some are private or smaller rooms, but most have shared bathrooms and common areas. You'll usually get your meals here, too, but it's likely to be breakfast and dinner. Along popular trails, high passes, and scenic ridgelines. 60-90 Euros per night (this includes your meals).
Alpine Refuges with More Comfort:

A more comfortable rifugio, sometimes with private rooms, better showers, nicer views, and finer dining.

These are for you if you have more room in the budget, but still want to experience a classic rifugio.		 These rifugios usually have more private rooms with a little more luxury. They are still relatively simple compared to hotels, but offer more comfort than a traditional rifugio. Near key trails, some scenic peaks, and some popular routes. 100-150 Euros per night.
Hotels, Guest Houses, and B&Bs:

These types of accommodation are less rustic if you're looking to be a bit more comfortable on your trip.

There is a wide variety located in the Dolomites, ranging from budget to luxury. 		Private rooms and ensuite bathrooms are typical. Some hotels are likely to have full services, like a spa, a gym, and a bar. You're more likely to find these in towns or valleys, rather than on the high trails. They might not be suitable if you're planning on doing multi-day treks. 100-200+ Euros per night.
Apartments/Self-Catering:

Flats or chalets with a kitchen, bathroom, living area, and bedrooms.

These are good for longer stays or those travelling in larger groups. 		This type of accommodation offers more space and privacy. You can also cook your own meals, which might help you save money if you're on a budget. You'll find these in the local villages at the bottom of valleys, and less in the high areas of the Dolomites. 50-150+ Euros per night.

The main season for the rifugios is late June to late September. Outside of this period, many will close or offer a very limited service.

For popular trails, huts can fill up early, so we recommend booking 3-5 months in advance, sometimes more if you want to stay in a specific one.

Top 5 Best Hikes in the Dolomites

The Dolomites aren't short of breathtaking hikes, stunning plant life, and calming wildlife, so advertising this list as 'the best' isn't totally accurate. You could argue they all are.

However, there are hikes that are more popular and stand out for various reasons, so with that in mind, here are our top 5 favourite hikes.

Note: Since most trails in the Dolomites are numbered and signposted, it's difficult to go wrong, even if you're not an experienced hiker. Always stick to the path where you can and do your research before heading out there.

 

#1 Tre Cime di Lavaredo Circuit

Distance: 10km

Time: 3-4 hours

Difficulty: Easy-Moderate

Location: Sexten Dolomites, border of Tyrol and Belluno

This circular trail is probably one you've already heard of if you're planning a trip to the Dolomites, and for good reason.

The Tre Cime di Lavaredo circuit is an extremely popular hike, and that's down to its unforgettable mountainous beauty. 

Free from anything technical, this hike is ideal if you're on a family getaway, or if you fancy something a bit lighter while you're visiting the region.

As this is such a popular circular hike, the car park can fill up pretty quickly, and there is a fee. To avoid disappointment, we recommend making car park reservations before you arrive, especially if you're going during the high season.

However, we do suggest heading there in the shoulder seasons to avoid large crowds and enjoy a more peaceful hike to take in the views of the spiked mountains.

#2 Seceda Ridgeline Hike

Distance: 7.7km

Time: 3-3.5 hours

Difficulty: Moderate

Location: Val Gardena Valley

@g_coooper Bro knew a spot… #dolomites #fyp #seceda ♬ Feel Good Inc. - Gorillaz & De La Soul

Credit: @g_coooper on TikTok.com

Situated in the Val Gardena Valley, the Seceda Ridgeline is a dramatic mountain edge in the Dolomites, known for its jagged edges and panoramic views into the distance.

There are various routes you can take up to the ridgeline, some even requiring ferratas. Today, we're talking about the Seceda – Rifugio Firenze – Col Raiser route.

You'll get to hike through valleys, forests, and, of course, experience the iconic view of the Odle/Geisler peaks from the top.

You just need a cable car to the top of Seceda from Ortisei, stop for the view, and follow the trail down to Rifugio Firenze. You'll then meander down to the Col Raiser cable car station, which will take you down to Selva.

You can either make your way back to your accommodation from here, or if you want to head back to where you started the hike (in Ortisei), you can get a bus or a taxi. 

Since this hike is essentially all downhill (hooray for the calves!), you'll likely need some hiking poles to take the pressure off your knees (boo for the joints).

Summer is the perfect time to tackle this hike, so you encounter less snow and ice, making it a pleasant, even relaxing walk under the warm rays.

You can either make your way back down via the same route or, if you like a challenge and fancy a more technical climb, some options use the lake as the starting point.

Hiking along some of the highest points in the Dolomites, this longer, more strenuous hike takes its toll, but the jaw-dropping views are more than worth it.

You can choose to use the cable cars for part of the hike if you don't feel up to it (we're not judging!), or you can take on the whole thing on foot.

This hike offers sweeping alpine vistas, unique rock formations, vast open landscapes of meadows, and an up-close look at the geology that defines the Dolomites.

If you're looking for something to fill the whole day, while being a rewarding hike without anything technical, this is the one for you.

Remember, you'll need to pay a fee for the cable car if you choose to use one, so check out the options and choose a pass that's right for you and your group.

Distance: 9.6km

The Cinque Torri and Rifugio Nuvolau hike is one of the best moderate day hikes in the Dolomites.

The loop combines epic alpine views, WWI history, and two of the most famous mountain landmarks, the iconic rock towers, and the Rifugio Nuvolau, one of the oldest and highest huts in the Dolomites.

For this hike, you can either take the chair lift from Bai de Dones to make the hike a little shorter and more suitable for families and dogs, or start from Passo Giau if you're a stronger hiker.

You'll experience the amazing rock formations with your own eyes, and even have a glimpse into the not-so-distant WW1 past at the open-air museum. Here, you'll find restored trenches and shelters.

The ridge is completely exposed, so be sure to check the weather and pack appropriately, but most importantly, be sure you’re a confident hiker who doesn’t mind heights. 

A Typical 7-Day Dolomites Itinerary

The Dolomites are vast, and there are hundreds of ways visitors like to spend their time in the stunning Italian region. But if you haven't yet figured out your itinerary, and would like some inspiration, we've created an example below.

It includes various popular hikes, including some we've talked about above, as well as where you'll stay for a 7-day trip.

Please note that if you book with a tour operator, they'll likely have their own itinerary to go off. You can always choose your operator based on the places you'd like to visit, or ask your guide to take you on a detour.

Here's a 7-day Dolomites itinerary for planning your self-guided trip to make the most of your visit. We've decided to show you a typical summer itinerary (June-early October):

Day 1: Arrive in Ortisei (Val Gardena)

Arriving at your destination after a long day(s) of travelling calls for light walks and relaxation before taking on any big hikes.

We recommend staying in Ortisei for two nights to settle in and explore the charming alpine town.

You can always walk 5km to Resciesa (or take the funicular) for a warm-up hike to stretch your legs and see some gorgeous sunsets.

The Val Gardena Card or the Dolomiti Supersummer Pass are recommended if you think you'll be using the cable cars and lifts throughout your trip.

Day 2: Seceda Ridgeline to Col Raiser via Rifugio Firenze

While you're in Ortisei, it would be a shame to miss the Seceda Ridgeline, so that is exactly where you're going to visit on day two.

You can find out more about this hike above, but trust us, it's not one to miss.

Enjoy the famous Odle/Geisler ridgeline view, descend via meadows to Rifugio Firenze, then to Col Raiser lift. You can then return to Ortisei by bus or taxi.

Day 3: Puez–Odle Altopiano Hike

Day three is all about getting your steps in, so today you'll hike along some of the highest points in the Dolomites.

There are options to use cable cars along the way, but since you're on a hiking holiday, we figured you'll probably take the whole 17km on foot. You can find more information on this hike above.

When you've returned to your accommodation, have some R&R and take a bus or taxi to the next location, Cortina, where you'll stay for four nights.

Day 4: Lago di Sorapis via Passo Tre Croci

Spend the day hiking through forests and mountainous landscapes to a turquoise glacial lake — the classic Dolomites landscape.

You can find out more about the specific hike above, but it is one of the most popular in the whole of the Dolomites, so well worth a mention.

It's best to avoid this on snowy/icy days due to the nature of the trail. If the weather turns, perhaps swap some days around.

Day 5: Cinque Torri & Rifugio Nuvolau Loop

Take the Cinque Torri chairlift or hike from Passo Giau to visit the fascinating WWI open-air museum, and hike up to Rifugio Nuvolau. A tough but rewarding hike.

If you want, you can even do this as an overnight hike if you want to stay in the traditional accommodation of the Dolomites - a rifugio.

You can then return via a different trail if you're feeling energised, or by chairlift if you need to rest those legs.

As this is one of the most photogenic ridges in the Dolomites, be sure to save some time for taking photos when you're up there and along the way. You'll regret not documenting the moment.

Day 6: Tre Cime di Lavaredo Loop

We have more information about this above, but as your penultimate day, you have to squeeze this hike in somewhere.

Perhaps the most famous in the Dolomites, this hike around the peaks is exactly what you think of when the Dolomites are mentioned.

Take in all the hike has to offer, and spend the evening relaxing, as it's (sadly) your final night in the region.

Day 7: Depart or Short Hike

If you have time and want to make the most of your last day, take an easy walk to Lago di Braies, Lago Federa , or Tofana viewpoint.

Afterwards, head to Venice, Verona, or Innsbruck to return to the UK. We recommend adding an extra night to your stay to explore these amazing cities. It's not a hiking holiday without some proper R&R at the end!

Hiking the Pyrenees should be on everyone's bucket list. Not just for the dramatic landscape, but because (strangely) it's one of the least-crowded mountain ranges, especially compared with the Alps. 

If you're looking for your next walking holiday, welcome to our guide to the Pyrenees!

The Pyrenees offer a diverse, unique destination with year-round activities and a fantastic hiking culture.

Think vast, crystal clear lakes, jagged mountains creating mesmerising backdrops, beautiful waterfalls, and much, much more. But what are the things you actually need to know before booking your trip? We cover it all in this guide.

For more details, start reading here or scroll to the different sections we cover:

  • Hiking in the Pyrenees FAQs
  • Map of the Pyrenees Mountain Range
  • Top 5 Best Hikes for Your Walking Holiday in the Pyrenees
  • Where to Stay in the Pyrenees for the Best Base
  • 5-Day Itinerary for Hiking in the Pyrenees
  • Essential Packing List for Hiking in the Pyrenees

Hiking in the Pyrenees FAQs

To ensure you make the most of your trip with the least amount of hiccups as possible, we've compiled the most commonly asked questions about the mountain range.

Here, we've covered everything from the best time to travel, prices, accommodation, and more.

Hiking holidays require an extra level of preparation, so we'd thought we'd cover all the bases. By the end, you'll be an expert in the Pyrenees without having gone yet!

Where are the Pyrenees?

The Pyrenees are a mountain range located in Southwest Europe, forming a natural border between France and Spain. The range stretches for about 450km from the Atlantic to the Mediterranean Sea.

The country of Andorra actually sits in the Pyrenees, making it a great place to visit while you're on your travels.

Map of the Pyrenees Mountain Range

To give you a better understanding of just where and how large the Pyrenees are, we've included a picture of the map below:

Credit: Blue Green Atlas

Are the Pyrenees Hard to Hike?

The difficulty of hiking in the Pyrenees depends on the specific route and terrain. Some trails can be challenging, with steep climbs and rugged paths, while others are more moderate and suitable for beginners.

It is important to properly research your chosen route and prepare accordingly before taking on any hike in the Pyrenees. This includes checking weather conditions, packing appropriate gear and supplies, and being physically fit for the level of difficulty.

However, even if you're not an experienced hiker, there are plenty of options for exploring the Pyrenees at a leisurely pace through scenic walks or guided tours. 

It's extremely diverse, so you'll always find something that suits you.

What is Hut-to-Hut Hiking in the Pyrenees?

Hut-to-hut hiking in the Pyrenees is a unique and rewarding way to explore the region's stunning landscapes while immersing yourself in its culture.

This style of trekking involves walking from one mountain hut, or refuge/refugio, to another, carrying only the essentials needed for the journey. 

The huts provide basic accommodation, often with communal sleeping areas, and meals can usually be arranged, allowing hikers to travel lighter and focus on the experience itself.

Routes can vary in difficulty, from easier paths suitable for beginners to more challenging trails that require experience and stamina.

It's a fantastic way to see the Pyrenees, but also to meet new people on the journey. Chances are, you'll do this with a group, so it's a great way to socialise.

Do You Need a Guide to Hike the Pyrenees?

Hiring a guide or going with a tour isn't essential for your trip to the Pyrenees. Self-guided hikes offer more freedom in terms of pace, sights, and stops, while allowing you to choose exactly where you hike.

However, sometimes a guide can enhance your experience, especially for those unfamiliar with the terrain or the challenges of mountain hiking.

Guides bring extensive knowledge of the region, including hidden spots, wildlife, and the area's history, which adds depth to the adventure. Plus, they can help ensure safety, particularly on more remote or demanding trails where navigation can be tricky.

If you're an experienced hiker with good navigation skills, you might feel comfortable tackling the trails independently. 

However, for beginners or those looking for an added layer of support and insight, having a guide can be good.

What are the Highest Peaks in the Pyrenees?

The Pyrenees mountain range boasts some of the highest peaks in Europe, with a total of 129 peaks reaching an elevation of over 3,000 meters.

The highest peak in the entire range is Aneto, standing at an impressive 3,404 meters. Other notable high peaks include Posets (3,375m), Monte Perdido (3,355m), and Vignemale (3,298m).

These high peaks not only offer stunning views of the surrounding landscape but also provide a challenge for experienced hikers and mountaineers. They require technical skills and proper equipment to reach the summit safely.

Aneto is often considered the most difficult peak to conquer due to its steep and rocky terrain. It is recommended to have a qualified guide when attempting this climb.

When is the Best Time to Hike in the Pyrenees?

The Pyrenees are a popular hiking destination during the summer months, typically from June to September. This is when the weather is at its best and the trails are most accessible.

However, it is important to note that even during these months, the weather can be unpredictable in the mountains. It's always advisable to check weather forecasts before embarking on a hike, and to be prepared for sudden changes in conditions.

Some hikers also prefer to visit the Pyrenees in the shoulder seasons of May or October. During this time, there are fewer crowds, but still mild temperatures and decent weather.

Winter hiking in the Pyrenees is not recommended for inexperienced hikers, as snow and ice can make trails treacherous.

That's why a lot of tourists flock to the Pyrenees for skiing and other winter sports during the cold season!

How Much Money is a Walking Holiday in the Pyrenees?

This depends on various factors, such as the length of your trip and whether you hire a guide or go by your own itinerary. But the accommodation you choose will make the most difference to the cost of your holiday.

Generally, a walking holiday in the Pyrenees can range from budget-friendly to more luxurious options.

For those looking for a budget-friendly option, camping is a popular choice. Campsites are plentiful throughout the region and offer affordable rates for tents or camper vans.

There are also mountain huts (they're called refuges in French and Refugios in Spanish — you'll hear both throughout this article), which offer a rustic and affordable experience of the Pyrenees.

If you prefer more comfortable accommodations, there are plenty of guesthouses, bed and breakfasts, and small hotels scattered throughout the mountains. These options often include meals and transportation to trails, making them a convenient choice for hikers.

For those seeking a more luxurious experience, there are also upscale hotels and resorts in the Pyrenees. These properties offer amenities such as spas, gourmet restaurants, and guided hikes.

Here’s a rough breakdown of what a hiking trip in the Pyrenees might cost, depending on your style of accommodation. 

The exact total will, of course, depend on duration, season, guided vs self‑guided, travel to/from the mountains, meals, transport and so on, but these figures give you a rough idea:

  • Budget/tent camping: If you bring your own hiking tent (or rent cheap gear) and stay at campsites or even wild camp (where permitted), you can keep accommodation costs as low as 8-9 Euros per night.
  • Mountain hut/refuge/refugio stays: Staying at refuge shelters, you usually get your meals included. On average, accommodation like this can cost 20-70+ Euros per night. This can be much more if you have guided hikes included, or plan to travel hut-to-hut.
  • Typical budget hotel: A 2-3 star mountain or valley hotel in the Pyrenees can cost 60-150 Euros per night, depending on the hotel's location.
  • Luxury hotel: If you opt for a premium experience, costs can really jump up. You can expect to pay upwards of 2000-7000 Euros for a whole week. This might include spa access, guided tours, with transfers included.

These prices don't include food, transport, flights in and out of the region, and other things like travel insurance. As you can see, this isn't a budget holiday, but well worth it if you value nature.

Just be sure to set out a budget initially, and do your research to see if you can find options to fit within it.

What are the Nearest Airports to the Pyrenees?

The nearest airports to the Pyrenees are located in Toulouse, Pau, and Lourdes. These airports offer both domestic and international flights, making it easy for travellers to reach the region from various locations.

From these airports, you can rent a car or take public transportation to get closer to the Pyrenees mountains.

Toulouse-Blagnac Airport is the largest airport in the region and is located about 2 hours away from the central Pyrenees. This airport offers flights from major cities, such as London.

Pau-Pyrénées Airport is another option closer to the Pyrenees mountains. Located just an hour away from the destination.

For those who prefer to travel by train, there are high-speed trains that connect major cities such as Barcelona, Madrid, and Paris to smaller towns near the Pyrenees. 

The TGV (Train à Grande Vitesse) or AVE (Alta Velocidad Española) are fast and convenient options for travelling.

Are There Any Permits or Restrictions I Should Know Before Hiking the Pyrenees?

There are generally no permits needed when hiking the Pyrenees. The only situation you may need one is if you fancy a spot of fishing on your hiking trip.

However, there are some considerations you'll need to make regarding restrictions. Some routes have none at all, but other hiking trails, like those in national parks, have regulations in place regarding camping, waste, and wildlife.

It is important to research and understand any required permits or restrictions before embarking on your hike to avoid any issues or difficulties during your trip.

What is Accommodation Like in the Pyrenees?

Accommodation in the Pyrenees caters to a wide range of preferences and budgets, offering something for everyone.

For those seeking a close-to-nature experience, camping is a popular option, with numerous campsites available throughout the region. Many of these campsites provide excellent facilities, such as showers, restrooms, and even small shops.

You should research the rules and regulations for wild camping in the Pyrenees, though. Wild camping is permitted in some places, but for the most part, there are designated camping sites to be used.

Alternatively, hikers can stay in mountain huts, which are scattered along popular trekking routes. These refuges often provide simple meals and a chance to connect with fellow travellers.

If you prefer more comfort after a day of hiking, charming guesthouses and traditional rural hotels are plentiful in villages across the Pyrenees, offering warm hospitality.

Top 5 Best Hikes for Your Walking Holiday in the Pyrenees

The Pyrenees, both Spanish and French, offer hundreds, if not more, beautiful and rewarding hikes, perfect for all abilities. From short and easy walks to challenging multi-day treks, there is something for everyone in this stunning mountain range.

While it's impossible to pick the best hikes from the region, we thought we'd show you some of our favourites, so you can get a feel for the kind of hikes you'd like to do.

To help plan your walking holiday, here are our top five Pyrenees hikes: 

GR10 Route (France)

Distance: 920km

Time: 45-60 days (depending on pace)

Difficulty: Difficult (physically demanding, not technical)

@placetobeee GR10 vu du ciel ⛰️ #voyage #bonplan #placetobe #travel #pyrenees ♬ som original - WE ARE 00h.03m 🇨🇭

Credit: @placetobeee on TikTok.com

The iconic GR10 route is worth mentioning, even if it takes over a month to complete. 

If you're on an extended holiday in the Pyrenees (some just head there to do this specific hike), the GR10 hike is a long-distance trail that runs coast to coast across the French Pyrenees.

From the Atlantic Ocean to the Med, this hike offers a little slice of everything. Rolling hills, glistening lakes, dramatic peaks, interesting wildlife, traditional villages — the list goes on, and on.

On a long-distance hike like this, trekkers will stay in mountain huts, like we talked about earlier, tents, or hostels for hikers. These often include meals, too.

Be warned, this trek isn't for the faint-hearted. While it isn't technical, it certainly is physically demanding, and you will need to allow for rests.

Thankfully, though, it’s a well-marked route, and you'll likely be heading out in a group, so you shouldn't go far wrong.

Just explaining this hike alone doesn’t do it justice, so get researching and see for yourself what all the fuss is about!

Pic du Midi d’Ossau (France)

Distance: 21.2km

Time: 9.5-10.5 hours (over a few days)

Difficulty: Moderate-Difficult

@amandine.lgt Pic d’Anayet - Pyrénées @Maëlle #sunset #pyrenees #montagne #hiking #mountain #rando ♬ ur the secret recipe - david kushner

Credit: @Kamandinelgt on TikTok.com

This is another multi-day hike we absolutely love in the Pyrenees. Although this one isn't quite a month long.

The Pic du Midi d'Ossau circuit is a multi-day hike that can be done in 2-3 days, depending on your pace.

While you will encounter steep climbs, rocky terrains, and a few technical areas (you won't need any specialist equipment, though), you'll also get to experience, at first hand, panoramic views of Pic du Midi d'Ossau, high-mountain lakes, and beautiful mountain meadows.

There are a few accommodation options for this one — Refuge de Pombie (mountain hut), wild camping (if you're brave!), and more traditional hotel and guesthouse accommodation in the larger nearby towns.

If you're not used to hiking in the snow, we recommend avoiding this route during the winter, because it can become a little tricky to navigate and potentially dangerous.

Ordesa Valley, Cola de Caballo Waterfall Hike (Spain)

Distance: 17.9km

Time: 5.5-6 hours

Difficulty: Moderate

@abelfdzz Espectacular 🤩 Cola de Caballo #cascada #natura #nature ♬ intro x chorus the night we met - aboutourfeelingss

Credit: @ablefdzz on TikTok.com

The Cola de Caballo Waterfall Hike is one of the most popular and accessible day hikes in Ordesa y Monte Perdido National Park, and for good reason.

It follows the stunning Ordesa Valley through forests, alongside rivers and waterfalls, all the way to the dramatic "Horse Tail" waterfall at the head of the valley.

There are some picture-perfect spots along the whole trail, ideal for making memories and experiencing the Pyrenees at their finest. It's also a loop, so you'll get to experience new sights the whole way around.

The path is wide and well-marked, allowing you to enjoy the hike without fear of getting lost or going off-trail.

As it's popular with visitors, expect crowds. If you want to avoid the main hustle and bustle, we recommend starting as early as possible.

Cavalls del Vent (Spain – Catalonia)

Distance: 77.1km

Time: 24 hr+ (over a few days)

Difficulty: Moderate-difficult

Another multi-day hike now, but this time, it's on the Spanish side, and we're actually in Catalonia.

This is a high mountain circuit through the Cadi-Moixero Natural Park, in the pre-Pyrenees (lower mountain ranges that run parallel to the main Pyrenean peaks), where the region meets the main mountain range.

Hikers, depending on fitness level and pace, take 4-8 days to complete this circular loop, and there is a selection of refugios where you can stay and get your meals along the way.

You'll get to see the iconic double-peaked mountain, Pedraforca Massif, Tosa d'Alp, another scenic summit, miles of fir forest, and spectacular wildlife.

If it's a hut-to-hut hike you're looking for, this is one of the best and least crowded options in the Pyrenees.

Lac d’Iraty & Dam Trail (France/Spain Border)

Distance: 10km

Time: 3 hours

Difficulty: Easy

Last but not least, if you're travelling with family and looking for a lighter hike, this trail will take you around a beautiful lake in the Basque Country at the base of the Pyrenees.

There's nothing technical or strenuous involved; it's just a thoroughly relaxing and enjoyable hike for a crisp morning or summer's afternoon.

Perfect for beginners, this route provides a gentle gradient, a turquoise lake (which you can swim in!), and lush green forest.

The definition of little effort for great reward.

The Best Bases for Staying in the Pyrenees

The Pyrenees are vast, and each location offers something completely unique, so how do you know where to stay for your hiking holiday?

When you're on a hiking holiday, your base needs to be close to a range of trails, with good enough amenities to be comfortable throughout your stay.

If you've chosen to stay in a fixed accommodation throughout your visit to the Pyrenees, we've listed some locations below, perfect for a hiking holiday with a range of accommodation nearby.

For those doing hut-to-hut hiking during your visit, or for those wanting to get into the full spirit of the Pyrenees by camping their way through the trip, we've also suggested some mountain huts and campsites to check out ahead of your stay.

They, too, are in excellent locations for an unforgettable hiking holiday.

5-Day Itinerary for Hiking in the Pyrenees

To give you the best overall picture of what a hiking holiday in the Pyrenees looks like, we've created a typical itinerary for 5 days on the Spanish side.

It includes a popular hike as well as a few quieter trails, with a mix of stays in mountain huts, camping, and base-village accommodation for a well-rounded experience.

Of course, you can adjust as you see fit, but hopefully this will give you an idea of what your itinerary could look like.

Note: If you’re travelling with a tour operator, you will likely follow their itinerary. If you want to see specific things or do specific hikes, let them know, and they may make adjustments.

Day 1: Arrival and Warm-up Hike

Arrive in Torla-Ordesa and set up camp in one of the many campsites in the area. If you don't fancy that, there are plenty of indoor local lodgings to choose from.

In the afternoon, after you've had time to relax and settle in, hike into the valley of Ordesa. A great introductory hike is the walk from Pradera de Ordesa up the valley floor to the first waterfalls (e.g. Cascada de la Cueva).

Day 2: Full Valley Hike to Cola de Caballo

Yesterday, you hiked up to Pradera de Ordesa; today, you'll ascend past that, through the forest and meadows, to the iconic waterfall at the head of the valley — Cola de Caballo Waterfall.

You can read more about this hike further up in the article.

Then, in late afternoon, continue to a refugio (like the Refugio de Góriz), or return to Torla for the night.

If you choose to stay in a hut, be sure to prebook.

Day 3: Move Out to Tena Valley

Depart early for the Tena Valley region. You can either get a bus or drive from Torla to Sallent de Gállego.

From Sallent, you have the perfect opportunity to hike into the higher lakes region and stay overnight in a mountain hut (like Refugio Respomuso), or camp nearby if permitted.

Day 4: Alpine Ridge/Lake Traverse

From your hut, if you're a more experienced hiker, ascend to ridges or high lakes and enjoy the panoramic views the Pyrenees are so famous for.

If you fancy it, you can even summit a moderate peak (keep within non-technical terrain if you lack experience or aren't with a guide).

You can then make your descent to the next hut or camping area. There may be others doing the same route as you, so it's a great opportunity to meet new people. You could even get a bit of a hiking group going!

Day 5: Descent

From the mountain hut, make your way back down to the nearest valley, maybe via a scenic route, finishing in a charming village or accessible road for transport back to Torla if you're leaving the Pyrenees the same way you arrived.

Be sure to factor in some well-earned R&R at the end! If you have a night left, spend it in a hotel with a few luxuries you missed while trekking.


Essential Packing List for Hiking in the Pyrenees

Packing for your trip to the Pyrenees will vary depending on the kind of hiking holiday you want — camping, staying in hotels, or something different.

That said, we think it's important to give you the whole picture, which is why we've created the ultimate packing list as if you were going camping. So, if you're staying in hotels, you can ignore some of the following sections.

A hiking holiday means you need stuff, and a lot of it, for that matter. Packing needs to be precise, and you must remember to bring the essentials.

You'll, of course, need to bring personal items like medication, devices, chargers, and toiletries, but we trust you to pack them without our guidance!




Here's our recommended packing list for Pyrenees trekking, with details to follow (plus some recommendations!):

For varied mountain conditions, layers will be your best friend. It's best to pack too much and be prepared for every weather possibility, than pack too little and be too cold or hot while you're out on a hike.

So, since mountains like the Pyrenees have plenty of unpredictable weather, here is a list of the clothing you should pack, no matter what season you're travelling in.

  • Moisture-wicking base layers.
  • A lightweight mid-layer, like a fleece or lightweight jacket.

Why Do I Need A Water Bottle On a Hike?

Staying hydrated is super important when hiking. It keeps your energy up, helps you stay cool, and keeps your body working at its best.

Even on short hikes, you’ll lose water through sweat, especially in hot weather or during tough climbs. That’s why carrying a water bottle is a must.

It makes sure you’ve got safe drinking water on hand to avoid dehydration, which can leave you feeling tired, dizzy, or unfocused (definitely not ideal on tricky trails!).

For more essential hiking gear, check out our ultimate hiking checklist for hikers of all levels.

Top Tip: If you invest in a water bottle with a filter, you can refill from water sources along the way and stay refreshed for the entire hike.

What Size Water Bottle is Best for My Hike?

The best size water bottle for your hike depends on a variety of factors, as well as personal preference.

For shorter, easier hikes in mild weather, a smaller bottle (around 500ml to 1 litre) might suffice. However, for longer or more strenuous hikes, especially in hot weather, you’ll need to carry more water (at least 2 to 3 litres) to stay properly hydrated.

Your fitness levels also play a role, as you may need to drink more if you’re working harder on steep ascents or challenging terrain.

You should also consider whether you’re comfortable carrying a larger, bulkier bottle, or if you’d prefer a smaller one and plan to refill from water sources along the way, particularly if you have a filtered bottle.

Will My Camping Water Bottle Be Suitable For Hiking?

This is another situation where it depends on the bottle and your personal preferences. If your camping water bottle is a bulky 8-litre water carrier that you decant into cups in your camp, it's probably not ideal for a hike.

However, if you have a smaller water bottle that you refill at camp, this should be fine to take on your hike.

Narrow Mouth Vs Standard Mouth Vs Wide Mouth

You'll have seen all these types of bottles in brick and mortar outdoor stores, on our website, and in this article, but what's the difference, and what does it mean for your hiking hydration?[in boxes]

Narrow Mouth Bottles

Narrow-mouth bottles have a small opening, making them ideal for preventing spills and easy to drink from while on the move.

They’re particularly useful during hikes where you may not have time to stop and carefully pour water. However, the small opening can make them challenging to clean and refill, especially if you use ice or need to add hydration powders.

Pros:

  • Prevents spills during drinking.
  • Easier to drink from while walking.
  • Compact and often lightweight.

Cons:

  • Difficult to clean and dry.
  • Tricky to refill, especially with larger water sources.

Standard Mouth Bottles

Standard mouth bottles strike a balance between narrow and wide mouth designs.

They offer a moderate opening that makes them easier to refill and clean compared to narrow-mouth types, while still being manageable for spill-free drinking. They’re a versatile option for hikers who want a practical, all-around bottle.

Pros:

  • Easier to clean and refill than narrow-mouth bottles.
  • Allows controlled drinking without frequent spills.
  • Compatible with many filters and lids.

Cons:

  • May still be slightly restrictive for adding ice or mixing powders

Wide Mouth Bottles

Wide-mouth bottles have large openings, which makes them the easiest to clean, refill, and add ice or powders to. They’re particularly useful for long hikes where frequent topping up or cleaning is required.

However, the wide opening makes precise drinking on the move more difficult, and they can be prone to spills if not handled carefully.

Pros:

  • Easiest to clean and refill.
  • Compatible with ice cubes and hydration powders.
  • Offers versatility for multi-use scenarios.

Cons:

  • Higher chance of spills while drinking.
  • Bulkier and may not fit some bottle holders.

Is an Insulated Water Bottle Better Than an Uninsulated One?

For hiking, an insulated water bottle is generally a better choice than an uninsulated one.

Insulated bottles maintain your drink's temperature, keeping water cool on hot days or tea warm on chilly hikes. This significantly improves comfort and hydration on long treks, especially in extreme weather. They also reduce exterior condensation, keeping your gear dry.

While uninsulated bottles are lighter and cheaper, they don't offer temperature control. This can lead to warm water in summer or cold drinks in winter.

For hikers who prioritise performance and comfort, the advantages of an insulated bottle outweigh its slightly heavier weight.

Final Words: What is the Best Overall Water Bottle For Hiking?

Choosing the best water bottle for hiking depends on your priorities and the type of adventures you take.

If you’re heading into remote areas and need to purify water from natural sources, bottles like Lifestraw are a great option. With built-in filtration systems, they make it easy to stay hydrated safely.

For hikers on a budget who want something durable and reliable, Nalgene bottles are a solid choice. They’re affordable, tough, and perfect for those who need a dependable option.

Ultimately, the right water bottle comes down to your specific needs, budget, and personal preferences.

title: What Is Thru-Hiking & Should You Give It A Go?
author: Laurence Kay
excerpt: Hiking is a popular pastime, but true enthusiasts are always looking for ways to make it more challenging. Enter, thru-hiking. But what is thru-hiking, and should you give it a go? If you've completed all your local hiki
html:
Hiking is a popular pastime, but true enthusiasts are always looking for ways to make it more challenging. Enter, thru-hiking. But what is thru-hiking, and should you give it a go?

If you've completed all your local hiking trails and are looking for something different, trying a different approach can be just what you need. Instead of taking your time on a long trail, thru-hiking is all about completing it in one go.

Find out whether thru-hiking could be the right challenge for you with our in-depth guide.

Thru-Hiking At A Glance:

  • Thru-hiking is the complete end-to-end journey of a long-distance trail in one continuous push, often over weeks or months.
  • It requires extensive preparation, covering route research, resupply planning, physical training, and lightweight, durable gear.
  • Typical thru-hikes range from 100 to several thousand miles, with completion times depending on fitness, terrain, and daily mileage.
  • Unlike section hiking or backpacking, thru-hiking demands sustained endurance, mental resilience, and the ability to live self-sufficiently on the trail.
  • Popular options include UK routes like the West Highland Way and global trails such as the Appalachian Trail, Pacific Crest Trail, and Camino de Santiago.

What Is Thru-Hiking?

Thru-hiking is when you hike a whole long-distance trail from one end to the other, all in one go! We're talking trails that are often hundreds of miles long.

It takes months of serious dedication, grit, and a ton of planning to pull off. Think trails like the famous Appalachian Trail, the Pacific Crest Trail, or the Continental Divide Trail in the US.

Unlike a quick day hike, thru-hiking plunges you deep into nature for a really long time. It's a huge mental test just as much as a physical one.

But for those looking for adventure, personal growth, and a deep connection with the natural world, it's an incredibly rewarding experience.

What Counts As a Thru-Hike?

While there’s no universal distance requirement, many thru-hikes span hundreds of miles.

Purists aim to cover every mile of the trail on foot, adhering strictly to its official route, while others may take occasional detours or skip sections due to weather or logistical challenges.

Ultimately, the essence of a thru-hike lies in the commitment, perseverance, and immersive experience of traversing the trail in one epic, continuous adventure.

Thru-hiking vs Section Hiking vs Backpacking

Thru-hiking requires careful planning, including route mapping, resupply logistics, and packing essential gear.

Physical and mental preparation are key, with training focused on endurance, strength, and resilience.

Hikers must also consider time commitments, budgeting, and skills like navigation and first aid. With proper preparation, thru-hiking can be a challenging but rewarding adventure.

Section Hiking

Section hiking involves completing a long-distance trail in smaller segments over time, offering flexibility for those with work, family, or other commitments.

It allows hikers to align trips with personal schedules or seasons, making it ideal for those seeking a less demanding alternative to thru-hiking.

Perfect for beginners or those with limited time, section hiking lets adventurers build skills while enjoying the experience of long-distance hiking.

Backpacking

Backpacking is a blend of hiking and camping where you carry all your gear, like a tent and food, for overnight trips in the wilderness.

It allows for a deeper connection with nature and is ideal for self-sufficient adventurers.

However, it requires careful planning, fitness, and outdoor safety knowledge for a successful trip.

How Long is a Typical Thru-Hike?

Thru-hiking can take weeks to months, with major trails like the Appalachian or Pacific Crest trails often taking multiple weeks or even months. Of course, the duration of the hike depends on the length of the trail, so let's take a look at what you can expect.

Thru-Hike Distance Ranges

Thru-hikes vary significantly in length, depending on the chosen trail. Here are some common distance ranges along with examples:

  • Short Thru-Hikes (160–320 km / 100–200 miles): Perfect for beginners or those with limited time, these hikes include trails like the Long Trail in Vermont (approx. 439 km / 273 miles, but shorter sections can be tackled) or the Wonderland Trail in Washington (approx. 151 km / 94 miles).
  • Medium Thru-Hikes (500–1,500 km / 300–1,000 miles): Medium-length thru-hikes often require a greater time commitment. Examples include the Camino de Santiago in Spain (varies based on route, with the popular Camino Francés at around 780 km / 485 miles) and the Arizona Trail (approx. 1,287 km / 800 miles).
  • Long Thru-Hikes (2,500+ km / 1,500+ miles): These epic trails demand months of dedication and are ideal for experienced hikers. Notable examples include the Appalachian Trail (approx. 3,540 km / 2,200 miles) and the Pacific Crest Trail (approx. 4,270 km / 2,653 miles).

Thru-Hike Timeframes

The duration of a thru-hike largely depends on several factors, including the trail length, the hiker's fitness level, experience, pace, and the conditions encountered along the way.

  • For shorter thru-hikes, such as those under 500 km (310 miles), hikers in good physical condition might complete the trail in 2 to 4 weeks, averaging around 20 to 25 km (12 to 15 miles) per day.
  • Intermediate thru-hikes, in the range of 800 to 1,500 km (500 to 930 miles), typically take about 1 to 3 months to finish, depending on pace and rest days.
  • For longer thru-hikes exceeding 2,500 km (1,500 miles), such as the Appalachian Trail or Pacific Crest Trail, many hikers dedicate 4 to 6 months to their journeys.

The completion time for these trails can vary widely, with some experienced hikers moving quickly while others prefer a more leisurely pace, stopping to fully enjoy the surroundings or adapt to challenges like weather or trail conditions.

Essential Gear for Thru-Hiking

If attempting a thru-hike sounds like your idea of a good time, you need to know how to pack for one! Here's our comprehensive list of the essential gear you'll need to complete a thru-hike.

Alternatively, download our thru-hike packing checklist to make preparing for your trip a breeze!

GPS devices or smartphone apps, such as Gaia GPS or AllTrails, offer useful digital support but should not replace traditional tools.

A waterproof map case will protect your maps from the elements, and it's wise to pack backup batteries or a portable charger for electronic devices.

Familiarise yourself with your chosen tools before setting out to ensure you can confidently use them during your hike.

You also can't forget about investing in high-quality dehydrated expedition meals. These meals are specifically formulated to provide the calories and nutritional balance needed for sustained physical exertion, making them a reliable choice to keep you well-fueled and ready for the next stretch of your adventure.




✓ Water Filtration & Hydration

Staying properly hydrated is absolutely critical during any thru-hike, often marking the difference between a successful journey and a prematurely ended one.

Because of this, having a reliable method for water filtration or purification is a non-negotiable part of your gear list. While natural water sources like crystal-clear streams or serene alpine lakes might appear pristine and inviting, they can often harbour unseen dangers.

These include harmful bacteria, parasites such as Giardia or Cryptosporidium, or even viruses, all of which could lead to severe gastrointestinal distress or other serious illnesses that would quickly derail your adventure.

A high-quality water filtration or purification system, like the LifeStraw Peak personal water filter, effectively removes or inactivates these contaminants, ensuring that you can safely drink from virtually any natural source without constant worry about your health.

Find out what the difference is between filters and water purifiers.

Convenient water storage is just as important as safe water. Hydration bladders offer significant advantages over traditional water bottles on long hikes. We particularly like the Hydrapak Pioneer water bladder.

They allow you to carry more water, distribute weight evenly in your pack, and enable hands-free sipping through a drinking tube.

This makes it easier to stay consistently hydrated, which helps prevent dehydration, maintain energy levels, and avoid muscle cramps.

Layering your clothing is crucial for thru-hikes. This is because weather conditions and your activity level can change a lot. Dressing in layers lets you easily adjust to temperature changes, keeping you comfortable and safe.

A common layering system includes:

  • A base layer: Wicks sweat away from your skin.
  • An insulating layer: Keeps you warm.
  • An outer layer: Protects against wind and rain.

This system allows you to add or remove clothing as needed, preventing you from getting too hot or too cold. It also helps you stay ready for sudden weather shifts often found in the backcountry.

By taking some of the strain off your legs and knees, trekking poles reduce joint impact, which is especially helpful during steep climbs or descents.

They also lower the risk of slips and falls by keeping you steady on tricky surfaces like loose gravel or wet trails.

A good pair of trekking poles can make your hike more comfortable and help you stay confident as you move toward your goal. We particularly like the lightweight 3F UL Gear C1 Carbon Fibre Trekking Pole.




✓ First Aid & Safety Essentials
