When going on a hike, it’s important to carry basic first aid supplies for minor injuries like cuts, blisters, or insect bites. But for a thru-hike, it’s a good idea to upgrade to a more complete first aid kit.

Thru-hiking often means spending long periods in remote areas where help might not be close by.

A thorough first aid kit can be crucial in an emergency, giving you the tools and supplies to handle more serious medical issues until you can get professional help.

We recommend the BCB Elite Explorers Kit for a strong pre-filled option. Alternatively, you can read our guide to building a first aid kit for a more tailored approach.




What to Expect on a Thru-Hike

Thru-hiking means trekking long distances over several days or months. It’s a challenging but rewarding experience.

Along the way, you’ll encounter varied terrain and unpredictable weather with limited access to amenities. It's essential to pack light, durable gear and have enough food and a way to purify water.

Mental strength is just as important as physical fitness, as the journey requires perseverance and the ability to adapt.

Despite the challenges, you'll be rewarded with stunning landscapes, unique wildlife, and a strong sense of community with fellow hikers.

Remember: Planning and preparation are key to a safe and enjoyable trip.

How to Prepare for a Thru-Hike

Thru-hikes aren't a spur-of-the-moment adventure. They require careful planning and preparation to make sure they're successful, and you and your group stay safe.

Steps to Prepare for a Thru-Hike:

  1. Research Your Route
    Study the trail you plan to hike, including its length, terrain, weather conditions, and resupply points. Understanding the specifics will help you tailor your gear and strategy.
  2. Train Physically
    Build your endurance through regular hiking, walking, or backpacking, gradually increasing the distance and weight you carry. Incorporating strength and flexibility exercises can also reduce the risk of injury.
  3. Select the Right Gear
    Invest in lightweight, durable, and weather-appropriate gear. Camping essentials include a reliable backpack, sleeping bag, tent, and proper footwear. Test all equipment beforehand to ensure comfort and functionality.
  4. Plan Your Supplies
    Organise food, water, and first-aid supplies carefully. Consider how often you’ll need to resupply and map out accessible points along your trail.
  5. Practice Essential Skills
    Learn important survival skills such as navigation, setting up camp, purifying water, and first aid. Confidence in these can make your hike safer and more enjoyable.

By following these steps, you’ll be better prepared to take on the challenges of a thru-hike and fully appreciate the adventure ahead.

Thru-Hiking Distance Trails in the UK

We've mentioned a lot of popular thru-hiking trails in far-flung places, but you don't need to have a passport to dip your toe into the world of thru-hiking.

Popular UK Thru-Hiking Trails

Here are some of the most popular thru-hiking trails in the UK:

  • West Highland Way (Scotland): A 96-mile trail stretching from Milngavie to Fort William, offering stunning views of lochs, glens, and rugged landscapes.
  • Pennine Way (England): Known as one of Britain's toughest long-distance walks, it covers 268 miles from Derbyshire to the Scottish Borders.
  • South West Coast Path (England): Spanning 630 miles along the coastline of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, and Somerset, it's Britain's longest National Trail.
  • Coast to Coast Walk (England): A 192-mile trail from St Bees on the Irish Sea to Robin Hood's Bay on the North Sea, crossing three national parks – the Lake District, Yorkshire Dales, and North York Moors.
  • Hadrian's Wall Path (England): An 84-mile walk following the remnants of Roman history, stretching from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway.
  • Offa's Dyke Path (Wales): A 177-mile trail roughly following the England-Wales border, with stunning views and historic landscapes.
  • The Great Glen Way (Scotland): This 79-mile trail from Fort William to Inverness takes you along the iconic Caledonian Canal and Loch Ness.
  • The Ridgeway (England): Often described as Britain's oldest road, this 87-mile trail runs from Overton Hill in Wiltshire to Ivinghoe Beacon in Buckinghamshire.
  • The Cotswold Way (England): A 102-mile route offering picturesque countryside views from Chipping Campden to Bath.
  • The Southern Upland Way (Scotland): A challenging 212-mile coast-to-coast route from Portpatrick to Cockburnspath.

What Makes UK Thru-Hiking Unique?

Thru-hiking in the UK offers a unique experience, thanks to its rich history, diverse landscapes, and well-developed trail system.

Many trails wind through historical areas, letting hikers explore ancient monuments, old villages, and even castles.

The landscapes are incredibly varied, ranging from rugged highlands and serene lochs in Scotland to rolling hills, wooded valleys, and dramatic coastal cliffs in England and Wales.

Each trail provides a distinct scenic journey. Plus, a well-maintained network of public footpaths and long-distance routes makes planning multi-day hikes simple.

Many routes also pass through villages and towns, offering accommodation, local food, and chances to meet friendly locals. This makes the adventure rewarding and memorable.

Thru-Hiking Trails Around the World

If you're interested in completing thru-hikes beyond our shores, here are some of the most popular trails around the world:

  • Pacific Crest Trail (USA): Stretching over 2,650 miles, this trail traverses diverse landscapes, including deserts, forests, and mountain ranges, from Mexico to Canada.
  • Camino de Santiago (Spain): Renowned for its cultural and spiritual significance, this historic pilgrimage route offers multiple paths, the most popular being the Camino Francés.
  • Appalachian Trail (USA): Spanning 2,190 miles across the Eastern United States, this iconic trail is famous for its scenic beauty and challenging terrain.
  • Te Araroa (New Zealand): Covering approximately 1,900 miles, this trail showcases New Zealand's stunning landscapes, from beaches to mountains.
  • Great Divide Trail (Canada): Running along the Canadian Rockies, this challenging trek offers breathtaking views and remote wilderness experiences.
  • Tour du Mont Blanc (France, Italy, Switzerland): Encircling the Mont Blanc massif, this 110-mile route combines alpine scenery with charming mountain villages.
  • Bibbulmun Track (Australia): Spanning nearly 620 miles, this trail navigates through Western Australia's diverse ecosystems, from forests to coastal terrain.
  • Kungsleden (Sweden): Covering 270 miles in Swedish Lapland, this route offers pristine arctic landscapes and a chance to witness the Northern Lights.
  • Overland Track (Australia): A 40-mile trek through Tasmania's wilderness, featuring rugged mountains, lush valleys, and unique wildlife.
  • Hayduke Trail (USA): A challenging 800-mile route through the desert southwest, passing through iconic areas like the Grand Canyon and Arches National Park.

Final Thoughts: Is Thru-Hiking Right for You?

Thru-hiking demands a lot: preparation, time, and money. You need to plan your route, get gear, and commit weeks or months to the journey.

It takes serious dedication and organisation. But for those who accept the challenge, it's an unmatched chance to test themselves, connect deeply with nature, and experience some of the world's best trails.

From Australia's rugged Overland Track to the vast deserts of the Hayduke Trail, the rewards of finishing such a huge adventure often far exceed the difficulties.

If you're unsure what hiking trails you want to tackle, check out our hiking guide series, where we cover popular hikes from the Inca Trail to Kilimanjaro.

author: Laurence Kay

html:
It's an age-old camping question: Cast iron vs. titanium cookware, which is best? The short answer is that it depends. The long answer is laid out in this in-depth guide comparing the pros and cons of both options.

From family camping trips to solo backpacking adventures, knowing you have the best camp cookware in your kit provides peace of mind and makes planning meals easier.

So, let's dive into the differences between these two reliable cookware materials.

The Quick Answer

Feature Cast Iron Titanium
Ideal Setting Home Kitchen, Car Camping, Campfire Backpacking, Mountaineering, Ultralight
Weight Very Heavy (Extreme Thermal Mass) Extremely Light (Featherweight)
Heat Retention Excellent (Stays hot forever) Poor (Cools very fast)
Heat Distribution Good (Once heated) Poor (Prone to Hot Spots)
Maintenance High (Requires seasoning, prone to rust) Low (Rust-proof, generally non-reactive)
Best For Searing, Braising, Baking, Frying Boiling water, Rehydrating meals, Minimalism

 

Cast Iron Cookware: The Heavyweight Champion

PetroMax Dutch Oven w/ Legs

Buy Now

PetroMax Fire Skillet w/ Pan Handles

Buy Now

PetroMax Loaf Pan w/ Lid

Buy Now

PetroMax Cast Iron Saucepan w/ Lid

Buy Now

Cast iron has long been a stalwart of experienced cooks both in kitchens and in camping circles, but why is it such a beloved material for cooking with?

The Science of Cast Iron Heat Retention

The high thermal mass of cast iron is one of its standout qualities. Thermal mass refers to the material's ability to absorb, store, and radiate heat consistently.

Cast iron’s density allows it to hold heat exceptionally well, even after cold ingredients are added to the pan.

This is crucial for tasks like searing, where maintaining a steady, high temperature ensures a perfect crust forms on the food without drastic temperature fluctuations.

Best Use Cases:

Cast iron's excellent heat retention makes it perfect for various cooking methods, from searing steaks and deep-frying to baking bread and cornbread with Dutch ovens.

Pros and Cons of Cast Iron

  • Pros:
    • Virtually indestructible
    • Excellent heat retention
    • Natural non-stick surface (when seasoned)
    • Affordable
    • Adds iron to food
  • Cons:
    • Extremely heavy
    • Takes a long time to heat up (fuel use issues)
    • High maintenance (seasoning, rust risk)
    • Reactive to acidic foods (strips seasoning)

Cast Iron in the Outdoors

Cast iron cookware is best suited for car camping or permanent campsites due to its significant weight and size.

While cast iron offers excellent durability and heat retention, these qualities come at the cost of portability. It is simply too heavy and cumbersome to carry over long distances, making it impractical for hiking or backpacking trips where every ounce matters.

However, for scenarios where transport is not an issue, cast iron remains a fantastic choice for outdoor cooking, providing reliable performance and versatility.



Titanium Cookware: The Ultralight Specialist

NatureHike Titanium Lightweight Cookware

Buy Now

TOAKS Titanium Pot w/ Pan

Buy Now

TOAKS Titanium Pot w/ Bail Handle

Buy Now

TOAKS Titanium 6.5” Frying Pan

Buy Now

Another much-loved cookware material is titanium, which brings its own unique set of strengths to the table, especially for outdoor cooking enthusiasts.

The Science of the Strength-to-Weight Ratio

Titanium's incredible strength enables cookware to be manufactured with ultra-thin walls, drastically reducing its overall weight.

This unique property makes titanium cookware an ideal choice for ultralight backpacking trips where every gram counts.

The thin walls allow titanium to conduct heat quickly, making it exceptionally efficient at boiling water.

This efficiency not only saves precious fuel but also reduces the time needed to prepare hot beverages, a critical convenience when you're out in the wilderness with limited resources.

Best Use Cases:

Titanium cookware is excellent for boiling water quickly, making it ideal for preparing tea, coffee, and dehydrated meals.

Its efficiency and lightweight nature make it a perfect choice for hikers and backpackers.

Pros and Cons of Pure Titanium

  • Pros:
    • Incredibly lightweight
    • Rust-proof and non-corrosive
    • Non-reactive to all foods (pure titanium)
    • High melting point (camp-safe)
    • Nearly indestructible.
  • Cons:
    • Severe hot spots (poor heat distribution)
    • Very poor heat retention (cools instantly)
    • High cost
    • Food burns easily.

Modern Titanium-Coated Pans vs. Pure Titanium Cookware

Modern titanium-coated non-stick pans and pure titanium cookware both carry the "titanium" name, but they serve very different purposes.

Titanium-coated non-stick pans are designed for home use, offering durability, convenience, and ease of use. These pans typically have an aluminium or stainless steel base coated with a titanium-reinforced non-stick layer. This design ensures even heat distribution, good heat retention, and a surface that's easy to cook on and clean.

They’re great for everyday tasks like frying eggs or sautéing vegetables. However, the titanium layer is part of the non-stick coating, not pure metal, and can wear down over time with heavy use or improper care.

Pure titanium cookware, on the other hand, is built for durability and portability, making it ideal for outdoor enthusiasts. Unlike titanium-coated pans, pure titanium doesn’t have a non-stick surface and doesn’t distribute or retain heat as well.

However, it’s extremely lightweight, corrosion-resistant, and nearly indestructible, making it perfect for camping. It’s ideal for tasks like boiling water or cooking simple meals in tough conditions.

In summary, titanium-coated non-stick pans are best for home kitchens, offering practicality and ease for daily cooking. Pure titanium cookware, meanwhile, is made for outdoor adventures, focusing on durability and portability.




The Ultimate Head-to-Head Comparison

Metric Cast Iron Titanium Winner
Thermal Conductivity (Heat Spread) Low-Moderate Very Low Cast Iron (Better for cooking)
Thermal Retention (Heat Hold) Excellent Poor Cast Iron
Weight/Portability Impractical for carrying Excellent for carrying Titanium
Durability (Lifetime) Multi-Generational Multi-Generational Tie (Both are incredibly tough)
Cost Low to Moderate High (Premium) Cast Iron
Health/Reactivity Reacts with acid; adds iron Non-reactive; inert Titanium
Cleaning Requires careful scraping/oiling Very Easy (especially for boiling) Titanium




The Verdict: Choosing the Right Tool for the Job

Choosing the right material comes down to its main roles. Cast iron retains heat exceptionally well, making it ideal for consistent, flavorful cooking in the kitchen or over a campfire.

Titanium, however, is lightweight and portable, perfect for hikers needing quick, hassle-free meals outdoors.

The choice depends on whether you value cooking performance or portability.

Choose Cast Iron If:

  • You cook at home or car camp.
  • Your primary goal is searing, deep frying, or achieving a deep, caramelised crust.
  • You value food quality and heat consistency over weight.
  • You are willing to maintain and season your pan.

Choose Titanium If:

  • You are an ultralight backpacker, climber, or bikepacker.
  • Your primary goal is boiling water quickly (for coffee, tea, or rehydrating meals).
  • You need the absolute lightest, most compact, and rust-proof gear for the trail.

title: Wild Camping Rules: How to Pitch Up Without Breaking the Law
author: Laurence Kay
excerpt: Wild camping is booming in popularity, but with increased popularity, it's even more important to follow the wild camping rules to avoid communities and authorities clamping down on the practice. If you're new to wild ca
html:
Wild camping is booming in popularity, but with increased popularity, it's even more important to follow the wild camping rules to avoid communities and authorities clamping down on the practice.

If you're new to wild camping, you may not be aware of the rules and regulations surrounding it. But fear not, we've got you covered with our guide on how to pitch up without breaking the law.

Wild Camping Rules At A Glance:

 

  • Wild camping rules vary across the UK, with Scotland allowing it on most unenclosed land, while England and Wales generally require landowner permission.

  • Dartmoor is the main exception in England, where wild camping is legally permitted in designated areas when guidelines are followed.

  • In places like the Lake District and Snowdonia, wild camping is informally tolerated on high ground if campers arrive late, leave early, and leave no trace.

  • Responsible wild camping means no fires, no litter, minimal impact, and being ready to move on if asked.

Following local rules and Leave No Trace principles helps protect access rights for future campers.

The Legal Map: Where Can You Actually Wild Camp?

Each region of Britain has different rules when it comes to wild camping, which can make it harder if you're looking to wild camp your way around the country.

Scotland: The Gold Standard

Scotland, under the Land Reform (Scotland) Act 2003, offers some of the best outdoor access rights in the UK, allowing people to camp legally on most unenclosed land.

This law ensures everyone can enjoy Scotland’s stunning countryside while following responsible access rules.

To make the most of these rights, it’s important to follow the Scottish Outdoor Access Code, which advises campers to avoid littering, respect wildlife, and stay away from homes and farmland.

Some areas, like Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park, have additional restrictions.

Due to high visitor numbers and environmental concerns, a seasonal permit system for wild camping is in place from March to September.

These permits help protect the area and promote sustainable use. Always check for local restrictions and plan ahead for a safe and enjoyable wild camping experience in Scotland.

England & Wales: The "Permission First" Rule

Wild camping in England and Wales is considered civil trespass if done without the landowner's consent.

This means that, technically, setting up a campsite on private land without permission is not a criminal act but a civil matter.

Landowners have the legal right to ask you to leave their property, and it is always advisable to respect their wishes and seek consent beforehand.

While some landowners may grant permission, many areas remain off-limits, making it essential to research and plan carefully to avoid disputes or disruptions.

The Dartmoor Exception (2026 Update)

In May 2025, a Supreme Court ruling re-established the legal right to wild camp on Dartmoor Commons without landowner permission.

This decision overturned previous restrictions, making Dartmoor the only area in England and Wales where this right is legally protected.

The ruling was a victory for outdoor enthusiasts and conservationists, highlighting the importance of public access to nature.

To protect this right to wild camping, it's important to follow Leave No Trace principles and the guidelines set by the Dartmoor National Park Authority (DNPA).

If you're planning a trip, use the official DNPA camping map to see where wild camping is allowed.

The "High-Fell" Tolerance

While England and Wales have limited legal rights to wild camp, the Lake District and Snowdonia (Eryri) have developed an informal tolerance towards responsible wild camping.

This unwritten "high-fell" agreement allows campers to pitch their tents discreetly above the fell line, away from paths and valleys, provided they adhere to Leave No Trace principles.

Camping in these areas is typically accepted for a single night, as long as visitors avoid disturbing wildlife, leave no litter, and cause no lasting impact on the landscape.

Both National Parks encourage this careful and respectful approach, recognising its value for those seeking solitude and a deeper connection with nature, while balancing the need to preserve these cherished environments.

The "Leave No Trace" Masterclass

We've mentioned the Leave No Trace principles a few times already, and if you're a seasoned camper or outdoorsman, you'll already be familiar with them.

If not, here's a quick overview of the Leave No Trace philosophy:

  • Arrive Late, Leave Early - The "Dusk till Dawn" Rule 

This guideline encourages campers and outdoor enthusiasts to minimise their impact by arriving at sites late in the day and leaving early the next morning.

By doing so, you'll limit your interaction with wildlife during their most active hours and reduce the potential for disturbing their natural routines. It’s a simple practice that promotes harmony with nature while leaving less evidence of your visit.

  • Toilet Etiquette - The "6-6-200" Rule 

When answering nature’s call in the backcountry, follow the "6-6-200" rule. Dig a cathole six inches deep and six inches wide, and ensure it's at least 200 feet (about 70 adult steps) away from any water sources, trails, or campsites. 

This keeps water sources uncontaminated and ensures minimal disruption to the environment. For toilet paper, one easy solution is to use dog poo bags to carry it out.

  • Fire vs. Stoves - Why Open Fires Are a Red Line

While a traditional campfire might seem appealing, the ecological impact of open fires cannot be overstated. Collecting wood can harm fragile ecosystems, and fires leave scars on the landscape that can last for years. 

Instead, opt for high-efficiency stoves like Soto or Jetboil, which are compact, reliable, and significantly reduce your environmental footprint. 

By using these stoves, you’ll practice a responsible way to cook that aligns with Leave No Trace values.

  • Waste Management - "If You Carry It In, Carry It Out"

This rule is simple yet essential. Whatever you bring into the wilderness, be prepared to carry it out. Proper waste management keeps ecosystems clean and safe for wildlife. 

Take it a step further by picking up litter left behind by others. Each act of care contributes to preserving these spaces for future generations and aligns with the true spirit of Leave No Trace.

Equipment: Staying Safe and Discreet

Staying safe and discreet while wild camping is key to a successful trip for both you and the wildlife around you. 

Below are some of our top recommendations for wild camping equipment. For a more in-depth look, check out our 17 wild camping essentials.

Discreet Shelter

Earthy-toned tents and tarps, such as those in shades of forest green, brown, or grey, are widely considered essential for blending into natural surroundings while wild camping.

These colours mimic the hues commonly found in forests, meadows, and other outdoor environments, making your presence less noticeable to both wildlife and other campers.

This not only helps maintain the unspoiled aesthetic of the area but also ensures minimal disturbance to animals in their natural habitats.

Also, using these subdued tones demonstrates respect for the environment and minimises the visual impact of human activity, aligning with the principles of responsible and low-impact camping.



Lightweight Gear

Heavy festival tents are not allowed on Dartmoor because of the need to protect its unique environment. As a National Park, Dartmoor’s delicate ecosystems require campers to minimise their impact.

Festival tents are often bulky, hard to transport, and leave a larger environmental footprint. They are also made with less durable materials, which can lead to damage, litter, and harm to the landscape.

These tents are discouraged in other areas for the same reasons, as they don’t align with responsible camping practices. Instead, lightweight and portable tents are recommended to make carrying easier, reduce disturbance, and follow "leave no trace" principles.



Water Safety

Carrying a lot of water on outdoor trips is a hassle. A better way to stay hydrated is to use water filters and purifiers. These lightweight devices let you clean water from natural sources like streams and rivers, so you don't have to carry it all with you.

  • Water filters remove impurities, sediment, and harmful microorganisms.
  • Purifiers take it a step further by also eliminating viruses.

To use one, just collect water and follow the device’s instructions, which might involve pumping or squeezing.

Using a filter or purifier reduces your pack weight and gives you access to safe drinking water on your adventure. Just make sure to choose one that's right for the environment you'll be in.



What Happens if You're Asked to Move?

When exploring nature or venturing into unfamiliar areas, it's essential to respect private land and adhere to the "Be Nice" rule.

This unwritten guideline reminds outdoor enthusiasts to be courteous and cooperative if asked to leave private property. It's important to understand that trespass is typically a civil matter, not a criminal offence.

However, if you refuse to leave after being asked, the situation could escalate to "Aggravated Trespass," which is a criminal action under UK law.

By maintaining a respectful and understanding attitude, you can avoid conflicts and ensure your outdoor activities remain enjoyable and lawful.

On a practical note, always try to keep your kit organised so you can pack up in 5 minutes if a landowner asks you to move!

Conclusion: Preserving the Right to Roam

Responsible camping today is essential for safeguarding the freedom to enjoy the great outdoors for future generations. By sticking to local regulations, respecting landowners, and leaving no trace, campers help demonstrate that the right to roam can coexist harmoniously with private and protected lands.

Every camper’s responsible behaviour today serves as a powerful statement that these privileges are valued and should remain available for years to come.

title: Car Camping vs. Wild Camping: Which One is Right for Your Next Adventure?
author: Laurence Kay
excerpt: Car camping vs. wild camping, both options offer unique experiences and adventures for outdoor enthusiasts. While they may sound similar, there are some key differences between the two that can help you decide which one
html:
Car camping vs. wild camping, both options offer unique experiences and adventures for outdoor enthusiasts. While they may sound similar, there are some key differences between the two that can help you decide which one is right for your next adventure.

Whether you've tried one and are curious about the other or you're looking to venture outside of regulated campsites for the first time, it's important to understand the benefits and drawbacks of both car camping and wild camping. Let's dive deeper into each option.

The Core Differences: At a Glance

Feature Car Camping Wild Camping
Access Roadside, laybys, or campsites On foot, boat, or bike
Gear Weight Weight doesn't matter (bring the cast iron!) Ultralight is essential
Legality Often restricted (Road Traffic Act) Legal in Scotland; "Permission required" in most of the UK
Facilities Often near toilets/pubs Zero facilities (dig a hole)

Legality: The "No-Go" Zones for Vehicles

Because car camping is quite different to wild camping, there are some specific no-go zones that apply to vehicles that don't apply to wild campers.

The "Roadside" Myth

In Scotland, the Right to Access allows people to explore the outdoors responsibly, including wild camping, but it explicitly excludes motor vehicles.

This means the legal protections for wild camping under the Land Reform (Scotland) Act 2003 do not apply to camping in your car. Parking up and sleeping in your vehicle by the side of a road is considered "roadside camping" rather than "wild camping."

While many travellers enjoy this practice, it falls outside the intended spirit and legal framework of wild camping, which is focused on non-motorised, low-impact camping in remote areas.

It’s essential to check local guidance and ensure you're complying with any regulations or restrictions when roadside camping in Scotland.

Dartmoor 2025/2026 Update

It is important to note that while backpack wild camping continues to be legally protected on Dartmoor, camping in a vehicle remains strictly prohibited.

This distinction is crucial, as camping in a vehicle does not fall under the rights granted for wild camping in the area.

Engaging in vehicle camping on Dartmoor can result in fines and enforcement action, so visitors are urged to adhere to the regulations to preserve the integrity of the national park and avoid legal repercussions.

Always ensure your camping activities align with the guidelines to help maintain Dartmoor's natural beauty for everyone to enjoy.

England & Wales

In England and Wales, trespass is a civil offence, not a criminal one. This means you can't be arrested for it.

However, if you refuse to leave or aggravate the landowner, things can escalate to aggravated trespass which is a criminal offence.

This is far more likely to happen if you've driven a vehicle onto their land without permission, as it causes more damage to the ground and more disruption than a tent.

Whether you're wild camping or vehicle camping, it's essential to get the landowner's permission first to avoid any issues. Asking for consent helps build good relationships with landowners and ensures they remain welcoming to responsible campers.

By respecting private property, campers can help maintain a balance that allows for sustainable and lawful access for everyone in the future.

Pros and Cons of Car Camping Vs Wild Camping

Car Camping

  • Pros: High comfort, no weight limit, easy "bail out" if the weather turns, great for families.
  • Cons: Noisy roads, limited privacy, "stealth" concerns in urban areas.
  • Best for: Weekend road trips and basecamps for hiking.

Wild Camping

  • Pros: Total silence, waking up to incredible views, true "Leave No Trace" experience.
  • Cons: Physically demanding, requires technical gear knowledge, and is weather-dependent.
  • Best for: Solo adventurers and those seeking a "reset" from modern life.

Our Top Equipment Picks For Car Camping

When it comes to car camping, your equipment needs are notably different from those required for wild camping.

Since you're not carrying your gear on your back, there's no need to worry about weight or compactness. This gives you the flexibility to bring larger and more comfortable items that can enhance your experience.

For example, while a good sleeping bag is essential for keeping warm, you won’t need a sleeping mat because you’ll already have the comfort of your car as a base.

The Golden Rule: Leave No Trace

Whether you're exploring the wilderness in a Land Rover or spending the night in a 1-man tent, the principles of Leave No Trace (LNT) are non-negotiable. Here are the basic rules you should be following:

  • Plan Ahead and Prepare: Research the area, pack efficiently, and ensure you're equipped for minimal impact.
  • Dispose of Waste Properly: Carry out all rubbish, including biodegradable items, and never leave waste behind.
  • Respect Wildlife: Observe animals from a distance and avoid interfering with their natural behaviour.
  • Minimise Campfire Impact: Use a portable stove where possible and only build fires in designated areas if allowed.

  • Wild campers should adhere to the rule of pitching their tents at dusk and leaving at dawn. This practice minimises the impact on wildlife and ensures that natural habitats are respected.

title: The JustSupplies Guide to Solo Camping Safety & Self-Reliance
author: Laurence Kay
excerpt: Solo camping safety should be your top priority before and during any unaccompanied trip. While solo camping isn't necessarily dangerous, it does have a zero margin for error and requires a bit of extra planning to keep
html:
Solo camping safety should be your top priority before and during any unaccompanied trip. While solo camping isn't necessarily dangerous, it does have a zero margin for error and requires a bit of extra planning to keep yourself safe.

When it's just you against the wilderness, you need to have the appropriate skills and gear to handle a situation without immediate external help.

To help you master the art of self-rescue, our guide provides you with the framework you need to stay safe while enjoying solitude in the UK's wild spaces.

Solo Camping Safety At A Glance:

  • Plan thoroughly before you go: leave a detailed itinerary (“dead man’s handle”), check mountain-specific forecasts (Met Office or MWIS), and identify escape routes using OS Maps.
  • Use reliable communication backups: don’t rely on the 999 signal myth. Carry a PLB or satellite messenger and manage battery life with fully charged power banks.
  • Carry a customised first aid kit with critical additions such as SAM splints, haemostatic dressings, water purification tablets, and a whistle for distress signalling.
  • Choose campsites carefully: avoid widow makers, camp 30–50m from water, follow strict fire safety rules, and adjust precautions for summer heat or winter cold.
  • Manage hydration, body temperature, and personal security by filtering water, using a 3-season sleeping bag, trusting your instincts, and minimising attention when camping solo.

 

Pre-Trip Safety Strategies

A large part of staying safe while on solo camping adventures is actually done in the planning stages. Making sure you're prepped and ready for being alone against the elements can save you when the going gets rough.

Here are our top tips for putting pre-trip safety strategies in place:

1. Leaving a Dead Man's Handle

As with any trip, you should always inform a friend or family member of when and where you're going, but with solo camping, you need to be more detailed.

We recommend providing your trusted loved one with a detailed itinerary of your trip to help raise the alarm as soon as possible if something goes awry and you can't contact anyone yourself.

A detailed itinerary should include:

  • Parked car location
  • planned route (detailed trail route)
  • Planned camp spots
  • A call-by time (When they should call Mountain Rescue if they haven't heard from you)

2. Avoiding The Weather Trap

We all know to check the weather when planning a camping trip, if only to make sure we have the right gear with us, but the BBC weather app or your phone's default weather widget doesn't cut it when you only have yourself to rely on if things take a turn.

Using the Met Office's Mountain Forecasts or the MWIS (Mountain Weather Information Service) will give you a much more comprehensive and accurate overview of the weather conditions throughout your trip and will help you prepare properly.

3. Doing a Terrain Recon

Even if you're planning to trek a well-known, well-worn trail, it's important to do a terrain recon to make sure you're prepared if something happens on the trail.

If you're hiking at a wet time of the year (any time in the UK!), there can be a risk of landslides, mudslides, or fallen trees that can block your intended path.

We recommend using OS Maps to identify potential escape routes in advance. These routes should be the fastest path to a road, not just the fastest back to your car, as this gets you to a possible rescue quicker if necessary.

Preparing Reliable Communication Methods

We all have a mobile phone these days, but they're not always the most reliable form of communication, especially when you're heading off-grid and into the wilderness.

To prevent you from being cut off from civilisation, here are our top tips for prepping reliable methods of communication with loved ones or emergency services.

Feature Mobile Phone Satellite Messenger (Garmin) PLB (Personal Locator Beacon)
Reliability Low (Signal Dependent) High (Global Coverage) Highest (Direct to SAR)
Two-way Messaging Yes Yes No
Battery Life 12-24 Hours 10-20 Days 5+ Years (Standby)
Best For Casual/Near Civilisation Long Treks / Remote "Life or Limb" Emergencies

1. The 999 Myth, Busted

Many hikers rely on the idea that you can still phone 999 if you don't have any signal, but this isn't exactly true and could leave you high and dry at the worst possible time.

While it's true that you can call 999 if you can't get a signal from your specific mobile provider, if there's no signal in the area at all (a true dead spot), then you won't be able to make that all-important call. That's why you need a backup method of communication when camping alone.

2. Using Satellite Technology

PLBs (Personal Locator Beacons) and Satellite Messengers are essential tools for safety and communication in remote areas. While both help you get assistance when needed, they have different features and uses.

Feature Personal Locator Beacons (PLB) Satellite Messengers
Primary Purpose Dedicated emergency distress signal. Emergency SOS + non-emergency check-ins.
Communication One-way: Outbound signal to rescue services only. Two-way: Send and receive texts/emails to anyone.
Subscription Fees None. One-time purchase cost only. Required. Monthly or annual service plans.
Reliability Highest. Powerful signal; works in extreme conditions. High. Reliable, but the signal can be weaker than a PLB.
Extra Features No-frills; GPS location tracking only. Location sharing, social media updates, and weather.
Battery Life Long-term. Typically 5+ years (no charging needed). Short-term. Rechargeable, similar to a smartphone.
Best For Serious "Life or Limb" emergencies only. Keeping in touch and routine safety updates.

Both devices are valuable, but choosing between a PLB and a Satellite Messenger depends on your needs, budget, and how much communication you want during your adventures.

3. Employing Power Management

EVO Repeller 3-in-1

Buy Now

When heading into remote or challenging environments, looking after the battery life of your communication devices is crucial.

Having a fully charged powerbank and making sure all your devices are fully charged before you leave means that even if things take a turn, you'll have the charge to make emergency calls or use GPS apps.

If you're on a longer trip, we'd recommend either keeping the active use of your devices to a minimum to preserve the battery life or bringing a larger battery pack that can provide enough energy to charge your devices multiple times.



Solo First Aid Kit Essentials

When you're by yourself in the wilderness, small cuts and minor injuries can quickly become serious if they're not properly treated, so having an appropriately stocked first aid kit is crucial when solo camping.

While there are many first aid kits you can purchase already stocked, we always recommend adding to these pre-made first aid kits to customise them to the terrain you're covering.

Solo camping first aid kits should cover:

  • Blisters
  • Open wounds
  • Sickness
  • Blunt Trauma
  • Pain relief
  • Immobilisation


Critical Additions to Basic First Aid Kits

Buying a basic first aid kit is a good start, but there are a few critical things you should add to your kit to keep yourself safe on your solo adventures.

SAM Splints are an essential addition, particularly for dealing with sprained ankles when you still need to make it back to your car. These lightweight and mouldable splints provide necessary support, allowing you to keep moving safely.

Haemostatic Dressings, on the other hand, are a lifesaver for significant cuts, especially when handling sharp tools like bushcraft knives. These dressings help to control heavy bleeding effectively until further medical help is available.

Water Purification Tablets are vital for making natural water sources safe to drink if you find yourself stuck and without clean water for a few days.

A strong whistle, like the BCB Howler Whistle, in your kit can be used to perform the six blasts that form the international distress signal, helping rescuers locate you if you’re immobile or trapped in an emergency.


A 1-day wilderness first aid course teaches you the skills to handle emergencies in the wild. You'll learn how to treat injuries like broken bones, hypothermia, and severe bleeding, as well as perform CPR in challenging conditions.


Risk Mitigation: Camp Site Selection & Security

When you're camping alone, you're solely responsible for mitigating the risks you take. To help you stay safe when solo camping, here are our top tips for staying safe and secure.

Basic Camp Set Up Safety

Before setting up camp, check the area for hazards like "widow makers", which are dead or unstable branches that can fall without warning, especially in high winds or after rain. Look up and scan the tree canopy for hanging branches or decaying trees. Avoid pitching your tent beneath them to stay safe.

When camping alone, fire safety is critical. Choose a site away from trees, dry grass, or flammable materials, with at least a three-meter cleared area. Use a fire ring or designated fire pit if available, and keep water or soil nearby to control the flames.

Never leave your fire unattended, and fully extinguish it before sleeping or leaving.

Set up camp 30–50 meters from rivers, lakes, or streams to reduce risks like flash flooding or soggy ground.

Seasonal Safety Concerns

Of course, the time of year you undertake your camping trip can come with specific safety concerns you need to be aware of.

Summer Safety Tips

  • Stay Hydrated: Drink plenty of water throughout the day to avoid dehydration, especially in hot weather. Carry electrolyte tablets or sports drinks to replenish lost salts.
  • Protect Against the Sun: Wear sunscreen with a high SPF, a wide-brimmed hat, and UV-protective sunglasses. Opt for lightweight, breathable clothing that covers your skin to minimise sunburn risk.
  • Avoid Overexertion: High temperatures can cause heat exhaustion or heatstroke. Plan strenuous activities for the early morning or late evening when it's cooler and pace yourself appropriately.
  • Be Aware of Wildlife: Summer heat may increase wildlife activity. Secure your food properly and stay vigilant to avoid encounters.
  • Choose an Appropriate Campsite: Find shade where possible and avoid camping in areas prone to excessive heat buildup, such as bare rock faces.

Winter Safety Tips

  • Dress in Layers: Wear thermal, moisture-wicking base layers, insulating mid-layers, and a windproof, waterproof outer layer. Avoid cotton, which absorbs moisture and loses heat retention.
  • Prevent Hypothermia and Frostbite: Keep extremities warm with insulated gloves and thick wool socks. Cover exposed skin, especially on your face, when temperatures drop significantly.
  • Stay Dry: Wet clothing can accelerate the cooling of your body. Pack extra dry clothes and use waterproof gear to protect against snow or rain.
  • Build a Windbreak: Set up your tent in a sheltered area to avoid direct exposure to harsh winds.
  • Stay Nourished and Warm: Eat calorie-rich foods to maintain energy levels and keep your body temperature up. Use an insulated bottle to prevent your water supply from freezing.
  • Carry Emergency Supplies: Always pack a space blanket, hand warmers, and a signal device in case of extreme cold or emergencies.



Social Safety Concerns

For all solo campers, but especially women, it is essential to remain vigilant about social safety while camping.

One effective tactic is to practice ghost camping, which involves arriving at your campsite at dusk and departing at dawn. This approach minimises the time spent in one location, reducing the likelihood of drawing attention.

Trust your instincts; if a campsite feels "off" or if you encounter someone who makes you feel uneasy, don’t hesitate to move on. Your safety and peace of mind are far more important than staying in a particular spot.

You can also improve your tent's security by using locking carabiners to "lock" your tent zips from the inside while you sleep. This simple step adds an extra layer of safety and can help you sleep more soundly knowing your tent is secured.

Sustenance & Health: The Invisible Risks

When exposing yourself to the elements, there are some invisible risks that can make or break your solo camping trip.

Managing Your Hydration Levels

Nalgene 32oz Bottle

Buy Now

Dehydration is a serious concern when camping or spending extended periods outdoors. It can lead to poor decision-making, reduced cognitive function, and physical effects like clumsiness, which can increase the risk of accidents.

Staying hydrated is essential to maintaining both mental clarity and physical coordination, especially in unpredictable environments.

To avoid dehydration, consider investing in smart water filtration systems like LifeStraw bottles, which allow you to easily and safely filter water from natural sources.

Always monitor your water intake and refill whenever possible to minimise these risks.



Managing Your Body Temperature

Even in the summer, temperatures can plummet to 0°C, especially on mountain trails where the environment is more unpredictable.

This drop in temperature can be particularly challenging when camping alone, as there's no one to share body heat with in the colder hours of the night.

For this reason, it is crucial to invest in a reliable 3-season sleeping bag that offers adequate insulation and protection against unexpected chills.



Final Thoughts: Empowerment Through Preparation

Solo camping puts your outdoor skills to the test. It requires resilience, resourcefulness, and a connection with nature. When you're out in the wilderness alone, you rely completely on your own abilities to survive and thrive.

Safety isn't about being afraid; it's about being prepared and capable. Being capable means understanding your environment, knowing the risks, and having the skills to handle them.

Solo trips can be an empowering experience, showing you what you can achieve when you trust yourself and respect the outdoors.

title: The Ultimate Guide to Stealth Sleeping Systems
author: Laurence Kay
excerpt: Standard camping gear is designed for visibility and comfort, but stealth requires the opposite: low profile, neutral tones, and rapid deployment. That's why having solid stealth sleeping systems is a crucial part of any
html:
Standard camping gear is designed for visibility and comfort, but stealth requires the opposite: low profile, neutral tones, and rapid deployment. That's why having solid stealth sleeping systems is a crucial part of any off-grid camping kit.

Whether you're new to stealth camping or want to improve your powers of invisibility, knowing how to build a sleeping system that allows you to vanish into the treeline and leave no trace by sunrise is key.

Stealth Sleeping Systems At A Glance:

There are three main types of stealth sleeping systems:

Hammock Sleeping Systems

Hammock sleeping systems consist of a lightweight hammock, suspension straps, and a rainfly. They provide a comfortable and elevated sleeping experience, making them a popular choice for stealth camping. However, they typically require trees or sturdy anchor points to set up.

Bivvy Sleeping Systems

Bivvys are essentially waterproof sleeping bags that provide minimal shelter. They are lightweight and compact, making them convenient for stealth camping in remote areas. Bivvys also offer excellent protection from the elements, but can be uncomfortable for extended periods due to limited space.

Tarp Sleeping Systems

Tarp systems involve using a simple tarp as a makeshift shelter. They offer the most flexibility in terms of setup and can be easily adjusted depending on the terrain and weather conditions. However, they require more skill and practice to set up efficiently.

Anatomy of a Stealth Sleeping System

One piece of gear alone doesn't make a system, and while you want to keep your kit to a minimum when you're stealth camping, you need multiple components to keep you comfortable and warm overnight.

The Three Pillars of Stealth Gear

  1. Functional and practical shelter
  2. Adequate insulation from the elements
  3. Footprint management

Pillar 1: The Shelter

Shelter is the most important part of your stealth camping gear, especially in the UK, where the weather can change through three seasons in a day.

The Bivvy Bag

3F UL Gear Tyvek Bivvy Bag

Buy Now

Bushman Hideout Warm Bivvy

Buy Now

 

OneWind Solo Bivvy Tent

Buy Now

The bivvy bag is often considered the best option for stealth camping because of its low profile, minimal footprint, and ease of use. Its compact design helps it blend into the environment, making it less noticeable than a traditional tent. This is especially useful when discretion is important.

The bivvy bag also aligns with the principles of Leave No Trace, as it leaves almost no impact on the landscape. Another big advantage is how quickly it can be set up or packed away, allowing campers to stay mobile and efficient.

These features make the bivvy bag a must-have for anyone wanting to camp stealthily and responsibly.

 

The Micro-Tarp

Micro-tarps are a great solution for outdoor enthusiasts looking for both comfort and concealment. Lightweight and compact, they provide enough coverage to protect you and your gear from the elements while staying low-profile.

A 1.5m x 2.5m tarp is a good size, offering flexible setup options for different terrains and conditions. Configurations like the "plough point" or "lean-to" help you blend into your surroundings while keeping you shielded from wind and rain.

These setups are ideal for stealth camping or minimalist adventures, offering protection without drawing attention.

 

The Low-Drag Tent

When stealth camping, a low-profile tent is essential. Choose one under 1 metre in height to stay discreet and blend in with your surroundings. Tunnel tents are great for this.

This makes it harder to spot, even in open areas. Tents in natural colours like green or brown also help you stay hidden, making them perfect for stealth camping.

Read our guide to choosing the right tent to avoid excess weight.

 

Pillar 2: The Insulation

When you're stealth camping, insulation is all about having warmth without the bulk. Not only do thick sleeping bags weigh more, but they also make you more obvious when you want to be incognito.

The Sleeping Bag

When choosing a stealth sleeping bag, a central zip is an important feature to look for. It makes getting in and out quick and easy, especially in tight spaces like small tents or hidden campsites.

A central zip is also practical for making quick exits if you need to pack up and leave in a hurry. This design adds both convenience and preparedness, making it a great option for anyone who values functionality while stealth camping.

 

The Sleeping Mat

A good sleeping mat is essential for a comfortable night's sleep, providing insulation from the cold ground and cushioning for your body. However, when stealth camping, it's important to choose your sleeping mat wisely.

Avoid crinkly ultralight air mats that rustle like a crisp packet with every movement, as they can easily give away your position. Instead, look for self-inflating options or closed-cell foam mats.

These alternatives are silent while still offering excellent comfort and support, making them ideal for staying both stealthy and well-rested.

 

Liners and Layers

A silk or thermal sleeping bag liner is an excellent way to enhance the versatility of your gear without adding bulk or complexity.

By slipping one into your lightweight 2-season sleeping bag, you can effectively boost its warmth, turning it into a 3-season option.

This small addition can make a big difference on cooler nights, providing extra insulation without increasing your pack size or making packing up more difficult.

 

Pillar 3: Footprint Management

When it comes to stealth camping, you need to be mindful of the footprint you're leaving during your camp and after you've left. 

Here are our expert tips on how to manage your footprint to leave as little trace as possible after you leave.

Light Discipline

When you're stealth camping, you'll inevitably need to do things in your camp after dark, so a head torch is a key part of your kit.

With that being said, to stay as hidden as possible and to avoid disrupting local wildlife, you should switch from the bright white LED mode to the less harsh red or green LED modes. This preserves night vision and reduces splash visibility.

 

Ground Footprint

3F UL Gear Lanshan Footprint

Buy Now

OneWind Ultralight Ground Sheet

Buy Now

Using sleeping bags, ground sheets, and other footprint gear that fit your body size is important for a few key reasons.

  1. It reduces the area you disturb while camping, helping to protect the natural environment and avoid damage to plants and soil.
  2. Compact gear is lighter and easier to pack, making your load easier to carry, which is especially important for stealth camping.

Bulky items take up more space and make it harder to stay discreet and mobile, which are both crucial for successful stealth camping.

Reflective Removal

When stealth camping, removing reflective cords, panels, and stickers from your gear is essential to staying undetected.

Reflective elements can catch and amplify light from headlamps, flashlights, or even moonlight, making your location more visible to others.

By eliminating these reflective surfaces, you reduce the chance of drawing attention to your campsite.

For reflectors that cannot be removed, it’s recommended to cover them with sniper tape. This durable, non-reflective tape effectively conceals shiny surfaces while still being easy to remove if needed.

Seasonal Configurations

 

Feature Summer Stealth Winter Stealth
Shelter Bug Bivvy + Small Tarp 4-Season Bivvy + Hooped Tent
Bag Snugpak Jungle Bag Snugpak Softie Expansion
Colourway Olive Drab / Camo Coyote / Brown / Grey

The Strike and Fade Approach

The strike and fade approach to stealth camping focuses on minimal disturbance and rapid deployment to maintain a low profile.

Below are the key elements of the strike and fade methodology:

The 20 Minute Rule

A crucial principle of stealth camping is the 20-minute rule. Aim to arrive at your chosen location at dusk, allowing you to use the diminishing light to obscure your movements.

From the time you arrive, you should be fully settled for the night within 20 minutes. This includes setting up your shelter and organising your gear quietly and efficiently.

Minimising your exposure time is essential to avoid drawing attention.

Cold Camp vs Hot Camp

When preparing your camp, you must decide whether to keep it a cold camp or a hot camp. A cold camp involves consuming only cold food and drink, thereby eliminating the need for any heat sources.

This ensures there are no visible light or smoke signatures, which are detectable even from a distance.

On the other hand, a hot camp requires additional considerations, such as using flameless heaters to warm meals or liquids discreetly. These devices produce less heat, light, and smoke than traditional methods but still carry a slight risk of detection.

Pack-to-Sleep Method

To maximise readiness, adopt the pack-to-sleep method. This involves keeping your rucksack either inside your bivvy bag or securely tucked at the foot end of your shelter.

This setup ensures that in the event of a disturbance, you can swiftly grab your gear and vacate the site within seconds, leaving minimal trace behind. This level of preparedness is vital for maintaining stealth and safety in unpredictable situations.

Final Thoughts: Preparation is Key for Stealth Camping

Stealth camping is undoubtedly a skill that takes time and practice to master. Observing the environment, staying silent, and leaving no trace are crucial competencies, but having the right gear can significantly ease the learning curve.

The right equipment not only enhances your efficiency but also helps you remain inconspicuous and prepared for any unexpected situations.

html:
The Great British summer is made for camping trips and hiking, with walkable mountains and gorgeous national parks, but the reality is more clouds of midges in the highlands and ticks in the New Forest. So, having the best UK bug repellents is key to a good trip!

Not all bug repellents are equal, with some melting plastic gear and others too weak to deal with persistent UK midges. With our team's expertise in surviving British summers, we've picked the most effective bug repellents to keep your adventures bite-free.

Best UK Bug Repellents: Top Picks at a Glance

  • Smidge Repellent (Picaridin-based) – Best overall for UK conditions, offering strong, odourless protection against midges with a water-resistant formula.
  • Mosquito Nets (Cocoon & Highlander) – Most effective for heavy infestations or travel, providing full physical protection day and night.
  • Citronella & Repellent Lanterns – Best natural/DEET-free option, ideal for campsites and outdoor spaces without damaging gear.
  • Flextail Repellent Devices – Best for families and camping setups, creating a safe, chemical-free protective zone around tents and seating areas.
  • After Bite & Zap Ease Relief – Essential for bite treatment, helping to quickly soothe irritation when prevention isn’t enough.

Understanding the "Big Three" Active Ingredients

Before we dive into our top picks, you need to understand the big three active ingredients that pop up in the most effective repellents.

DEET

Often regarded as the gold standard in bug repellents, DEET is renowned for its effectiveness and long-lasting protection against a wide range of biting insects.

However, its powerful formulation comes with a drawback. DEET can damage synthetic fabrics and plastics, such as watch straps, glasses, and various gear. Exercise caution when applying it around your essential items.

Picaridin (Icaridin/Saltidin)

Picaridin is a modern favourite and an excellent alternative to DEET. It has gained popularity for being odourless, non-greasy, and safe for use with most synthetic materials and gear.

With strong insect-repelling capabilities and none of DEET's drawbacks, Picaridin is a reliable choice for those prioritising comfort and practicality.

Citriodiol (Oil of Lemon Eucalyptus)

For those seeking a natural or plant-based option, Citriodiol, derived from oil of lemon eucalyptus, stands out as the most effective choice.

While not as long-lasting as DEET or Picaridin, it provides robust protection against insects and is an eco-friendly option for nature enthusiasts who prefer sustainable solutions.

Permethrin

Permethrin differs from other repellents as it is specifically used for treating clothing, gear, and outdoor fabrics rather than being applied directly to the skin.

When properly treated, clothing infused with permethrin provides long-lasting protection against insects, making it a practical choice for those spending extended periods in bug-prone environments.

Top Picks: Best UK Bug Repellents by Category

Not all bug repellents work for all bugs, so we've split our top picks into categories to help you find the best bug repellent for your camping trip.

Lightweight, portable, and easy to use, mosquito nets are an indispensable part of your travel kit for ensuring health and comfort in high-risk regions.


Best Natural/DEET-Free:

When looking for effective ways to protect yourself and your belongings, DEET-free or natural repellents offer a fantastic alternative.

These options are less likely to damage clothing or gear, making them ideal for both personal use and outdoor equipment.

Mosquito repellent candles, like Citronella Tealights, and lights like the Evo Repeller Mosquito Repeller Lantern are excellent additions to your protective measures, creating an insect-repelling barrier in outdoor spaces.


Best for Families/Kids:

Mosquito repellent pads are an ideal choice for camping trips with kids, ensuring your camping area stays free from mosquitoes and bugs.

These pads, like the Flextail Mosquito Repellent Mat, are easy to use, portable, and can be placed around tents, seating areas, or even near dining setups to create a protective barrier.

These handy electric repellents are free from harmful chemicals and don't require topical application on sensitive skin.

Simple yet effective, repellent pads offer peace of mind so you can focus on enjoying your outdoor adventure.

These are also great for festival trips to keep your hungover mornings free from bugs!


Best for Bite Relief:

After Bite Classic Pen

Buy Now

Zap Ease Bite Relief

Buy Now

Even with the best repellents, some bug bites are unavoidable, especially when camping or hiking. That's why it's a good idea to have bug relief products on hand.

Products like the After Bite Classic Pen or the Incognito Zap Ease Bite Relief can instantly soothe the itch and irritation from bites.

Using these can help you avoid scratching, which can lead to more discomfort or infection.


The "Midge Factor": Why the UK is Different

While mosquito repellents can be effective against many biting insects, they often fall short when it comes to the notorious Scottish midge.

This is because midges are much smaller than mosquitoes, with a wingspan of just a few millimetres, allowing them to bypass certain netted deterrents.

Their tiny size means they can easily manoeuvre through gaps larger than their microscopic bodies. That’s why a reliable midge net becomes indispensable in heavily infested areas.

When choosing a midge net, the mesh size is critical. Look for one with over 1000 holes per square inch to ensure it provides an effective barrier against these persistent pests.

A well-fitted midge net not only prevents bites but also offers peace of mind during outdoor activities.

Protecting Your Gear: The DEET Warning

DEET is a powerful and effective insect repellent, but it comes with a downside when it comes to your synthetic outdoor gear.

Acting as a solvent, DEET can break down materials such as plastics, waterproof coatings, and synthetic fabrics. This means that tents, waterproof jackets, and even the screens of electronic devices like GPS units can suffer damage if exposed to DEET.

The substance can cause fabrics to weaken, coatings to peel, and screens to cloud, compromising the functionality and durability of your gear.

It's essential to take precautions, such as applying DEET-based products away from your equipment, to protect your investment while staying insect-free.

Gear Safety Table

Repellent Effectiveness Against Insects Gear Safety Additional Notes
DEET High Risk of damage to plastics, waterproof coatings, and synthetic fabrics. Avoid direct contact with gear.
Picaridin High Safe for synthetic materials and plastics. Odourless, and doesn’t stain gear.
Natural (e.g. Citronella, Lemon Eucalyptus) Moderate Generally safe for all gear. Requires frequent reapplication.

 

Using the right repellent can help you balance insect protection with gear longevity. If your outdoor plans rely heavily on synthetic equipment, consider alternatives like picaridin or natural repellents to minimise potential damage.

Expert Tips for Maximising Protection

  • Layering: For the best protection, apply sunscreen first and allow it to absorb into your skin for at least 20 minutes before applying insect repellent. This ensures both products work effectively without compromising each other's performance.
  • Focus Areas: Pay extra attention to your ankles and wrists when applying repellent. These areas are common entry points for ticks and other crawling pests, so ensuring they're covered can significantly reduce your risk of bites.
  • The "Double Defence": Combine strategies for optimal protection by treating clothing like socks and trousers with Permethrin, a long-lasting insecticide. For exposed skin, use a repellent containing Picaridin for comprehensive coverage against bugs.
  • Timing Awareness: Be mindful of peak activity times for midges and other pests. These are typically at dawn and dusk, so plan your outdoor activities accordingly and increase your protection during these hours.

Conclusion: Getting the Best Insect Protection For Your Trip

Choosing the right insect repellent depends on where you'll be. If you're hiking in the Highlands where midges are common, you'll need a high-strength repellent designed for them.

For a garden BBQ in the city, a milder repellent for mosquitoes and other flying insects should be enough.

Matching your repellent to your environment ensures it works effectively without using stronger chemicals than necessary.

title: How much does it cost to start camping?
author: Laurence Kay

html:
How Much Does It Cost to Start Camping in the UK? A Realistic Beginner Budget Guide (2026)

If you’re thinking about getting into camping in the UK, one of the first questions you’ll probably ask is:

“How much does it actually cost to start camping?”

The honest answer is — less than most people think.

After over 30 years of camping experience, starting back in Scouts and continuing through wild camping and lightweight backpacking, I’ve helped plenty of beginners get their first setup together. A realistic beginner budget isn’t thousands of pounds — it’s about making smart choices and buying the right gear the first time.

In this guide, I’ll walk you through:

  • realistic starter costs

  • What gear do you actually need

  • hidden expenses beginners don’t expect

  • what not to waste money on

  • and how to build a setup that lasts for years

Whether you’re planning your first campsite trip or working toward wild camping later, this article will give you a clear starting point. 🏕️

The Real Cost of Starting Camping in the UK

Let’s start with realistic numbers.

Based on experience helping beginners build their first setups, here’s what you should expect:

Setup level Estimated cost
Entry-level beginner setup £300
Comfortable long-term setup £450
Buy once, cry once setup £1000

You can spend less than £300 — but that often leads to replacing gear quickly.

It’s usually better to buy reliable mid-range equipment that performs well and lasts longer, rather than ultra-cheap gear that struggles in British weather.

What Equipment Do You Actually Need to Start Camping?

Beginners are often surprised how small the essential kit list really is.

Here’s what you genuinely need for your first overnight trip in the UK.

Shelter

This can be:

  • a tent

  • or a tarp setup

Tents are easier for beginners and better for early confidence. Tarps are excellent once you gain experience or move into lightweight camping.

Sleeping Bag

A good sleeping bag makes or breaks your trip.

UK conditions mean even summer nights can feel cold — so don’t cut corners here.

Head Torch

A head torch is essential, not optional.

It keeps your hands free while:

  • cooking

  • setting up camp

  • packing gear after dark

Rucksack

Your pack needs to comfortably carry everything.

Avoid oversized expedition packs — beginners often go too big and overpack as a result.

Good Boots

Footwear is one of the smartest investments you can make.

Comfortable, supportive boots help prevent:

  • blisters

  • fatigue

  • ankle injuries

Cooking System

A simple gas stove setup is ideal for beginners.

Reliable starter stove systems from brands like:

  • Fire Maple

are lightweight, dependable, and excellent value.

Multi-Layer Clothing

Layering is essential in the UK outdoors.

Think:

  • base layer

  • insulation layer

  • waterproof outer shell

Avoid cotton where possible.

Spork

Simple. Lightweight. Does the job.

Reusable Water Bottle

Reliable hydration matters more than beginners expect.

A Typical Beginner Camping Setup Budget Breakdown

Here’s how a realistic £300 beginner setup often looks.

Item Estimated cost
Tent or tarp £80–£120
Sleeping bag £60–£100
Sleeping mat £30–£60
Rucksack £40–£80
Cooking system £30–£60
Head torch £15–£30
Water bottle £10–£20

That’s enough gear to safely and comfortably complete your first trips.

The Biggest Hidden Costs Beginners Don’t Expect

These are the extras that catch people out.

They’re not expensive individually — but they add up quickly.

Parking Fees

Especially common at national parks and countryside access points.

Fuel Costs

Travel is often the biggest hidden expense.

Remote campsites and trailheads aren’t always close to home.

Camping Gas

You’ll need replacement gas canisters regularly.

Water Containers

Essential once you start staying away from serviced campsites.

Clothing

Weather-appropriate layers matter more than people expect in the UK.

Food

Simple camp meals are affordable — but still part of your planning budget.

Campsite Costs Across the UK

If you’re just starting out, campsites are the best place to begin.

Typical UK prices look like this:

Campsite type Cost per night
Wild camping £0
Basic campsite field £15
Standard pitch £25
Serviced pitch £40

For beginners especially, starting on campsites builds confidence before moving into wild camping later.

Should Beginners Start With Wild Camping?

Short answer:

Usually no.

Wild camping is fantastic — it’s how many experienced backpackers prefer to travel — but beginners benefit from learning the basics first on campsites.

Campsites help you practise:

  • pitching your shelter

  • organising your kit

  • cooking outdoors

  • staying warm overnight

Once those skills feel natural, wild camping becomes far more enjoyable.

Don’t Waste Money on These Beginner Mistakes

One of the easiest ways to overspend when starting camping is buying the wrong things first.

Here are three common traps.

Overpriced Brand Names

Expensive doesn’t always mean better.

Reliable mid-range equipment often performs just as well for beginners.

Brands like:

  • Onewind Outdoors

  • Fire Maple

  • TOAKS

  • 3FUL Gear

offer excellent performance without premium-brand pricing.

Heavy and Bulky Equipment

This is especially important if you plan to backpack.

Heavy kit:

  • reduces distance you can travel

  • increases fatigue

  • makes trips less enjoyable

Lightweight gear improves your experience immediately.

Buying Too Much Gear Too Soon

You don’t need everything straight away.

Start simple.

Add equipment as your experience grows.

Why Spending Slightly More Early Saves Money Later

A common beginner question is:

“Should I just buy cheap gear first?”

Sometimes that works — but often it doesn’t.

Better-quality gear:

  • performs better in bad weather

  • packs smaller

  • weighs less

  • lasts longer

A £60 upgrade now can prevent replacing a £40 item later.

Over time, that approach saves money.

A Comfortable Beginner Setup (£450 Budget)

At around £450, your setup improves noticeably.

You’ll typically gain:

  • lighter shelter

  • warmer sleeping system

  • more reliable stove

  • better backpack comfort

  • improved waterproof layers

This is the level where most people start genuinely enjoying camping rather than just trying it.

The “Buy Once, Cry Once” Setup (£1000 Budget)

If you already know camping is something you’ll stick with, a £1000 setup builds a lightweight system that can last for years.

At this level you’ll usually get:

  • compact shelter

  • high-quality sleeping bag

  • lightweight cooking setup

  • durable backpack

  • reliable waterproof clothing

Many experienced backpackers still use gear bought at this level years later.

A Simple Strategy for Building Your First Camping Kit

Here’s what I usually recommend to beginners:

  1. Start with campsites

  2. Buy reliable mid-range gear

  3. Keep your kit lightweight

  4. Avoid unnecessary extras

  5. Upgrade gradually as experience grows

This approach keeps costs sensible and enjoyment high.

Final Thoughts: Camping in the UK Doesn’t Need to Be Expensive

Starting camping in the UK doesn’t require specialist equipment or a huge budget.

A realistic starting point is around £300, with £450 giving a much more comfortable long-term setup.

More important than spending money is buying the right equipment and learning how to use it well.

Start simple, build confidence on campsites, and expand your setup as your experience grows.

That’s the approach we recommend at JustSupplies Outdoors — practical, reliable gear and skills that help you enjoy time outside from your very first trip. 🌲🔥

title: Beginner Camping Gear Checklist UK: Everything You Need for Your First Trip

html:
Beginner Camping Gear Checklist UK: Everything You Need for Your First Trip

Getting ready for your first UK camping trip can feel overwhelming — tents, sleeping bags, cooking gear, clothing, and all the little extras add up fast.

After 30 years of camping experience — from Scouts to wild backpacking — I’ve helped beginners streamline their gear and avoid unnecessary spending. This checklist is designed for beginners with zero kit, giving you everything you need to get started confidently.

If you haven’t already, check out our realistic UK camping budget guide to see how much it costs to start camping and how to plan your setup according to your budget.

Shelter: Tent or Tarp

Your shelter is your most important piece of kit. For beginners, I recommend starting with a tent, as it’s easier to set up and offers more protection against UK weather.

Checklist:

  • Lightweight 1–2 person tent (or beginner-friendly tarp setup)
  • Groundsheet or footprint to protect the base
  • Tent pegs and guy lines

Brands I trust for beginners include:

  • Onewind Outdoors – durable, affordable tents
  • 3FUL Gear – excellent for lightweight setups

Sleeping System

A warm, comfortable sleep setup makes camping enjoyable rather than miserable.

Checklist:

  • Sleeping bag (suitable for UK summer nights or year-round if needed)
  • Sleeping mat for insulation and comfort
  • Pillow or stuff sack for head support

Brands to consider:

  • Snugpak
  • TOAKS

Cooking Essentials

Cooking outdoors is simple with the right gear.

Checklist:

  • Lightweight camping stove (gas or multi-fuel)
  • Fuel canisters
  • Compact cookware (pot, pan, mug)
  • Spork or utensil set
  • Reusable water bottle

Brands I recommend for beginners:

  • Fire Maple – reliable, beginner-friendly stoves
  • TOAKS – lightweight and durable

Clothing and Footwear

UK weather is unpredictable. Multi-layer clothing is essential.

Checklist:

  • Base layer (moisture-wicking)
  • Insulation layer (fleece or light jacket)
  • Waterproof outer layer
  • Comfortable hiking boots
  • Warm socks
  • Hat and gloves if camping in spring/autumn

Lighting and Navigation

Even short summer nights can get dark fast.

Checklist:

  • Head torch (keeps hands free)
  • Spare batteries
  • Compass or smartphone with GPS app

Backpack and Carrying Gear

Your rucksack is the home for all your gear.

Checklist:

  • Comfortable rucksack (sized for overnight or multi-day trips)
  • Rain cover for backpack
  • Packing cubes or dry bags for organisation

Safety and Extras

Beginner campers often forget these essentials:

Checklist:

  • First aid kit
  • Map and guidebook
  • Whistle or emergency signal
  • Lightweight knife or multi-tool

Optional Items for Comfort

  • Lightweight camping chair
  • Small camp towel
  • Notebook or journal
  • Lightweight camera

Tip: Beginners often overpack. Focus on essentials first. You can add extras once you’ve tried camping and know what works for you.

How Much Will This Gear Cost?

You can pair this checklist with your budget guide from How Much Does It Cost to Start Camping in the UK?.

Typical costs:

Budget level Gear & essentials cost
Beginner (£300) Basic tent, sleeping bag, stove, clothing
Comfortable (£450) Upgraded sleeping system, lightweight stove, better rucksack
Buy Once, Cry Once (£1000) High-quality, ultralight setup for long-term use

Starting simple keeps costs down, avoids decision fatigue, and ensures your first camping trips are enjoyable.

Final Tips for Beginners

  1. Start on campsites first – get your setup and skills right before moving to wild camping.
  2. Invest in quality essentials – better-performing gear often lasts longer and makes camping easier.
  3. Keep it lightweight – avoid carrying unnecessary items; it reduces fatigue.
  4. Gradually expand your kit – add extra comforts as you gain experience.

Following this checklist will give you a solid foundation to enjoy camping in the UK, whether you’re pitching your first tent in a local campsite or heading out on a multi-day backpacking adventure.

Whether you're on a family camping trip or a challenging multi-day hike, fueling yourself and your team is crucial in the wilderness. Having a strong camp kitchen setup can make feeding your campmates much easier and more enjoyable.

We've taken our wealth of experience with camp cooking equipment and trying to cook in a range of outdoor conditions to put together our ultimate guide to help you set up a functional camp kitchen without making your gear too heavy to carry.

Camp Kitchen Setup: Key Takeaways

  • Choose a setup that suits your trip: folding kitchen units for convenience, modular tables for flexibility, or bushcraft systems for minimalist cooking.
  • Use the right stove for your needs, from multi-fuel stoves for reliability to double burners for groups or wood burners for eco-friendly cooking.
  • Organise your space into clear zones: cold storage, prep, cooking, and clean-up to streamline workflow and reduce stress.
  • Protect your setup from the elements with windshields, tarp shelters, and stable surfaces to improve safety and efficiency.


The Foundation: Choosing Your Worksurface Strategy

The first thing you need to think about if you want a fully decked out camp kitchen is the type of worksurface you want to use.

The Dedicated Kitchen Unit:

All-in-one folding units are a convenient, compact choice for camp kitchens, but they have both pros and cons.

Their biggest advantage is portability. These units fold down into a small size, making them easy to carry and store. They also save space and setup time by combining multiple features like workspaces, storage, and stove windshields into one package.

However, their main drawback is stability. Because they are lightweight and foldable, they can be wobbly on uneven ground. Their packable design can also mean they are less durable, especially if made with thinner materials.

If you prioritise a small pack size and an integrated setup, an all-in-one unit is a great choice. But if you need a sturdier, more robust kitchen, you might want to look at other options.




The Modular Table Setup:

Seasoned campers often prefer separate, height-adjustable aluminium tables because of their versatility and practicality.

These tables can be customised to suit different tasks, whether it’s preparing food, eating meals, or organising camping gear. The height adjustability ensures comfort, allowing users to set them at the perfect level for various activities, even on uneven terrain.

Aluminium tables are also highly durable and lightweight, making them easy to transport while withstanding the rigours of outdoor use.

By opting for modular setups with separate tables, campers gain the flexibility to create a kitchen or dining area tailored to their specific needs.

The Tailgate/Drawer System:

This approach is particularly beneficial for car campers and van-lifers, who often require a customised and efficient setup to maximise functionality in limited spaces.

By tailoring the setup, you can organise your gear more effectively, ensuring easy access to essentials while maintaining a clutter-free environment.

The modular nature of this system allows you to adapt your layouts to suit specific journeys, whether it's a weekend getaway or an extended expedition, providing both convenience and comfort for life on the road.

The Bushcraft Alternative:
